#1416. Wesley Fofana has a shot at redemption after shocking first half in Man United win, Estevao cements his status as Chelsea's fan favourite - and why Romeo Lavia was their star man, writes KIERAN GILL

Published: 02:01 EDT, 1 November 2026 | Updated: 04:27 EDT, 1 November 2026

There is something called the Science of Scare Project.

It is a study ranking the most frightening films of all time by measuring an audience’s reaction to watching them. Via their average heart rate, highest spike, time between heartbeats, and so on.

Halloween enthusiasts consulting this year’s eerie list found the spookiest ever was a 2012 supernatural horror called Sinister. That received a 'Scare Score' of 96/100. It beat The Conjuring (88/100), Paranormal Activity (73/100), Texas Chainsaw Massacre (65/100), and so on.

If only the good folks behind this scientific study had hooked up the Chelsea fans at Stamford Bridge. It would have been intriguing to know the fluctuating activity of their hearts as they watched Wesley Fofana flirt with gifting Manchester United the opening goal.

We would have seen the spikes occur whenever he was involved. Chelsea’s major mistakes came from the 25-year-old Frenchman, who will be needed more while Maxence Lacroix is recovering from his hamstring injury.

Xabi Alonso has told us Lacroix is facing ‘a few weeks’ on the sidelines, but sources around the player have suggested he may not return until 2027. That information has also been stood up by the odd contact at the club.

Chelsea’s major mistakes came from the 25-year-old Frenchman, who will be needed more

Chelsea supporters were thrilled they got to watch Estevao (left) and now he has given Alonso a selection headache

Which is worrying for Alonso and Co. While Chelsea wound up winning 2-0 against an abysmal United team now hovering over the relegation zone, Fofana’s first half was a shocker.

First, he was burgled of the ball by the halfway line. Amad countered, and while he should have made more of the chance, he won a corner. United scored from this attacking phase, but Chelsea survived when VAR decided the scorer, Matheus Cunha, was offside.

Then, Fofana misjudged a long pass to leave Amad with only Mike Penders to beat. Chelsea got away with that one, too.

This followed what happened at Anfield on Wednesday when Chelsea exited the Carabao Cup. Fofana swapped football for volleyball at a Liverpool corner to hand them their penalty equaliser. At the shootout, he was the unfortunate soul who skied the decisive spot-kick to confirm defeat.

If Alonso had any other senior central defenders available on his bench, he might have made the change at half-time versus United. He did not, and so Fofana survived a hooking.

To Fofana’s credit, he calmed after the break. He was the one clattered to win Chelsea their penalty and earn Lisandro Martinez his second yellow. There was even a point towards the end, when Chelsea were leading 2-0 against United’s 10 men, that he was trying to pass from the back.

Bruno Fernandes stood in his way and so he simply nutmegged his opponent to find Valentin Barco. As Fofana jogged by Fernandes immediately afterwards, he rubbed it in a little, laughing at United’s captain with a little finger-wagging gesture.

That told us the confidence is there, though Chelsea fans will continue to fear he is a player too prone to a clanger, rather than a centre back who cost £75million from Leicester City in 2022.

Even before his errors here, there were pieces penned by other websites suggesting he should be seen as the worst signing of the BlueCo era. Thanks to his driving infringements, we know how much he earns, too. More than £200,000 per week, his lawyer had to tell Lavender Hill Magistrates' Court in January as his client reached a remarkable 50 points on his licence.

It is fair to say he has not lived up to the hype which accompanied his arrival with injuries having hampered his career. But here is a small chance at redemption. Lacroix may miss the remainder of 2026, and Fofana will be needed. Chelsea would love him to reduce his 'Scare Score' which, in the first half of this win over United, was rivalling Sinister’s record.

Those of us inside Stamford Bridge did not notice it. We thought Bryan Mbeumo had sent his shot straight into the crossbar. But then we saw Penders celebrating, and the slow-mo replays.

Penders got his fingertips to it. He stopped any chance it had of creeping underneath the crossbar to reduce the scoreline to 2-1. The 21-year-old Belgian earned this clean sheet.

It was good to see. He had a nightmare against Tottenham, there is no hiding from that. He punched a cross into his own goal to give Spurs their opener in that 2-0 defeat. But at Liverpool in the Carabao Cup, he responded well. Then here against United, he would not be beaten.

There has been talk of Chelsea rushing back Martinez from his jaw injury, maybe by having him wear a protective mask. But Penders performing like this may mean that is not necessary.

The loudest cheer when the line-ups were announced was reserved for Estevao, followed by Stamford Bridge chanting ‘Stevo, Stevo’. They love him, and they are right to love him.

He had to wait a long time for his first Premier League start of the season. Arguably too long.

But he seized his opportunity. Estevao scored two goals – alas, both were disallowed for offside – but he was forever involved. Chelsea supporters were thrilled they got to watch him, and now, he has given Alonso a selection headache because it was a showing which said he should start more.

Daily Mail Sport reported in our Chelsea Confidential column this week how there had been no fallout between Alonso and Estevao, despite speculation suggesting otherwise. His exclusion from the line-up was down to tactical and technical decisions.

When Estevao thought he had scored for the second time, he ran over to Alonso to give him a hug. When substituted, there was another cuddle. All is fine in that relationship, even if the 19-year-old Brazilian is itching to play more.

Lavia was actually the best performer in this victory. It was his winning of the ball that led to Rogers scoring

Jordan Henderson fell ill and so was unable to start his sixth successive match for Chelsea.

But that afforded an opportunity to Romeo Lavia. He had completed his first full 90 in a competitive game for Chelsea at Liverpool in the Carabao Cup. Then, a day before this Premier League visit of United, he was told he would need to start again.

Despite TNT Sports being blinded by Morgan Rogers’ fine opener – they gave him the player-of-the-match award – Lavia was actually the best performer in this victory. It was his winning of the ball that led to Rogers scoring. He then completed yet another full 90. You wait for one bus, then two come along at once.

#1415. Harry Kane embraces his family during special Ballon d'Or presentation at Bayern Munich - before England skipper MISSES a penalty in chaotic draw!

Published: 06:28 EDT, 1 November 2026 | Updated: 06:29 EDT, 1 November 2026

Harry Kane received a hero's welcome as he returned to action for Bayern Munich for the first time since winning the Ballon d'Or.

Kane was crowned as the best player in the world on Monday night, becoming the first English player to win the award since Michael Owen in 2001 on what was an emotional evening for the former Tottenham star.

His success came off the back of a stunning year with Bayern and England, with the forward netting a staggering 73 goals during the 2025-26 season.

Kane's goals spearheaded the German side's domestic Treble, while he also captained his country to third place at the World Cup.

And, ahead of Bayern's clash against Borussia Dortmund on Saturday night, Kane received a special presentation at the Allianz Arena.

With both sets of players and match officials lined up on the pitch, Kane was welcomed out of the tunnel while holding his new prized possession in his hands.

Harry Kane presented his Ballon d'Or trophy to Bayern Munich fans and players on Saturday

Kane received a hero's welcome from Bayern fans and his team-mates as he walked out

Kane was also greeted by his family, including his four children, ahead of the match

Bayern's players and fans gave Kane a standing ovation as Land of Hope and Glory played over the stadium's sound system.

The England skipper was serenaded by the home faithful, although some Dortmund fans could be heard to be booing him.

Waiting on the pitch were his family, including his wife Kate, four children, his parents and his brother Charlie, and he greeted them all as he came out.

Kane then took a microphone and addressed the home fans by saying: 'I’m extremely proud to be a Bayern player.

'The support you’ve shown me since I arrived is incredible. I’m extremely proud to present this to you. I hope to win many more titles with you.'

Unfortunately for Kane, his on-pitch return didn't perhaps go as planned as he missed a penalty as Bayern drew 2-2 with Dortmund.

Kane had the chance to mark his honour further after Konrad Laimer had put Bayern ahead, but he smacked his spot kick against the bar.

Serhou Guirassy then equalised for Dortmund, and although Kane assisted Dayot Upemecano's response, which put his side 2-1 up, former Wolves flop Fabio Silva equalised for the visitors in the 89th minute.

Kane addressed the crowd on the pitch where he highlighted his pride at playing for Bayern

Meanwhile, after winning the award on Monday, Kane had made sure to pay tribute to Bayern.

He said: 'Without you guys [Bayern Munich team-mates] and the rest of the team it wouldn't be possible, the way you guys push me, the way we compete, so thank you very much.

'To Vinny [Vincent Kompany]. I know he is at home or still in the hospital. Wishing you well. I hope this gave you a bit of energy. To all the staff, the we way train and the way you push us, it is a credit to yourself.

'Since I have been with you I have improved as a player, improved as a person and a leader.

'It is an honour to play for Bayern Munich, to represent you is a real privilege and I am glad to be bringing this trophy back to Bayern Munich.'

#1413. Barry Sees Blues Beat Newcastle Again

Thierno Barry's eighth goal of the season proved enough for Everton to beat Newcastle for the second time in the space of four days in a 1-0 win at St James' Park.

Having triumphed 3-1 in the Carabao Cup at Hill Dickinson Stadium, the Blues left the North East with three Premier League points this time around.

Following a dominant first-half display, Everton got their reward four minutes after the restart when keeper Lukas Hornicek spilled Tyrique George's low shot, allowing Barry to tap home from a yard out.

That proved decisive to continue the Toffees' fine recent record at St James' Park – with a third victory on the trot – as David Moyes' men moved up to seventh in the Premier League table.

Moyes made two changes from the team that beat the Magpies 3-1 in the Carabao Cup at Hill Dickinson Stadium four days earlier – Jarrad Branthwaite returning from a concussion protocol and Harrison Armstrong preferred to Hayden Hackney in central midfield.

Branthwaite partnering James Tarkowski in central defence saw Jake O'Brien switch to right-back, with Merlin Röhl getting the nod ahead of Tyler Dibling to play in front of the Irishman.

Buoyed by their success over Matthias Jaissle's team on Merseyside last week, the Blues made an excellent start and did not look back in a dominant first half that had everything but a deserved opener.

Röhl was the first to threaten when he collected a pass from Thierno Barry and drove a rising first-time angled shot narrowly over the bar, before Barry failed to get a clean connection from seven yards out after Jarrad Branthwaite headed down Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall's free-kick into the striker's path.

Everton then had two more opportunities to edge ahead in two minutes of first-half added-time. Dewsbury-Hall's glorious curling cross from the left edge of the area narrowly evaded O'Brien lurking at the back post. And the Toffees' No.8 turned provider again seconds later, getting the freedom down the left flank to cut back to Armstrong, who screwed his first-time finish wide when well placed from 12 yards out.

Thankfully, the Toffees did not have to wait long to find the back of the net after the restart. Four minutes into the second half, James Garner slid George in through the left channel and, when the winger's shot squeezed through the hands of Hornicek, Barry was left with the simple task of tucking home from a yard out.

With the wind in their sails, Everton went close to a second as Branthwaite's header was turned over the bar by Hornicek, before the Newcastle keeper did the same with Dewsbury-Hall's whipped shot from 25 yards out.

And from the resulting corner, Garner picked out O'Brien at the back post to nod down a goalbound header which Hornicek did well to turn behind.

Having done little to worry Jordan Pickford up until the hour mark, the hosts went so close to levelling when substitute Yoane Wissa nodded into Anthony Elanga at the back post who squeezed a finish under the England No.1 but, thankfully, the ball rolled along the line before being booted clear by Tarkowski.

As the inevitable Newcastle pressure grew trying to find a leveller, substitute Jacob Ramsey hit a volley from the edge of the area with 11 minutes remaining that crept inches past the left-hand post.

Then, as eight minutes of injury-time approached, Wissa looked to apply a finish from close range only to be denied by the legs of Pickford.

And that was to prove crucial as Everton saw out the closing stages, Ramsey being given his marching orders with seconds remaining after picking up two quick yellow cards for late tackles on substitute Hackney and then Armstrong.

#1412. The cheats prosper: Man City thrash 10-man Liverpool

Just when the Premier League and the world outside of east Manchester and Abu Dhabi needed Liverpool to step up, to strike back, to make a point, they faltered. Maybe it was unfair to expect them to do so, given the circumstances. But unfairness, lack of clarity and uncertainty are all prevailing moods in English football at present.

How we had rubbed our hands in anticipation of Manchester City having to play their first league fixture here at Anfield after being found guilty of industrial-scale fraud with 114 of the 115 financial charges being proven against them.

It felt apt that it was at the home of Liverpool, who, along with Arsenal, possess the strongest sense of grievance at having been denied trophies and glory by City’s cheating. As expected, there were banners everywhere at Anfield. “A generation of supporters cheated,” one read and it summed up the depth of the anger.

Their fans would surely create the kind of bear-pit atmosphere that would leave City in no doubt at the vitriol that will rain down on them from now on. At every away ground. Liverpool could set the tone. The defiance.

This is a team who can stir the blood, surf the emotion and triumph against the odds more than any other; who have a proud history of doing so. Who feel the injustice at its most acute and could feed off that.

In the end Liverpool suffered their first defeat of the season. Their first under Andoni Iraola. And comprehensively so. It could not have come at a worse time for them and for the Premier League, and for the fans of every other club who wanted to see City humbled. On the pitch.

There was another sense of injustice. Up until the dismissal of Ryan Gravenberch, Liverpool were the better side. Especially as they attacked the Kop in the second half, drawing saves from Gianluigi Donnarumma, and began to build the kind of momentum that has, over the years, appeared to suck the ball into the net.

Ryan Gravenberch is OFF 🟥 https://t.co/IVIHNzqw6k

The midfielder’s first yellow card looked harsh. His second, for a foul on substitute Jérémy Doku was less so (but still not clear-cut) and it meant Liverpool had to play the final third of the game with 10 men. Instead of weaponising that; they wilted and the fans directed their frustration at referee Chris Kavanagh, believing he was lenient towards City.

This is not a slight on Iraola, but it is hard to imagine Jürgen Klopp not riding that wave of emotion more effectively and wringing more out of the available players. Turning to the fans; imploring them; cajoling them.

Instead it was City making the statement with an extraordinary power play as they scored three times in 13 minutes, inspired by Doku, whose cameo made him man of the match. For several reasons. What if they run away with it this season before being sanctioned, probably sometime in the spring? Where will that leave the competition?

In the face of City’s power and the adversity of losing Gravenberch, Liverpool simply could not cope. They were already depleted – without Dominik Szoboszlai, Alexander Isak, Hugo Ekitike and Cody Gakpo – and needed some of their other big signings to respond.

A small point to make, in amongst everything else, but Liverpool have recruited a jewel in Jeremy Jacquet. He is going to take care of Erling Haaland at every opportunity and this is the battle that will have so much of a bearing on the contest. Haaland only needs a second to make a difference - Jacquet cannot switch off at any stage.

Fernandez’s whipped, dipping strike from outside the box is caught by Alisson. That is City’s first shot of the game.

Will Liverpool regret not capitalising on how frantic and emotional it was in the opening 20 minutes? Certainly it appears to have calmed down a bit since then with Manchester City gaining more control which will delight their head coach Enzo Maresca. There’s a little bit of frustration detectable from the home fans.

Haaland fails to adequately clear a Liverpool corner, looping the ball into the air. Mac Allister tries an ambitious overhead kick, but his attempt is off-target. In the next phase of play, Munoz’s low, long-range strike is gathered by Donnarumma.

City are growing into the game as Cherki clips a searching pass over to Semenyo. The ball is slightly overhit, forcing the winger out too wide, allowing Liverpool to regroup. The hosts fly up the other end, with the busy Munoz running at O’Reilly. The City left-back has to match him stride for stride before conceding a corner.

Gravenberch tries to find Munoz with a threaded pass through City’s backline. However, O’Reilly defends expertly, shielding the ball back to his goalkeeper.

Liverpool need more from Wirtz and Barcola. Both big-money attackers have been on the periphery. With Isak, Gakpo and Szoboszlai all absent, Iraola needs the duo on the pitch to deliver.

Liverpool have been aggressive and on the front foot, but we’re still waiting for a noteworthy chance to be created here at Anfield. City haven’t been spectacular, but they’ve done just about enough so far.

Kerkez fires in a cross and there’s a miscommunication between Guehi and Donnarumma, with the centre-back slicing a clearance instead of allowing the goalkeeper to gather the delivery. Barcola can’t capitalise on the loose ball and City get away with one there.

Let’s not kid ourselves about what we are seeing at the moment. There is a lot of noise but nothing has happened to light a fire and the onus has got to be on Liverpool’s players to step this up considerably. This occasion, more than anything, is crying out for someone to play how the supporters are feeling and it’s not there yet. It’s been tame and Manchester City are, accordingly, comfortable.

City motor forward on the counter through Cherki, whose delightful touch takes him away from Mac Allister. From inside his own half, the Frenchman dribbles to the edge of Liverpool’s penalty area. He attempts to play a one-two with Fernandez, but the pass is cut out by Jacquet.

Manchester City have not got going, as of yet. The defiant message from the club is they would not let the verdict affect them. They have defended well enough but have barely strung a passing sequence together against a Liverpool side who appear be playing off pure emotion.

Gravenberch is bossing this game in midfield. Another powerful run from deep results in a delightful nutmeg on Fernandez, who slips over. Liverpool’s energy has been really impressive. City need to ride out this early storm.

It’s getting heated at Anfield! Mac Allister and Anderson clash sparking a scuffle between both sets of players. It threatened to boil over for a second, but the drama quickly calms down and play resumes after the referee has a word with the two captains.

All fairly difficult to stomach, the Manchester City fans’ performance at kick-off. Inflatable bananas to signify nostalgia for the late 1980s, when these were all the rage after the club’s relegation to Division Two? The City of Sheikh Mansour are about as far removed from the era of Jimmy Frizzell as is possible to imagine, with their colossal wealth enabling cheating on an unprecedented scale. And as for the Poznan during You’ll Never Walk Alone? When Liam Gallagher asks Oasis fans to perform this backwards dance during next year’s tour, I suspect there will not be quite the same take-up.

There’s an early flashpoint as Koumas puts Guehi under serious pressure, causing the defender to fall to the ground and grab the ball with his hands. It’s not a foul and Liverpool are given a free kick. The hosts want Guehi booked and Araujo sprints over to the referee waving an imaginary yellow card, but gets one himself.

Amid all the build-up and backstory to this extraordinary fixture it is remarkable that 21-year-old Lewis Koumas is making his first Premier League start as Liverpool’s makeshift centre-forward. And he has started well.

A spell of Man City possession has slightly quelled the atmosphere. On paper, you would have to say the away side’s starting 11 is superior to Liverpool’s.

Liverpool make a fast start as Gravenberch effortlessly turns Fernandez and Munoz darts inside of O’Reilly. The winger’s shot is smothered by Guehi, but the early signs are encouraging for the hosts.

City get us under way at Anfield. This is one we’ve quite literally all been waiting for.

A roaring rendition of YNWA is bellowed by Anfield, which is in full voice. City players huddle together and go over to clap their fans in a show of solidarity.

In the corner of the stadium, where the Sir Kenny Dalglish Stand meets The Kop, there is a white banner with black paint proclaiming: “A generation of supporters cheated” - none of this is bothering the Manchester City fans, who are going back a generation and have a raft of inflatable bananas. (It was a craze in the 1980s, for you younger readers). Anyway, let’s get on with the game and what an opportunity this is for young Lewis Koumas, who has produced the individual performance of the season so far for Liverpool against Tottenham in the Carabao Cup. He needs to be a scampering, scurrying menace once again.

The Kop has now started a chant of “you cheating b-------” you know what you are. Doubt it will be the last time we hear that this afternoon. They are now singing “going down, going down, going down”.

No chance of hearing the names of the Manchester City players as the team is read out by the PA announcer. He is drowned out by the boos, jeers and whistles from the Liverpool fans. The atmosphere is certainly starting to build.

A re-imagining of Oasis’ Wonderwall at the front of the Kop. “And after all,” the banner reads, “you really robbed us all.”

Andoni Iraola told Sky Sports: “He came back from the international break with an overload. He felt a tight hamstring.

“He tried somehow pushing through training, but he was not feeling 100 per cent.

With just over 15 minutes until kick-off, here’s a recap of the two sides.

When asked if the mindset and mood are right for him to do his job, the City boss replied: “Yes. Absolutely. Yes.

“The mood is good, the mindset is good. Now it’s time to start the game - finally!

“It [togetherness] is very important; the mix between the players and the fans, everyone.

The Manchester City players are out for their warm-up and, dare it be said, they were greeted with apathy by the Liverpool fans. Not even the murmur of a boo when Erling Haaland and Co emerged. It surely will be very different when kick off comes.

The current City players found themselves in a peculiar situation as none of this is their fault, but they’ll be the ones who receive the brunt of abuse from rival fans as the public-facing figures of the club. They’ll need to be braced for a hostile reception at every away ground in England.

However, you can expect Anfield to turn up the heat to one of the highest levels, given how alleged City’s actions have impacted Liverpool’s trophy haul.

Jurgen Klopp’s Liverpool finished second in the 2018-19 season, accumulating a staggering 98 points, while winning 30 matches and losing just once. City incredibly pipped them to the Premier League trophy by one point. A strikingly similar scenario occurred in the 2021-22 campaign, with Liverpool placing as runners-up with 92 points. You guessed it, City had 93.

What’s done is done, and ultimately we are entering a territory of ifs, buts and maybes. However, if City’s appeal against the charges is unsuccessful and the guilty verdict is upheld, then Liverpool would have unfairly missed out on historic success and lifelong memories.

Since City last kicked a football in anger, they have been found guilty of 114 of the 115 charges levelled at them by the Premier League in a verdict that has shaken professional football to its very core. The club have appealed and the extent of their punishment now rests with an independent panel. Until then, though, the show goes on and City’s players and staff must compete knowing that their every move now comes with a caveat.

City have put up a united front and on Thursday Maresca and Haaland duly delivered the party lines, the City head coach revealing that the feeling among his charges was “fantastic”. “[My players] know what we can control is the football side – they are not worried at all about different things,” Maresca said, before adding that he trusts the club “completely”. City maintain their innocence and many of Maresca’s peers have remained tight-lipped on the case, though Manchester United head coach Michael Carrick admitted this week he has questions, while Régis Le Bris urged football’s governing bodies to be “relentless” in safeguarding competitive integrity.

Given all that has happened, it would be easy to forget that this is, for now, a top-of-the-table clash and has been one of the Premier League’s marquee rivalries since the days of Guardiola-Jürgen Klopp. Liverpool fans have never been ones to roll out the red carpet when City are in town, but the ill feeling and belligerence will only intensify at Anfield this time around owing to the events of the past weeks.

#1411. A chip off the old block? Wayne Rooney's son Kai, 16, is dazzling in Man United's academy after scoring FOUR goals in a game - insiders reveal the secrets behind his rise

By LUKE AUGUSTUS, ASSISTANT SPORTS EDITOR

Published: 07:00 EDT, 1 November 2026 | Updated: 07:06 EDT, 1 November 2026

Just over 24 years ago, a 16-year-old footballing phenomenon called Wayne Rooney made his mark with that goal for Everton against Arsenal.

Fast-forward to now and his eldest son, Kai, enhanced his burgeoning reputation while in action for Manchester United's Under 18s on Tuesday.

The 16-year-old, who turns 17 on Monday, scored four goals for the young Red Devils in a 6-0 thrashing of Burnley's U18s in the Under-18 Premier League North.

His four goals showed his repertoire of skills as the forward scored two with his preferred left foot, one with his head and the other a fine run that was finished with his right foot.

His four goals came in 44 minutes across half-time - with the latter three coming in a devastating 15-minute second-half spell (49, 63 and 66 minutes).

As Manchester United's own match report on their website details the teenager 'was the star of a clinical showing after the break from Darren Fletcher's side'.

Kai Rooney opens the scoring at Burnley for our #MUAcademy U18s 💪Watch live coverage on MUTV ⤵️ pic.twitter.com/KFr8B2hWNY

Kai Rooney scored four goals for Manchester United U18s as they thrashed Burnley U18s 6-0

One of his goals came was a penalty during Tuesday's Under-18 Premier League North fixture

Rooney's father Wayne scored that goal against Arsenal as a 16-year-old for Everton in 2002

Rooney then followed that performance with another goal in Saturday's comeback 4-1 win at Blackburn Rovers U18s, although he was later sent off for two bookable offences.

Just like his dad Wayne, Kai is fixated on football and is following in his father's footsteps in a number of ways.

As detailed by Daily Mail Sport in January, one of those is with regards to diet.

Akin to his famous father - who is United's all-time record goalscorer - in his Old Trafford heyday, Rooney Jr eats plenty of carbohydrates two days before a game. This then changes to salmon and rice followed by rice pudding the night before matches.

His dietary discipline has been recognised by those within the United academy - who are impressed by Rooney's focus.

The teenager does allow himself some respite at times though with the family's go-to is Chinese takeaway 'WowYauChow' in Altrincham. As revealed in Manchester United Confidential, crispy chilli beef is a particular favourite of the rising footballer.

Cooking has also become a passion for Rooney off-the-pitch and he is also fluent in Spanish - a trait that will only stand him in good stead in the multicultural world of football.

Rooney has had to deal with accusations of nepotism, due to the legendary figure of who his dad is, but he has always wanted to form his own path - even from a younger age than he is now.

'Kai told Wayne to stop coming to football games when he played grassroots tournaments and stuff, because he used to get swarmed, and he couldn't even watch the game,' his mum Coleen explained during her time in the I'm A Celebrity… Get Me Out Of Here! jungle almost two years ago.

Kai is pictured with parents Coleen and Wayne signing his Man United contract when younger

Rooney is fixated with football like his father but wants to forge his own career within the sport

'How do you say to all of these kids, "Go away, I'm watching my son?" Adults, it's different, you could speak to them, so he [Kai] just said, "Oh, dad, there's no point you coming because you don't even watch me play anyway". Which is sad, but it can't be helped.'

Speaking in August 2024, Rooney underlined that he is intent on doing things his own way.

'I'm trying to make a name for myself, not try and be my dad because I'm my own person,' Kai said back in August 2024.

'I want to see how my career goes, obviously try to do the best I can and try to reach the biggest stages.

'I'm just focusing on me and to try to not let any pressure get to me and just keep working on me day by day, month by month.'

Rooney Jr has copied his father's diet when he was a professional - which includes salmon

His parents, meanwhile, have been keen to stress that they are keeping the pressure off their young son.

'He has great coaches at Manchester United, so I take a stand-off approach,' Wayne told the BBC last year.

'I speak to him, but for me it’s all about his mentality and his mindset, to make sure he keeps enjoying it – that’s the main thing for me.'

Meanwhile Coleen told The Times earlier this year: 'He’s lived it (being Wayne's son) from a young age. When we used to go to matches when he was younger, he’d get a lot of people coming up saying, "Oh, are you Wayne Rooney’s son?"

'But he’s strong-minded, always has been. I’ve got no worries in the way he deals with it.'

A Puma ambassador since he was 12, Kai used to play football in laceless boots after previously breaking both of his feet.

The youngster was signed up by Puma at the age of 12 - and has pursued a football career

Against Burnley his boots had laces as he tied his opponents in knots, something he will look to continue to do as he makes his own way in the game.

And while replicating his father seems fanciful, the iconic 'remember the name' piece of commentary could be updated for Kai in the future.

#1410. Tumour assembloids recapitulate tumour–CAF–T cell crosstalk in renal cancer

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Dynamic interactions between tumours and their microenvironment are crucial for cancer progression and therapeutic outcomes1,2. However, our understanding of these relationships remains limited by the constrained capacity of current human model systems to manipulate diverse cellular components and to interrogate complex tumour–stroma crosstalk. Here we generated combinatorial, mix-and-match tumour assembloids by conditionally reconstituting multiple components of human renal cell carcinoma, including cancer cells, cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) and tumour-infiltrating immune cells. Using genetically engineered renal cell carcinoma assembloids with humanized mouse models, we uncovered mechanisms by which CAFs coordinate interactions between tumour cells and CD8+ T cells to maintain non-cell-autonomous CD8+ T cell stemness and drive responsiveness to anti-PD-1 therapy. These interactions operate through a tumour–CAF–T cell signalling axis in which tumour-derived WNT induces CAF expression of activin A, which enhances CD8+ T cell stemness and sensitivity to PD-1 blockade. In non-responders, we also identified a subset of WNT-unresponsive CAFs that do not produce activin A, which leads to impaired CD8+ T cell stemness and resistance to therapy. Together, these findings establish a tumour–CAF–T cell axis as a key determinant of heterogeneous responses to immune checkpoint inhibitors. Moreover, tumour assembloids provide a versatile platform for mechanistic dissection of the tumour microenvironment and evaluation of personalized immunotherapy strategies.

Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) have substantially improved the prognosis and survival of patients with various solid cancers3, including melanoma4,5,6, non-small cell lung cancer7,8 and bladder cancer9,10,11. However, the overall response rate remains around 30%, which leaves many patients without clinical benefit12. The mechanisms that underlie this heterogeneous response remain poorly understood, which limits the ability to predict and improve ICI efficacy in individual patients.

Recent advances in immunotherapy suggest that the tumour stroma has a pivotal role in shaping responses to ICIs, functioning both as a facilitator and a barrier to effective antitumour immunity1,2. Diverse stromal components engage in continuous reciprocal communication with tumour cells to influence tumour progression and therapeutic responses. A major challenge in defining how the tumour stroma shapes ICI responses is the lack of experimental systems that accurately recapitulate these dynamic, multicellular interactions with high human relevance. Recent advances, including patient-derived xenografts13,14,15, humanized mouse models16,17,18 and ex vivo culture of human tumour tissues using air–liquid interface (ALI) techniques19,20, have improved the representation of human tumour architecture and complexity. However, precise manipulation and tracking of individual cell types and their interactions in these systems are challenging, which limits detailed mechanistic analyses of tumour–stroma–immune crosstalk.

In this study, we developed patient-derived, combinatorial, mix-and-match tumour assembloids from individuals with renal cell carcinoma (RCC). These assembloids recapitulate dynamic interactions among tumour cells, CAFs and CD8+ T cells and reflect patient-specific responses to immunotherapy. By integrating genetically manipulated assembloids with humanized mouse models, we identified a signalling axis that governs tumour–CAF–CD8+ T cell crosstalk and the mechanisms that underlie differential responses to ICIs. Our findings provide mechanistic insights into heterogeneous ICI responses and establish a platform for developing strategies to enhance immunotherapeutic efficacy across diverse malignancies.

To investigate the cellular and molecular basis of heterogeneous ICI responses in RCC, we established patient-specific tumour assembloids21 that faithfully recapitulate therapeutic responses by reconstituting autologous tumour cells, CAFs and tumour-infiltrating immune (TII) cells from RCC tissue samples (Extended Data Fig. 1a). Pretreatment tumour tissue samples from six patients before ICI therapy were used to generate tumour organoids (Extended Data Fig. 1b and Supplementary Data 1). Organoids from all patients were successfully propagated; however, with prolonged culture, cells negative for carbonic anhydrase IX (CA9−) progressively dominated, an effect that is probably due to in vitro growth advantages (Extended Data Fig. 1c). To overcome this technical difficulty, CA9+ and CA9− cells were isolated and separately maintained as distinct organoid populations (Extended Data Fig. 1d). The resulting CA9+ organoids contained canonical clear-cell RCC-associated somatic alterations, including VHL mutations and other recurrent driver events, whereas no detectable VHL mutations were identified in the CA9− organoids (Extended Data Fig. 1e–h and Supplementary Data 2). Both populations maintained clear-cell histology with distinct morphological and immunohistological features (Extended Data Fig. 1d).

Next, we generated patient-specific RCC assembloids by reconstituting CA9+ and CA9− populations with patient-matched CAFs and TII cells at ratios reflecting the cellular composition of the corresponding primary tumours. These assembloids were cultured for 7 days (Extended Data Fig. 1a). Patient-derived CAFs and TII cells were isolated and expanded separately (Extended Data Figs. 2 and 3), a process that largely preserved their major cellular compositions relative to the corresponding parental tumours. CAFs exhibited a phenotype similar to myofibroblastic CAFs (myCAFs) and comparable proportions of cells expressing key markers (Extended Data Fig. 2a–e). Conversely, TII cells preserved the overall composition of major immune cell populations despite modest shifts in specific subpopulations in some patients (Extended Data Fig. 3a–c).

To characterize assembloid formation over time, we performed time-course analyses at days 0, 3, 5 and 7. Cultures were initiated from dissociated single cells at day 0, and no organized tissue architecture was evident up to day 3 (Fig. 1a,b). Multicellular organization emerged by day 5, and by day 7, the assembloids recapitulated key structural and histological features of the matched parental tumours. In detail, tumour cells were associated with CAFs and were infiltrated by immune cells while maintaining >90% cell viability throughout the culture period (Fig. 1a,b and Extended Data Fig. 4a–c). The assembloids also retained the genetic alterations of the parental tumours (Fig. 1c,d, Extended Data Fig. 4d–i and Supplementary Data 3).

We also performed single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) of RCC assembloids and directly compared them with the corresponding parental tumour datasets at single-cell resolution. Through integrated analysis, we identified the major tumour microenvironment (TME) compartments in both RCC assembloids and parental tumours, including tumour cells, CAFs and diverse immune populations (Fig. 1e,f). Although cell-type proportions varied across patients, assembloids and matched parental tumours showed overall concordance in tumour, stromal and immune cell composition (Fig. 1g,h). Moreover, cell-type-specific transcriptomic comparisons revealed high similarity between assembloids and their matched parental tumours across multiple cell types (Fig. 1i and Extended Data Fig. 4j–o).

Notably, all patient-specific RCC assembloids faithfully recapitulated the therapeutic responses of their corresponding patients to ICIs. Treatment of RCC assembloids with anti-PD-1 antibodies for 7 days induced substantial tumour reduction and increased apoptosis in four patient-derived assembloids (P-1, P-4, P-5 and P-6). This result was confirmed through cleaved caspase-3 staining in tumour cells, and by the minimal apoptosis observed in CAFs and immune cells (Fig. 1j–l). By contrast, assembloids from two patients (P-2 and P-3) did not exhibit significant tumour cell death (Fig. 1j–l). The responses of individual assembloids to anti-PD-1 mirrored the clinical outcomes of the corresponding patients from which the assembloids were generated (Fig. 1m). Together, these findings establish that patient-specific RCC assembloids generated from autologous tumour cells, CAFs and immune cells are a robust experimental platform that recapitulates the histopathology and ICI responsiveness of parental tumours in the cohort analysed.

We next sought to investigate the mechanisms that underlie differential ICI responses in RCC. Assembloids established from responders contained a significantly higher proportion of stem-like CD8+ T cells (TIM3−TCF1+) relative to exhausted and differentiated cells (TIM3+TCF1−)22,23,24,25,26 than assembloids developed from non-responders (Fig. 2a). This result was consistent with the patterns observed in matched parental tumour tissue samples (Fig. 2b). Notably, depletion of stem-like CD8+ T cells markedly impaired anti-PD-1 responsiveness and tumour cell killing (Extended Data Fig. 5a), which indicated that these cells are required for effective anti-PD-1 responses23,24,27,28,29,30,31,32.

To determine whether T cell stemness is intrinsically programmed or maintained via non-T cell-autonomous mechanisms, we generated mix-and-match assembloids by reconstituting responder-derived and non-responder-derived TII cells with tumour cells and CAFs from the opposite group (Extended Data Fig. 5b). CD8+ T cells retained stemness only when combined with responder-derived tumour cells and CAFs, whereas non-responder-derived environments did not preserve T cell stemness (Fig. 2c). This result suggests that T cell stemness is maintained in a non-T cell-autonomous manner. To define the cellular components responsible for this effect, we generated combinatorial assembloids that lacked TII cells, tumour cells or CAFs (Extended Data Fig. 5c). Assembloids reconstituted with all three components from responder tumours preserved stem-like CD8+ T cells, whereas removal of either tumour cells or CAFs markedly reduced T cell stemness (Fig. 2d). Only assembloids containing all three components from responder tumours showed substantial tumour cell reduction following anti-PD-1 treatment (Fig. 2e). This finding demonstrates that both tumour cells and CAFs are required for maintaining T cell stemness and therapeutic responsiveness. Furthermore, lineage-tracing experiments showed that stem-like CD8+ T cells were primarily maintained through the expansion of pre-existing stem-like cells rather than de novo conversion (Extended Data Fig. 5d–f).

We next designed four experimental conditions using combinatorial assembloids to investigate how tumour cells and CAFs cooperate to maintain T cell stemness in responders (Fig. 2f–i and Extended Data Fig. 5g). Assembloids lacking both tumour cells and CAFs did not expand stem-like T cells, even when cultured with conditioned media (CM) from tumour cells (tumour-CM) or CAFs (CAF-CM) (Fig. 2f). This finding indicated that direct communication between tumour cells and CAFs is required. Notably, CAF-CM alone did not restore T cell stemness in CAF-deficient assembloids, whereas tumour-CM restored stem-like T cell frequencies in tumour-deficient assembloids to levels comparable to controls (Fig. 2g,h). These results suggest that tumour-derived soluble factors activate CAFs to produce stemness-supportive factors. Moreover, tumour-activated CAFs maintained T cell stemness through soluble factors. That is, when responder-derived CAFs were cultured in tumour-CM, stem-like T cells were preserved even without direct contact (Fig. 2i). Together, these findings provide support for a tumour–CAF–CD8+ T cell signalling axis in which tumour cells induce CAFs to secrete stemness-supportive factors. This process preserves stem-like CD8+ T cells in a non-T cell-autonomous manner to induce effective anti-PD-1 responses.

Comparative transcriptome analysis of CAFs from assembloids generated from responders and reconstituted with or without patient-matched tumour cells (Extended Data Fig. 5h,i) revealed 245 highly upregulated genes. Among these, we focused on seven genes that encode secreted proteins with potential roles in cell–cell communication (Extended Data Fig. 5i and Supplementary Data 5). Gene expression analyses of patient-derived CAFs showed that FGF2 and INHBA (which encodes activin-βA chain (also known as inhibin-βA chain)) were highly and consistently upregulated across all samples (Fig. 3a).

We generated genetically manipulated RCC assembloids by reconstituting patient-matched tumour cells and TII cells with responder-derived CAFs in which either FGF2 or INHBA was individually knocked down (Fig. 3b). INHBA knockdown (KD) abolished the maintenance of stem-like CD8+ T cells, whereas FGF2 KD had no significant effect (Fig. 3c). Moreover, assembloids containing CAFs with INHBA KD did not exhibit tumour reduction following anti-PD-1 treatment (Fig. 3d and Extended Data Fig. 5j). These findings indicate that activin A is a tumour-induced, CAF-derived effector that sustains CD8+ T cell stemness and is required for effective anti-PD-1 responses in RCC (Extended Data Fig. 5k–n).

We next investigated the tumour-cell-derived ligands responsible for INHBA induction (Extended Data Fig. 5o). RNA-seq of responder-derived tumour cells revealed 9,141 expressed genes (Extended Data Fig. 5p and Supplementary Data 6), of which 205 candidate genes were identified by regulatory potential scoring33 (Extended Data Fig. 5p and Supplementary Data 6). Intercellular communication analysis34 further revealed 14 signalling pathways and 37 predicted ligands with tumour-to-CAF signalling potential (Fig. 3e,f and Extended Data Fig. 5q). Analyses of freshly isolated tumour cells from responders identified three consistently expressed candidate factors: SEMA3B, TNF and WNT2B (Fig. 3g).

We therefore generated RCC assembloids containing responder-derived tumour cells with individual KD of SEMA3B, TNF or WNT2B, together with patient-matched CAFs and TII cells (Fig. 3h). WNT2B KD substantially reduced INHBA expression in CAFs and stem-like T cell populations across responders, whereas SEMA3B or TNF KD had minimal or no effect (Fig. 3i,j). Notably, assembloids containing WNT2B KD tumour cells did not respond to anti-PD-1 therapy. Specifically, they did not show significant tumour reduction compared with isotype controls (Fig. 3k and Extended Data Fig. 5r). These results demonstrate that tumour-derived WNT2B induces activin A expression in CAFs, which in turn sustains stem-like CD8+ T cells and promotes therapeutic efficacy of anti-PD-1 in RCC.

To investigate why non-responders do not have this signalling axis, we performed comparative transcriptomic profiling of tumour cells and CAFs from responders and non-responders (Extended Data Fig. 5s and Supplementary Data 7 and 8). The tumour cells displayed highly comparable transcriptomic landscapes between the two groups (Fig. 4a), with similar WNT2B expression (Fig. 4b). CAFs likewise showed largely similar transcriptomic profiles and predominantly myCAF features35,36 (Fig. 4c and Extended Data Fig. 5t); however, CAFs from non-responders exhibited markedly reduced INHBA expression (Fig. 4d). Notably, INHBA expression in CAFs from non-responders was not restored even when reconstituted with tumour cells from responders (Extended Data Fig. 5u,v). This result suggests that there is an intrinsic defect in the response of these CAFs to tumoural WNT signals. Indeed, mix-and-match assembloids containing responder-derived tumour cells and TII cells with non-responder CAFs showed poor responses to anti-PD-1 treatments (Extended Data Fig. 5w). Thus, resistance in non-responders is associated with a CAF-intrinsic defect in responding to tumour-derived WNT2B rather than an intrinsic difference in tumour cells. In support of this idea, CAFs from non-responders showed reduced canonical WNT–β-catenin target gene expression and deficient WNT pathway activation (Fig. 4e,f). Together, these findings demonstrate that impaired WNT responsiveness in CAFs is a substantial barrier to anti-PD-1 efficacy in RCC.

To pinpoint the molecular basis of WNT unresponsiveness in CAFs from non-responders, we analysed WNT-pathway-associated genes and identified 61 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) between responders and non-responders (Fig. 4g and Supplementary Data 8). Comparisons of 16 key WNT pathway regulators revealed 3 candidate genes of particular interest: FZD1, FZD6 and LRP6 (Supplementary Data 8). Analyses of freshly isolated CAFs showed that LRP6 expression was substantially reduced in non-responders (Fig. 4h).

We genetically engineered CAFs from non-responders to express LRP6 and reconstituted them with patient-matched tumour cells and TII cells (Fig. 4i and Extended Data Fig. 5x). LRP6 restoration reinstated INHBA and WNT target gene expression, restored the stem-like CD8+ T cell population and rescued anti-PD-1 responsiveness (Fig. 4i–k). Together, these findings indicate that there is a distinct subset of LRP6-deficient, WNT-unresponsive CAFs enriched in non-responders. Owing to a lack of activin A expression, these CAFs fail to sustain CD8+ T cell stemness and contribute to resistance to anti-PD-1 therapy (Extended Data Fig. 5y,z).

We next investigated the tumour–CAF–CD8+ T cell crosstalk identified in RCC assembloids using two additional experimental platforms: patient-specific in vivo humanized mice37,38,39 and ex vivo ALI organoids19,20 (Fig. 4l). In the humanized mouse model, RCC assembloids containing patient-derived tumour cells together with autologous CAFs were orthotopically transplanted under the kidney capsule of NOD.Cg-PrkdcscidIl2rgtm1Wjl/SzJ (NSG) mice (Extended Data Fig. 6a). Patient-matched peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) were then intravenously infused to reconstitute a human immune cell population, a process that achieved around 10% CD8+ T cells among human CD45+ cells (Extended Data Fig. 6b,c).

Anti-PD-1 extensively reduced tumour burden in mice transplanted with control tumours. By contrast, mice transplanted with responder tumours in which WNT2B was knocked down exhibited substantially blunted anti-PD-1 responses, which was accompanied by a reduction in the stem-like CD8+ T cell population without affecting overall immune cell infiltration, including CD8+ T cells (Fig. 4m and Extended Data Fig. 6d–i). For mice transplanted with tumours from a non-responder, tumours containing INHBA-expressing CAFs showed robust anti-PD-1 responses with significantly reduced tumour weight compared with IgG controls, along with increased stem-like CD8+ T cell populations. By contrast, mice transplanted with tumours with control CAFs remained resistant to treatment, despite comparable immune cell infiltration levels (Fig. 4m and Extended Data Fig. 6j–n).

We further examined the tumour–CAF–CD8+ T cell crosstalk using previously established ALI organoids19,20. WNT pathway inhibition in ALI organoids developed from a responder abolished the anti-PD-1-mediated reduction in tumour cells observed in control organoids (Fig. 4n and Extended Data Fig. 6o–r). Conversely, supplementation with recombinant activin A restored anti-PD-1 sensitivity and resulted in a substantial decrease in tumour burden relative to IgG-treated controls in ALI organoids generated from a non-responder (Fig. 4n and Extended Data Fig. 6o,s–u).

Together, these patient-specific humanized mouse and ALI organoid models, combined with genetic and pharmacological manipulations, demonstrate the pivotal role of the WNT–activin A–T cell stemness axis across multiple patient-relevant platforms. The data also highlight the robustness and translational significance of tumour–CAF–CD8+ T cell crosstalk in shaping anti-PD-1 responses.

We analysed scRNA-seq datasets from the pretreatment RCC tissue samples used to generate the RCC assembloids (Fig. 5a, Extended Data Fig. 7 and Supplementary Data 4). We identified 24 clusters representing the major TME compartments, including epithelial tumour cells, CAFs, endothelial cells, macrophages, CD8+ T cells and other immune cell subpopulations (Fig. 5b and Extended Data Fig. 7a–c). Overall, the proportions of these major cell types were similar between responders and non-responders (Extended Data Fig. 7d).
