#1393. HEARTS 1-2 HIBS - PLAYER RATINGS: Which midfielder ran the show at Hampden? Who missed chances to force extra time?

Published: 12:59 EDT, 1 November 2026 | Updated: 13:09 EDT, 1 November 2026

Hibs ripped up the form book to  claim a thrilling victory over city rivals Hearts in  the Premier Sports Cup semi-final at Hampden.

Despite falling behind to an early header by Claudio Braga, the Premiership's bottom-placed side came roaring back with goals from Martin Boyle and Jamie McGrath.

Hearts piled on the second-half pressure, but Marink Reedijk's side held firm to secure a place in the final against Rangers next month.

After a dramatic derby that will be remembered for years to come, Paul Forsyth assesses the individual performances.

Blameless for the two goals, he did his best to repel Hibs with a string of saves. Denied Passlack, Boyle and, in the closing stages, Klidge.

Had his hands full when Boyle threatened to run riot, but stuck to his task. Supported the attack well when Hearts grew desperate.

Caught flat-footed and square when Boyle stole in behind him to net Hibs’ equaliser. Otherwise solid enough when the pressure was on.

Man of the match Joe Newell celebrates with Jamie McGrath after their  team go 2-1 ahead

Bust a gut to cover and thwart Hibs’ explosive breaks. Produced a number of excellent blocks, most notably one that denied Elding.

Stood up well when Hearts needed him. His outstanding sliding block to thwart Passlack late in the game was as good as a goal.

Left the field after just 14 minutes with a horrible head knock, picked up when he nodded Calvin Miller’s cross narrowly wide.

Outnumbered in the first half, he looked lost in midfield. Far more influential when Hearts later got a grip of that department.

Stretched his opponents as Hearts grew into the game, but never really came up with a telling pass or effort on goal.

Caused all sorts of problems with his early crosses, only to become the latest addition to Hearts’ ridiculous injury list. Hobbled off before the interval.

Quiet in the first half, save for a perfect cross that Braga should have converted. Direct, dangerous and back to his best after the interval.

Claudio Braga misses a late chance to force extra time in the Premier Sports Cup semi-final

Opened the scoring from close range, but could and should have done more. Missed two free headers and had a powerful shot saved.

SUBSTITUTES: Wilson (Dhanda 83) (Magnusson 14), Guendouz (Miller 37), Benjaminsen (Kerjota 81)

Unused: Fulton, Williams, Kabore, Findlay, Pollock.

Nowhere to be seen when Braga nodded Hearts ahead from inside the six-yard box, but two saves, denying Braga and Guendouz, were massive.

Aggressive, positive and willing to give Hibs width in attack. Should have scored with an early chance after he was set up by Newell.

Fell asleep for Braga’s early opener, but settled into the game and was a pillar of Hibs’ defence when the pressure mounted.

Switched off to allow Braga a free header that slipped wide. His powerful header at the other end was directed straight at the goalkeeper.

Took full advantage of the early freedom he was given wide on the left. Responded well to later pressure, especially with a brilliant tackle on Kerjota.

Properly exploited Hearts’ depleted midfield with a strong, authoritative first-half display. Less influential after Hearts tweaked their set-up.

His positive, probing work was crucial to Hibs’ first-half dominance. Clipped the top of the crossbar with one shot. Set up his team’s second goal with another.

Strong and tactically aware. By stepping inside, he increased the midfield numbers, allowing McGrath to push forward and Passlack to overlap.

Playing off the front, he supported Elding at every opportunity. Reacted well to snap up the rebound for Hibs’ second.

Martin Boyle equalises for Hibs with a low shot that goes in off the goalkeeper and post

Inspirational talisman in attack. Transformed the game with a timely equaliser, which he stroked in off the goalkeeper and post. Almost scored a second.

Occupied Hearts’ backline without offering a sustained goal threat. His lovely hook over a square defence set up Boyle for the equaliser.

SUBSTITUTES: Klidge (Elding 74), Wright (Newell 74), Cadden (Boyle 85), Hanley (McGrath 85).

Unused: Smith, Iredale, Suto, Matondo, Abdulai.

Failed to cope with the early loss of Tomas Magnusson, which turned the game.

Gave his side numerical superiority in midfield, as well as the resources later  to protect their lead.

#1392. Arsenal’s big guns blow Lille away after the second string flop

There will be some games where Mikel Arteta has no choice but to tweak the XI, rest some tired legs and give his second-choice attackers the chance – although given the option he may wish to pick the same team every week.

The three big guns of his attack were primed and ready to come on in the next break in play when Arsenal at last broke through in this, their second Champions League league phase game of the season against some stubborn opposition from Ligue 1. Lille had sat deep against an Arsenal attack without Bukayo Saka, Martin Odegaard and Kai Havertz, and the French club were past the hour when it all finally broke.

That was a superb finish from Jurrien Timber who, with two touches, demonstrated that in the modern era even defenders are capable of the kind of moments of skill and composure that we once assumed were only within the capacity of the best attackers. He gave Arsenal the lead just as Mikel Arteta had decided he had seen enough from some of his second-choice attackers – Viktor Gyokeres, Noni Madueke and Mikel Merino. They had created some chances and at times looked promising, but as soon as the big three were on the difference was obvious.

“We had moments in the game in the first half … [when] we arrived in very dangerous positions,” Arteta said. “With a lot of advantage, our technical quality wasn’t good enough to deliver moments of real threat and especially to be able to sustain the attack, so we allowed certain transitions.” He said that he made some changes at half-time, as managers are wont to do, and that things improved but the real change was clear when he made the substitutions.

“It was a joy to watch,” Arteta said. “The three goals were unbelievable, the connections, the timings, the quality they delivered to score. Three different players and a lot of players participating in those goals, so overall very, very happy.” He had played Myles Lewis-Skelly at left-back again to give Riccardo Calafiori a rest. Saka had been ill during the week and not in a position to start.

In the opposing technical area was Davide Ancelotti, the 37-year-old son of Carlo, with his father’s trademark slow amble to the edge of the technical area. Young Ancelotti had drilled his team well, but once they were exposed to the high-pace recovery and sharp passing geometry of the Arsenal substitutes there was to be no coming back. Saka made the second for Eberechi Eze who had started the game on the left and the Arsenal No 7 scored the third himself. The home fans sang again about being champions of England and they certainly looked the part.

The Arsenal players wore black armbands to mark the passing, aged 94, of Ken Friar, the club’s life vice-president. Even Arteta, no sentimentalist, insisted on beginning his press conference with a tribute.

For Arteta’s players, there will be a much bigger test than this one in Munich next week against Bayern. Arsenal have already won in Naples but a victory at Bayern would be significant beyond that. Arsenal have won all but one of their 10 games this season – that big defeat at the Amex Stadium, almost one month ago. No goals for Gyokeres this season and a general acceptance that the time for persevering with him has passed. It could be ever-dwindling returns for him in terms of game-time as the season goes. Arteta starts his press conference with a tribute to Ken Friar: "There are people in football clubs that create an identity, create values and have a vision to create a future. The legacy that Ken is going to leave, to all of us and to our club, is going to be forever."

Since returning to the competition under Arteta in 2023, they have won all 12 home group-stage or league-phase matches, conceding just three goals.

Including knock-out games, Arsenal have conceded just eight goals in 20 home matches, keeping 15 clean sheets.

Lille’s manager is Davide Ancelotti, the son of Carlo, and you would assume he has picked up a few tips and tricks from his dad about success in this competition. Carlo, after all, has won the European Cup on five separate occasions. This is Davide’s second job as a manager, following a spell at Brazilian side Botafogo.

Some of Bukayo Saka’s finishing has been wayward so far this season, but the volume of chances coming his way bodes well. At this fledgling stage of the season, only Erling Haaland is averaging more non-penalty expected goals per 90 minutes in the Premier League.

As Sam Dean explores in this piece, Arteta seems to be encouraging Saka to take up more central positions inside the box.

Sam writes: “Is Saka becoming a proper penalty-box predator? It is too early to say for certain but it is absolutely clear that he is taking up different positions, closer to the opponents’ goal, this season. Not only when the ball is on the left flank, but also when Arsenal are attacking through midfield.”

Saka starts among the substitutes this evening, but will play his part towards the end of the game.

Lille are considering legal ⁠action after defender Tiago Santos suffered a serious knee injury following an “uncontrolled and dangerous” tackle in Saturday’s match ‌against Le Havre.

Santos, 24, suffered a ruptured anterior cruciate ligament and meniscal tear in his right knee and was carried off the pitch on a stretcher after being tackled by Le Havre midfielder Amir Richardson during the first half of Lille’s 1-0 victory.

The referee gave a foul for the tackle but did not issue Richardson with a caution.

Lille said the ‌tackle merited ‌a red card ⁠and that they had asked the league’s governing body (LFP) to refer the matter to its disciplinary committee. The club are also seeking an explanation of ⁠the video review process undertaken by match officials.

“LOSC is exploring all possible legal avenues and reserves the right to take any legal action necessary to obtain compensation for its losses,” the ​club said. “It will support Tiago in ‌any steps he decides to take to defend his rights.”

The artist Northbanksy has plumped for another Oasis-inspired dig at Manchester City, this time with Rui Pinto taking centre stage, the man whose leaked emails kicked off the Premier League investigation into City’s financial affairs.

A consequence of Piero Hincapie’s injury on Saturday (he hurt his ankle in a cool-down session after the game, embarrassingly) is that Myles Lewis-Skelly is seemingly now the backup left-back. Arsenal can’t trust Riccardo Calafiori’s body to play two games in a week and are clearly saving him for Premier League action on the weekend. Lewis-Skelly has been so impressive in midfield that it must be frustrating to change position now.

Bakwa is on loan from Nottingham Forest, while those at the Emirates with long memories will remember that Nabil Bentaleb played for Spurs. Only the knowledgeable shall boo.

Lille XI: Özer; Perraud, Alexsandro, Ngoy, Goffi; Bentaleb, André; Mukau, Haraldsson, Bakwa; Ueda

Subs: Gill, Srdanovic, Giroud, Sahraoui, Kjaergaard, Onal, Kouassi, Verdonk, Cossier, Perrin, Diaoune, Sajous

Bukayo Saka, Kai Havertz and Martin Odegaard drop to the bench, so some rotation from Arteta with a weekend trip to Nottingham Forest in mind, a venue where Arsenal have drawn 0-0 on their last two visits.

Arsenal XI: Raya; Timber, Konsa, Gabriel, Lewis-Skelly; Bruno, Rice; Madueke, Merino, Eze; Gyokeres

Subs: Meslier, Kepa, White, Mosquera, Salmon, O’Neill, Hashi, Saka, Odegaard, Havertz, Dowman

Will Olivier Giroud receive a warm welcome back to the Emirates Stadium? The Frenchman spent six years as an Arsenal player but burned a few bridges when he left the club for Chelsea, and then celebrated wildly when Chelsea beat Arsenal in the Europa League final of 2019. Now 40, Giroud has shown remarkable longevity and is unquestionably one of the best strikers of his generation. But can he hurt this formidable Arsenal defence? It’s a tough ask.

Olivier Giroud back at the Emirates ❤️ https://t.co/TPBgcNDsVW

Arsenal pay tribute to one of the club’s greatest custodians this evening following the news of Ken Friar’s death aged 92. Friar worked in various roles at the club across more than 70 years, and a bridge from Drayton Park to Emirates Stadium is named in his honour.

A statue at the end of the bridge is a nod to the chance meeting the 11-year-old Friar had with Arsenal manager George Allison in 1945, while playing football outside Highbury with his friends.

As Sam Dean wrote earlier today, finishing the story: “Allison was so impressed by Friar’s enthusiasm that he told him to report to his office at 9am the next day. Friar did as he was instructed and his reward was a job offer: he became a messenger at the stadium on match days. He was paid 12 and a half pence per week.”

Friar was a long-serving member of the Arsenal board, before stepping back in 2020 and becoming life president.

Arsenal’s players will wear black armbands.

A post shared by Sam Dean (@samjdean_tel)

After signing his new Arsenal contract last week, Mikel Arteta described May’s Champions League final defeat as “poison in his veins,” and last season’s campaign demonstrated the benefits of finishing top of the league phase.

Arsenal enjoyed home second legs all the way through to the final after winning eight from eight, and in a 50:50 draw they fell into a considerably kinder bracket.

Sometimes it can be hard to gauge the importance of these league-phase matches, but Arteta will strive for another perfect record to give Arsenal the best possible chance of going deep in the competition again.

Fixtures against Bayern Munich and Real Madrid are likely to determine whether Arsenal finish in the top two, but there is still a job to be done against Lille this evening.

Arsenal have played against 10 different French opponents in European competition but have never faced Lille, who are managed by Davide Ancelotti, son of five-time Champions League winner Carlo.

Lille sell their best players every summer. After finishing third in Ligue 1 last season they lost Ayyoub Bouaddi and Matias Fernandez-Pardo to Manchester City and Newcastle United for a combined £130m. They have claimed 10 points from their first five league games of the season and led Paris St-Germain 2-0 before being pegged back in stoppage time.

Leading the line for Lille is 40-year-old Olivier Giroud, who scored 105 Arsenal goals in 235 appearances between 2012 and 2018. After leaving the Emirates, Giroud went on to score against Arsenal for Chelsea in the 2019 Europa League final, but he can still expect a warm reception.

Arsenal’s home record in the Champions League has been formidable since they returned to the competition under Arteta in 2023. They have won all 11 home group-stage or league-phase matches, conceding just three goals (two of those were shipped against Kairat Almaty in a dead rubber).

Arteta’s scope for rotation has been reduced by injuries to Piero Hincapie and Martin Zubimendi, but tonight’s game should offer Eberechi Eze and Viktor Gyokeres a chance to impress, while Jurrien Timber needs minutes to build his fitness.

Former Manchester United manager Erik ten Hag has admitted that relegation from the Premier League is a genuine possibility for his old club amid their alarming start to the season.

The Red Devils find themselves 17th in the table with just seven points from their opening nine matches, sitting outside the relegation zone on goal difference following Saturday’s 2-0 defeat to Chelsea.

Speaking in an interview with ESPN Netherlands (quotes shared by Fabrizio Romano), Ten Hag was asked whether Manchester United could realistically find themselves fighting to avoid relegation from the Premier League.

The former United boss acknowledged that the possibility could not be dismissed, pointing towards the competitive nature of English football.

“In the Premier League it’s certainly possible, because all the teams are simply strong. They’re all strong squads, all good managers.

“And if you end up on the wrong side once and you really get into that vicious circle… yes, then it can become very, very difficult.”

? Erik ten Hag when asked by @ESPNnl if Man United relegation is a potential scenario: “In the Premier League it's certainly possible, because all the teams are simply strong. They're all strong squads, all good managers”.

“And if you end up on the wrong side once and you… pic.twitter.com/BdixMfFKJf

— Fabrizio Romano (@FabrizioRomano) November 2, 2026

Ten Hag’s chilling assessment comes as current manager Michael Carrick faces overwhelming pressure at Old Trafford.

Saturday’s 2-0 defeat to Chelsea at Stamford Bridge extended United’s winless run across all competitions to nine matches—their longest slump since 1984.

The result leaves the Red Devils sitting in 17th place with just seven points from nine games, sitting outside the relegation zone on goal difference alone.

With critical fixtures against AS Roma and Aston Villa looming, Carrick desperately needs to find answers before the situation becomes irreversible.

Ten Hag’s comments carry extra weight given his own complex, two-and-a-half-year spell at Old Trafford.

Arriving from Ajax in May 2022, the Dutchman enjoyed a strong debut campaign, securing a third-place Premier League finish and ending United’s six-year trophy drought by winning the 2023 Carabao Cup.

He followed it up by defeating Manchester City to lift the 2024 FA Cup. However, domestic form deteriorated sharply during his second and third seasons, blighted by severe injury crises, heavy derby defeats, and inconsistent tactical identity that ultimately led to his departure.

Despite the tumultuous end to his tenure, Ten Hag’s two domestic cup triumphs stand as the club’s last major silverware before Old Trafford plunged into its current crisis.

#1390. Erik ten Hag launches latest attack on Cristiano Ronaldo: Former Man United boss claims Portugal star's career was OVER by time he joined Juventus

By BEN WILLCOCKS, ASSISTANT SPORTS EDITOR

Published: 12:32 EDT, 1 November 2026 | Updated: 14:19 EDT, 1 November 2026

Former Manchester United manager Erik ten Hag has taken another swipe at Cristiano Ronaldo, claiming the Portugal icon's career was already over by the time he joined Juventus and eventually returned to Old Trafford.

The legendary forward's second spell at United ended acrimoniously after he launched a public attack on the club and Ten Hag, accusing the manager of 'betraying' him in a bombshell interview.

Ronaldo, whose United contract was terminated following his explosive criticism of the club, joined Al-Nassr in January 2023, while Ten Hag was eventually sacked in October 2024 after a disappointing run of results.

Last month, Ten Hag gave a wide-ranging interview to The Athletic in which he criticised Ronaldo for 'letting the team down' and accused the club's hierarchy of contributing to a 'toxic culture'.

The Dutchman has now doubled down on his criticism of the 41-year-old veteran once again, claiming Ronaldo could not 'make way' for the team.

'Every top team must embrace the top player, but the top player must also make way for the team. That was simply the problem with Ronaldo,' Ten Hag said in an interview on ESPN.

Erik ten Hag has claimed Cristiano Ronaldo's career was over by the time he returned to United

Ten Hag conducted a wide-ranging interview with The Athletic last week in which he hit out at the club's hierarchy for contributing to a 'toxic culture' - and lashed out at Ronaldo

'Let there be no misunderstanding on my part, he is of course a great player. He belongs among the greats of the world.

'But the reality is also that he hasn't been able to deliver for the last seven or eight years. From Juventus onwards, it was simply over.'

Ten Hag also praised Real Madrid, where Ronaldo statistically enjoyed the most prolific years of his career, for selling the superstar at what he believed was the perfect time.

'That is also Real Madrid's great gift,' he added. 'They see when a player is declining in level. Then they part ways at a moment when, to the outside world, they are still at their peak, but actually can no longer deliver.'

In Ten Hag's tell-all interview last month, he accused Manchester United's owners of 'breaking promises' over recruitment and blasted them for showing a lack of ambition in the transfer market.

His criticism of Manchester United came amid a turbulent spell for the club, with Lisandro Martinez and Bruno Fernandes both publicly criticising the board and manager Michael Carrick respectively in recent weeks.

Carrick was given a chance to put things right after United's chiefs met for crunch talks earlier this week in the wake of his side losing 4-1 to Como in the Champions League and 3-0 to Bournemouth in the Premier League.

According to Ten Hag, Ronaldo was not prepared to stand aside for the good of the team

Ronaldo, who now plays for Al-Nassr, is within touching distance of scoring 1,000 career goals

On Saturday, United met a similar fate as they were thumped 3-0 by Chelsea at Stamford Bridge, piling even more pressure on Carrick.

Red Devils legend Peter Schmeichel expressed his anger at Ten Hag speaking out against the club during this difficult period last week.

Speaking on The Overlap Daily, former United goalkeeper Schmeichel said: 'What really annoys me in everything that has happened in the past two weeks is Ten Hag coming out and saying that he wanted Declan Rice and Harry Kane, like he was a god.

'It's so ridiculous. He brought (Lisandro) Martinez in, (Matthijs) de Ligt. I mean he brought players in that are still there, how dare he go out and say that.

'Everybody knew we should sign Harry Kane. Everyone knows we should have signed Declan Rice, that's no secret. I don't know why we didn't do that.

'But you have now people stirring the pot where they should just keep calm and not talk and maybe talk about what they did for this football club themselves, or what they didn't do.

'He wasn't a success at Manchester United. Why does he feel the need to come out and say that?

'What he's saying is "I was let down by the club" and there might be an element of truth in that but he wasn't good enough. And then he went to Bayer Leverkusen, a team who had just won the Bundesliga, and then he got sacked within, what, three games?

Ten Hag also hit out at Manchester United's hierarchy amid a turbulent time for the club

Michael Carrick has been given a chance to turn things around after chiefs held crunch talks

'Maybe just take a step back and don't put yourself in that because then you will end up with someone like me criticising him, and there's no need for that. We don't need it in the narrative.'

Ten Hag was sacked by United in October 2024 after a string of poor results left the team 14th in the Premier League.

His future had been in doubt after he led United to a disappointing eighth-placed finish in the top flight a couple of months earlier, but victory in the FA Cup final over rivals Manchester City contributed to the club's decision to give him a contract extension in the summer after crunch talks in Ibiza.

He went on to replace Xabi Alonso at Bundesliga side Bayer Leverkusen the following season, but was sacked after just three games in charge, and he criticised the club's board for this 'unprecedented' decision.

Manchester City and Manchester United are both monitoring Villarreal right-back Alex Freeman after the United States international’s rapid rise in Spain.

The 22-year-old has established himself as Villarreal’s first-choice option on the right and built on that momentum with a strong 2026 World Cup under Mauricio Pochettino.

His pace, athleticism and ability to play across the back line have now put him on the radar of several major Premier League clubs.

According to Football Insider, Man City and Man United are among the clubs tracking Freeman closely.

City are understood to view him as a potential long-term solution at right-back, while United have also sent scouts to watch him as they continue planning a defensive rebuild.

Tottenham are in the race too, with Roberto De Zerbi assessing alternatives amid continued uncertainty around Pedro Porro’s future.

Freeman joined Villarreal in January 2026 and has since developed into a regular starter in both La Liga and the Champions League.

He also made the United States squad for the 2026 World Cup and featured in all five matches, further raising his profile.

A related CaughtOffside report also states that United, Chelsea and City are all tracking Freeman, while Villarreal remain in a strong position because he is contracted until 2032.

It is easy to see why both Manchester clubs are interested.

Freeman is quick, physically strong and comfortable progressing the ball from deeper positions. He can also operate across several defensive roles, which makes him especially attractive to teams looking for tactical flexibility.

For City, the appeal is obvious because Matheus Nunes is currently being used at right-back despite being a natural midfielder, while Rico Lewis and Abdukodir Khusanov provide alternatives.

United’s need may be even clearer. They are actively rebuilding their defence and have already been linked with several full-backs and centre-backs ahead of 2027.

Freeman’s long-term contract means they do not need to sell, and his value could rise further if he continues performing in Europe.

For now, both clubs appear to be monitoring rather than negotiating, but Freeman is quickly becoming one of the most interesting young right-backs on the market.

#1388. T and B cells recognize splicing-derived neutrophil neoantigens in lupus

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Proteome diversity is generated through alternative mRNA splicing1. In tumours, mis-spliced transcripts that contain intronic sequences, skipped exons or noncanonical donor/acceptor splice junctions resulting in frameshifts are often translated into neoantigens that drive anti-tumour immunity2,3. Here we report that neutrophils from patients with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), unlike neutrophils from healthy donors or patients with rheumatoid arthritis, contain many aberrantly spliced gene transcripts, the translation of which was predicted to result in novel amino acid sequences that are absent in normal splice variants or any other proteins. Twenty-one peptides derived from these novel amino acid sequences were detected by mass spectrometry on class I major histocompatibility complex molecules in patient samples. Co-culture of T cells from patients with overlapping sets of 15-mer peptides from the novel sequences resulted in the expansion of CD4+ and CD8+ T cells that were rapidly reactivated to secrete interferon-γ. T cell antigen receptor sequencing and re-expression transferred neoantigen reactivity to a reporter T cell. Serum from patients with SLE also contained IgG autoantibodies that recognized epitopes within the novel amino acid sequences. Our findings demonstrate that dysregulated mRNA splicing in SLE neutrophils generates neoantigens that have caused T and B cell activation, clonal expansion, IgG class-switch and autoimmunity.

SLE is a debilitating autoimmune disorder of unclear aetiology4,5,6. SLE involves multiple organs and is characterized by the presence of autoantibodies against nuclear proteins, nucleic acid-associated proteins and double-stranded DNA7. Although antigen-specific T cell responses8 have a substantial role, it is largely unknown what antigens the T cells respond to9. Mounting evidence also suggests that innate immune cells have a central role in driving the underlying mechanisms of SLE10,11,12,13,14, including the elevated levels of type I interferons found in most patients with SLE15. Neutrophils are increasingly implicated11,12,13,16,17,18 as sources of SLE autoantigens, including both nucleic acids and proteins, that are released during inflammatory cell death via processes such as NETosis13 and ferroptosis19. Although neutropoiesis is accelerated in SLE15, many patients are neutropenic, indicating increased neutrophil consumption. Neutrophils in SLE display widespread genomic hypomethylation, leading, in part, to a distinctive type I interferon-weighted transcriptional profile20, which differs from that in other autoimmune diseases, but bears much resemblance to that in neutrophils from SARS-CoV2-infected individuals21.

Alternative RNA transcript splicing begins during gene transcription and results in the nuclear export of mature mRNA variants that profoundly contribute to proteome complexity and molecular diversity1. Proteins that are translated from alternatively spliced mRNA often display substantial differences in molecular functions, stability and interactions with other proteins or nucleic acids. Alternative splicing can also modulate mRNA disposition, including degradation through nonsense-mediated decay (NMD)22. Alternative splicing occurs more frequently in autoantigen transcripts20 than in randomly selected proteins, and escape from NMD has been shown to cause autoimmunity23. Neutrophils represent an abundant reservoir of intracellular proteins and nucleic acids that potentially function as autoantigenic sources.

To comprehensively analyse alternative mRNA splicing, we created the RiboSplitter24 pipeline, which yields the translated protein products of splice variants. With this tool, we characterized 65,730 high-confidence alternative splicing events in 5,697 protein-coding genes in neutrophils from patients with SLE, of which 521 events in 356 genes were significantly different from healthy donors25. Here we focus on the SLE-restricted mRNA splicing events, referred to as ‘cryptic’ splicing events, that are predicted to generate novel protein sequences.

Thirty-four patients with SLE, representing a typical academic medical centre population (Supplementary Table 1), consented to blood donation. Healthy donors and patients with rheumatoid arthritis served as normal and disease controls, respectively. Immune cells and neutrophils were isolated, and the patients’ sera were stored frozen until use. RNA was isolated from neutrophils and used for stranded paired-end RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) (Fig. 1a) to a sequencing depth of approximately 50 million reads with 101 bp read length (Fig. 1b). We applied a minimum threshold of five reads to exclude stochastic low-frequency splicing artefacts, detecting a total of 271 cryptic splicing events in 130 genes in SLE neutrophils (n = 34), all of which were absent in neutrophils from the healthy donors (n = 20) and patients with rheumatoid arthritis (n = 15). The most abundant events were abnormal exon skips, followed by multi-exon skips, atypical 5′ or 3′ splice sites and intron retention (Fig. 1c). Several cryptic events were combinations of these mechanisms. A pathway analysis of the aberrantly spliced genes showed a strong bias for type I interferon-inducible genes (Fig. 1d), including the most frequently mis-spliced genes IFI44L, MX1, OAS1, RSAD2, XAF1, IFI27, MX1 and IFIT1. However, cryptic splicing events were also observed in genes that are not considered interferon-inducible, such as ABCG1, PSMF1 and OGG1 (Supplementary Fig. 1), indicating that expression level alone cannot explain the generation of these cryptic splicing events, although it could be a factor. As expected, read support for cryptic splicing events was lower than for non-cryptic events (Fig. 1e), but read support for cryptic splicing events that generated novel peptide sequences varied from 283 reads down to our cut-off threshold of 5 (median = 10).

a, Schematic overview of our experimental approach. BCR, B cell receptor; HC, healthy control; PMN, polymorphonuclear cells; RA, rheumatoid arthritis. b, Our computational pipeline. c, Categories of the cryptic splicing events. d, Pathway analysis of the aberrantly spliced genes. IFN, interferon. e, Average read counts for cryptic splicing events that generate novel amino acid sequences compared to all splicing events in the same gene transcripts in all 34 patients. Box plots represent second to third quartiles centred around the mean, and whiskers indicate ±2× s.d. f, Number of cryptic splicing events and genes that they affected in the individual patients with SLE. g, Total number of 9-mer and 15-mer peptides that the cryptic transcripts could theoretically generate. h, In silico-predicted neoantigens in genes undergoing cryptic splicing in each patient with the number of cryptic events in each. Right side, the number of predicted neoantigen peptides with high-affinity binding to their own haplotype of class I or II molecules. i, Venn diagram of total mRNA splicing and cryptic splicing (pink) events in SLE monocytes and neutrophils. j, Venn diagram of total mRNA splicing and cryptic splicing (pink) events in SLE and Sjögren’s disease neutrophils and healthy donor neutrophils treated with interferon. k, Venn diagram of total mRNA splicing and cryptic splicing (pink) events in SLE neutrophils and two SLE PBMC datasets. The interferon gene signature status of each patient is indicated as a purple (high) or pale blue (low) box.

Cryptic splicing events were detected in 33 out of 34 patients with SLE (Fig. 1f), but the total number of events and the genes that they occurred in varied among patients, from 45 events in 18 genes down to 1 event in 1 gene (Fig. 1f). These data also revealed that the precise pattern of cryptic splicing is relatively unique to each patient, although several genes are mis-spliced in up to 15 patients. For comparison, we analysed RNA-seq data from SLE monocytes (Fig. 1i), interferon-treated healthy donor neutrophils (Fig. 1j), Sjögren’s disease neutrophils (Fig. 1j), and two publicly available RNA-seq datasets of peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) from patients with SLE (n = 36 total) (Fig. 1k) using our pipeline and found that only one of the cryptic splicing events in monocytes and two in one SLE PBMC dataset, suggesting that these patterns of cryptic splicing are unique to neutrophils in SLE. Similarly, the acute myeloid cell line AML14, which represents an immature myeloid phenotype, lacked any cryptic splicing observed in SLE neutrophils. These datasets had higher sequencing depth, providing greater sensitivity for detecting splicing events than our SLE neutrophils (Supplementary Fig. 2a). Cryptic splicing correlated with interferon-inducible genes (Supplementary Fig. 2b), but not with anti-nuclear autoantibodies (ribonucleoprotein, Sm antigen, double-stranded DNA, Sjögren's-syndrome-related antigen A (SSA)), SLE disease activity index (SLEDAI), or steroid use (Supplementary Fig. 2c). A subset of cryptic events, particularly in many interferon-inducible genes, correlated with higher expression in those individuals with the cryptic events. However, in more than half of the genes, there was no such correlation (Supplementary Fig. 3a–d). This was also observed by calculating the per cent-spliced in (PSI) for the cryptic splicing events: for many cryptic events, PSI showed minimal change, although for the majority of cryptic splicing events PSI was much altered (Supplementary Fig. 3e).

Using RiboSplitter, we translated the observed cryptic splicing events into peptide sequences. The total number of 9-mer and 15-mer cryptic peptides that were optimal for class I and class II major histocompatibility complex (MHC) binding, respectively, varied between patients (Fig. 1g). To evaluate whether these peptides could bind MHC and be presented to T cells, we determined MHC class I and II haplotypes for each patient using arcasHLA (Supplementary Table 2) and ranked peptides derived from their individual set of novel amino acid sequences for binding using NetMHCpan-4.1 and NetMHCIIpan-4.026. We only considered peptides that did not match any known human protein sequences in Ensemble and in secondary BLAST searches. Individual patients with SLE varied in the number of potential neoantigen peptides with predicted high-affinity binding to their own haplotype of class I or II molecules (Fig. 1h): 86 peptides from 46 genes ranked in the top 2nd percentile, 65 of them in the top 0.5th percentile.

To experimentally confirm cryptic mRNA splicing events, we designed PCR primers flanking the splicing event that were designed to yield an amplicon of diagnostic size. In a patient with SLE with the multi-exon skip in USP18, this variant was visualized by the appearance of an amplicon corresponding to the predicted 207 bp (Fig. 2a). Sanger sequencing of this band verified its identity as the joined exons 6 and 11. In addition, there were bands of approximately 300 bp and 450 bp, representing the skip of 3 or 2 exons (rather than 4). The canonical splice form was also prominently present at the predicted size of 653 bp. These data validate the in silico detection of this cryptic splice variant.

a–e, The location of forward (F) and reverse (R) PCR primers to amplify diagnostic-sized fragments of five cryptic mRNA splicing events (left) in USP18 (a), ABCG1 (b), IFI44L (c), OAS1 (d) and MX1 (e). The PCR reaction products (middle) with the spliced exons in each band indicated and the sequence of the band corresponding to the cryptic variant. These results were obtained in 3–5 independent experiments for each event. f,g, Average reads of canonical splice junctions in all 34 patients (f) and read counts of the cryptic splice junctions in the same genes (g). n = 1–15. Box plots represent second to third quartiles centred around the mean, and whiskers indicate ±2× s.d.

Similarly, the cryptic ABCG1 exon skip was validated by the flanking PCR primers yielding a 203-bp band (Fig. 2b), the sequencing of which verified the joining of exon 8 to exon 10, as well as the canonical 352-bp band. The skip of exons 4 and 5 in the cryptic IFI44L variant was seen as a 101-bp amplicon (Fig. 2c) by flanking PCR primers and its sequence verified the joining of exon 3 to exon 6. The cryptic splicing of OAS1 (Fig. 2d) and MX1 (Fig. 2e), were validated by PCR with reverse transcription (RT–PCR) and Sanger sequencing of the relevant band in the agarose gel. All these data also illustrate that the cryptic splice variants are less abundant than the canonical or physiological splice variants, in agreement with the RNA-seq read counts (Fig. 2f,g).

Next we used an immunopeptidomics27 approach to determine if peptides derived from cryptic splicing were indeed translated and proteolytically processed for presentation on MHC28. This is vital, as transcripts with premature stop codons are frequently degraded by NMD29,30,31 and because the proteolytic processing creates skewing in the presented peptide repertoire. We immunoprecipitated class I MHC molecules from SLE neutrophils using an anti-pan HLA antibody and analysed the eluted peptides by targeted liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry (LC–MS/MS), using a custom reference database containing computationally predicted neoantigen peptides. These experiments yielded spectra matching 21 of the predicted novel peptides and their calculated daughter ions for a high confidence of identification (Fig. 3, Table 1 and Supplementary Fig. 4). We refer to the novel peptides identified by LC–MS/MS in HLA immunoprecipitates as bona fide neoantigens. By NetMHCpan-4.1 ranking, the majority of them fell into the highest-affinity group (Supplementary Fig. 5), with only one notable exception: the 10-residue peptide AGRRKEEEIL derived from a cryptic splicing event in MX1 which was predicted to bind the HLA haplotype of the patient with modest affinity, perhaps reflecting some post-translational modification that is not recognized in the LC–MS/MS, a mutation or modification of the HLA molecule in this patient, or a false negative prediction by NetMHCpan-4.1. Supplementary Table 3 summarizes the disease activity, interferon gene signature, cryptic splicing of interferon-inducible genes, and peptides derived from these genes in the 34 patients with SLE.

Left, schematic representations of the cryptic events in: USP18 (a), MYO15B (b), PHF11 (c), OAS1 (d), FCGRT (e) and MX1 (f). Middle, the translation products with the predicted neo-sequences indicated as purple boxes, normal sequences by orange boxes, and stop codons by a vertical red line. Right, the origin within the neo-sequences of the peptides detected in anti-HLA immunoprecipitates (IP) and their mass spectra, with precursor and daughter ions and idotp values.

Figure 3 also illustrates cryptic splicing events that generated novel amino acid sequences from which peptides bound to HLA were detected. For example, a cryptic splicing event in USP18 (Fig. 3a) involving a multi-exon skip to splice exon 6 to exon 11 resulted in a frameshift of exon 11 and translation of 24 codons (purple box in Fig. 3a) until an in-frame stop codon (indicated by a red line). The translated USP18 protein has a novel C terminus, from which an 11-amino acid peptide was identified with very high confidence (dot product of experimental and theoretical isotopic distributions (idotp) 0.99) in anti-HLA immunoprecipitates. A similar event in the transcript from MYO15B (Fig. 3b) excised exons 41–43, resulting in a frameshift in the translation of exon 44 (purple box in Fig. 3b), from which a 9-residue peptide was detected by LC–MS/MS in an anti-HLA immunoprecipitate from the patient predicted to have this cryptic splice variant.

A cryptic splicing event in PHF11 in another patient with SLE (Fig. 3c) generated a novel amino acid sequence by a different mechanism: an aberrant skip of exon 11, in which a stop codon normally terminates translation, resulted in a continued translation of 53 codons in the normally untranslated exon 12. The junction of exon 10 and this novel amino acid sequence yields an HLA-bound peptide FQAGCHTQL (idotp 0.92) in which the first 4 residues are encoded by exon 10, but the following 5 represent neo-sequences that are unique to the cryptic splicing event and have no match in a BLAST search. In the canonical isoform, exon 10 is translated in its intended reading-frame resulting in a completely different amino acid sequence (orange box).

A similar mechanism generated a novel amino acid product of an OAS1 transcript (Fig. 3d), where a cryptic splicing event representing both a skip of exon 6 (which occurs physiologically in transcript variant 10) and an altered 3′ acceptor site for splicing located 3′ of the stop codon in exon 7, resulting in the translation of 26 codons of exon 7 (purple box in Fig. 3d) until an in-frame stop codon (red line). Thus, the resulting OAS1 protein has a novel C terminus, which can give rise to the FLLTGVDL peptide that we detected by LC–MS/MS on HLA-A*02:01 in the neutrophils from the patient that carries this cryptic splicing event with 15 read counts.

A different mechanism generated a 32-amino-acid residue novel sequence from the aberrant splicing of the FCGRT transcript, in which 96 nucleotides of an inverted 302-bp AluJb element located in the 10-kb intron between exons 4 and 5 was spliced in to generate the novel sequence (Fig. 3e). A peptide encoded by the junction of exon 4 and the Alu sequence (NLEWKETGF) was detected by LC–MS/MS in anti-HLA immunoprecipitates. Further illustrative examples of splicing events that were unique to SLE included a two-exon skip plus an aberrant 3′ splice acceptor site in MX1 (Fig. 3f), resulting in a frameshift in the translation of exon 16, from which a peptide was identified by LC–MS/MS.

Supplementary Fig. 2 shows additional cryptic splicing events in ABCG1, RSAD2, DAAM2, IFIT1, IFI44 and IFI44L. The event in RSAD2 includes part of an intron consisting of a long interspersed element-1 (LINE1)-derived HAL1 (half-L132) retrotransposon, whereas the cryptic event in IFIT1 includes part of the intron containing an inverted AluSx element. Some of the events shown generated peptides that we identified in anti-HLA immunoprecipitates, whereas others did not.

Most of the cryptic splicing events yielding detectable neoantigen peptides occurred near the 3′ end of the open reading frame and therefore do not introduce premature stop codons that would result in NMD. Another set of peptides was derived from events that spliced in a portion of an intron—for example, an inverted Alu element—but did not introduce a premature stop codon.

To test whether class-switched IgG autoantibodies exist in our patient cohort against these neo-sequences, we synthesized a series of 15-residue peptides to cover, in a tiled fashion, the novel amino acid sequences generated by a set of cryptic splicing events observed in the highest numbers of patients with SLE. Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays (ELISAs) with these peptides revealed that many of the patients computationally predicted to express the selected neoantigens indeed had IgG that was reactive with the corresponding peptides (Fig. 4). Using the 95th percentile of the background reactivity of healthy donors as a cut-off, 17 out of 34 patients with SLE were positive for IgG recognizing the first IFI44L peptide, including 7 out of 9 patients who were observed to generate this neo-sequence at the time of blood draw for our RNA-seq. By contrast, peptides from the canonical amino acid sequence of IFI44L selected to have high affinity for the SLE risk allele HLA-DR3, did not show increased IgG reactivity in SLE compared with healthy donors (Fig. 4g). These results indicate that the IFI44L neo-sequence was generated chronically or episodically in these patients for a sufficiently long time to generate a B cell response leading to circulating IgG antibodies against this sequence. IgG autoantibodies also recognized peptides from the novel amino acid sequences in OAS1, MX1, IFI44 and RSAD2, with the fifth peptide generated by the frameshifted translation of MX1 exon 6 after the cryptic multi-exon skip and 3′ neojunction detected in 5 of 8 patients with SLE exhibiting this event.

a, ELISA with 39 SLE serum samples, including all 34 patients with SLE, and the 2 indicated overlapping 15-residue peptides derived from the total novel amino acid sequence (purple box) generated from the transcript of IFI44L. Blue dots indicate patients that were computationally predicted to generate this neo-sequence at the time of venipuncture. a.u., arbitrary units. b, ELISA for the second peptide (indicated), covering most of the neo-sequence (purple box) generated by cryptic splicing of RSAD2. c, Same as b, for the single 10-residue peptide covering the cryptic splice event in IFI44. d, Same as b, for the two peptides covering the neo-sequence (purple box) from OAS1. e, Same as b, for a peptide from the neo-sequence (purple box) generated by a cryptic splicing event in IFIT1. This peptide was chosen because it is predicted to bind the SLE-associated HLA-DRB1*15:01 with high affinity. f, Same as b, for three of the six peptides covering the second half of the neo-sequence (purple box) generated from MX1. The far right graph connects the reactivity towards the six peptides in each individual patient. g, Same as b, showing absence of IgG specific for three canonical IFI44L peptides in patients with SLE. All data include mean ± s.d. and the 95th percentile of the healthy donor cohort is shown as a dashed blue line.

Autoantibodies were also detected in some patients even when the cryptic splicing event generating the neoantigen was not observed. These either represent patients who had the cryptic splice form earlier, but not at the time of venipuncture, or events that were missed in our analysis because our RNA-seq depth of 50 million reads is estimated to give us approximately 60% coverage of mRNA splicing events33,34, indicating that there might be more splicing-generated neoantigens than we observed.

The presence of class-switched IgG autoantibodies that recognize the cryptic peptides suggests that neoantigen-specific T cells were involved and provided help for class switching and affinity maturation. To test this directly, we used a 14-day expansion and restimulation assay that was optimized for the detection of tumour antigen-specific T cells35. In this regimen, the antigen-specific T cells are activated and undergo several cell divisions, and then return to a resting state before restimulation on day 14 (Fig. 5a). PBMCs from patients including those in the RNA-seq cohort were incubated for 14 days in the presence of peptide pools consisting of 3–7 distinct 15-mer peptides covering the novel amino acid sequence of a cryptic splice variant, and restimulated on day 14 with each individual peptide separately, and assayed on day 15 for IFNγ and IL-17 production by ELISpot and analysed for activation using flow cytometry. T cells from one immunosuppressed patient with SLE (undergoing treatment with tacrolimus and prednisone) showed only weak reactivity, whereas T cells from nine other patients (Fig. 5b–e and Supplementary Figs. 9 and 11a), showed moderate to strong reactivity against several peptides, with T cells from each patient displaying a unique profile of reactivity. We also tested a set of control peptides. Three peptides from the canonical splice variant of IFI44L with high predicted affinity for class II MHC (DR3), and three peptides with random amino acid sequences lacking homology with any human proteins, did not activate any T cell response (Fig. 5e and Supplementary Fig. 9). IFNγ and IL-17 secretion were frequently detected, whereas IL-5 was rarely produced and was not increased by any of the peptides (data not shown). Both CD4+ and CD8+ T cells exhibited increased expression of the activation marker CD69 (Fig. 5g–i), but many individual peptides preferentially activated either CD4+ or CD8+ T cells. By contrast, T cells from healthy donors showed little response to any of the neoantigen peptides (Fig. 5j and Supplementary Fig. 10). In the patient represented in Fig. 5i, peptides derived from the cryptic variants of ABCG1, FCGRT, SERPING1, RSAD2, IFIT1, TBC1D15, MX1, IFI44L, and IFI44 stimulated CD8+ T cells, whereas peptides derived from cryptic variants of SERPING1, IFIT1, IFI44L and IFI44 stimulated CD4+ T cells. A statistical analysis based on T cell numbers in flow cytometry using χ2 test and adjusted for multiple comparisons, gave significant P values for many of these peptide responses (complete list in Supplementary Table 4).

Experiments were carried out in triplicate; data are mean ± s.d. c, Same as b, using T cells from a second patient with SLE. d, Same as b, using T cells from a third patient with SLE. e, Same as b, using T cells from a fourth patient with SLE, including control peptides.
