Single-cell sequencing of the T cell antigen receptor (TCR) β chain gene (TCRB) revealed that 105 cells in the starting cultures had approximately 89,400 different TCR sequences with a Simpson clonality index of 0.006, whereas the control cultures without peptide had 22,000 TCRs, also with low clonality. By contrast, two neoantigen peptides from IFI44L resulted in the notable expansion of several specific TCRs (Supplementary Fig. 11b), with Simpson clonality indices of 0.072 and 0.185. The copy number after PCR amplification (template frequency) of TCRs from the IFI44L-1 culture was increased from <1 to 6,366; that of the TCRs from the IFI44L-2 culture was increased from <1 to 1,832. Additional TCRs were also expanded, but to a lesser extent. The amino acid sequences of the unique complementary determining regions (CDRs) 1, 2 and 3 of the top ten TCRs are shown in Supplementary Fig. 11c.

To validate the neoantigen specificity of expanded T cell clones, we used throughput-intensive rapid TCR library sequencing (TIRTL-seq)36 to sequence expanded TCR α and β chain (TCRA/TCRB) pairs from the same neoantigen-stimulated cultures and then expressed the TCR pairs in a reporter T cell line, termed T-FINDER37. Figure 5k shows a TCR (TCR14) identified among the 18 tested, which responded vigorously to the IFI44L-2 neoantigen peptides presented by the patient’s own B cells. The T-FINDER cells with this TCR did not respond to 11 other neoantigen peptides or the 3 canonical IFI44L peptides (Fig. 5l), demonstrating high selectivity for the IFI44L-2 peptide. In addition, a pool of all six possible 10-mer peptides covering the sequence of the 15-mer IFI44L-2 did not activate the TCR14-expressing cells, indicating that the 15-mer IFI44L-2 peptide was presented on class II MHC. Thus, this TCR was derived from a CD4+ T cell in the patient with SLE.

Given that SLE neutrophils with cryptic splice variants result in neoantigen peptides presented on their surface class I MHC, as evidenced by our immunopeptidomics experiments, we stained SLE neutrophils with a monoclonal antibody that recognizes the N-terminal knob that is exposed in 20–24 copies on the extracellular face of polymerized perforin pores38 generated by cytotoxic T cells. We previously showed that this antibody detects poly-perforin pores on the surface of 15–45% of neutrophils freshly isolated from patients with rheumatoid arthritis as well as neutrophils treated with monomeric perforin38. Indeed, 0–20% of SLE neutrophils contained dots (Fig. 5m) of the same size as those in rheumatoid arthritis neutrophils, whereas neutrophils from healthy donors did not (Fig. 5n), indicating that cytotoxic T cells have encountered antigen on their surface and attempted to kill them via perforin deposition. The proportion of SLE neutrophils bearing poly-perforin pores was lower than that observed in rheumatoid arthritis (Fig. 5o).

These experiments demonstrate that neoantigen-specific T cells exist in patients with SLE at frequencies that can be estimated to reach 1–15 per million T cells, which is comparable to the frequencies of tumour antigen-specific T cells35. The presence of IgG autoantibodies that recognize neo-sequences suggests that some of the antigen-specific CD4+ T cells provided help to B cells—that is, they are either follicular helper T cells (TFH), which are are known to be expanded in SLE, or peripheral helper T cells (TPH).

Our finding that neoantigens are generated from aberrant mRNA splicing in SLE neutrophils introduces a potential new model for the pathogenesis of this disease. We propose that the appearance of neoantigens, rather than loss of tolerance, is the driving factor behind the escalating immune activation that characterizes this disease. In this scenario, the immune system acts as it is programmed to do: making every effort to eliminate the source of ‘foreign’ neoantigens. This may explain many features of the disease, such as its waxing and waning course, the broad range of organ manifestations and symptoms, and the strong immunosuppression required for treating active disease. This paradigm is also in agreement with the notable similarity in neutrophil expression profiles in SLE and SARS-CoV2 infected individuals21.

The importance of neoantigens is well-recognized in anti-tumour immunity, which is pivotal for cancer immunotherapy39,40, and in which altered self-peptides are recognized as foreign antigen by CD4+ and CD8+ T cells, ultimately resulting in tumour killing by CD8+ cytotoxic T cells. These tumour-specific peptides can be generated from point mutations in proteins41, cancer-specific post-translational modifications, intergenic translation products or aberrant mRNA splicing3,42,43, with aberrant mRNA splicing yielding the largest repertoire of neoantigens. Our findings in SLE are similar in that aberrant transcript splicing is widespread (detected in 33 out of 34 patients) and results in novel amino acid sequences with the capacity to yield neoantigens presented on class I and II MHC molecules. At a sequencing depth of 50 million, our estimated coverage of mRNA splicing events is about 60%. Thus, it is likely that many aberrant slicing events remained undetected in our analysis. Our mRNA splicing data also represents a single time point, while the presence of IgG autoantibodies against the novel amino acid sequences indicates that patients had been exposed to them over an extended time before our sample acquisition. Thus, it is possible that aberrant mRNA splicing is more widespread than our findings show. It may also vary over time, perhaps related to exacerbations interspersed with periods of low disease activity.

Neoantigens presented on class I MHC on the surface of SLE neutrophils would make them vulnerable to killing by cytotoxic CD8+ T cells, which are activated44 but decreased in number45 in SLE. Indeed, we detect poly-perforin pores on the surface of SLE neutrophils, which are known to be consumed at higher rates in SLE15. Perforin-mediated killing is more inflammatory than neutrophil apoptosis and may include other programmed cell death pathways11,13,46. In SLE, cytotoxic effector T cells have a CD38hiCD127− phenotype similar to that of CD8+ T cells in checkpoint inhibitor-induced arthritis and viral infections47, a phenotype that can be induced in vitro by type I interferons47.

The processing of nascent transcripts begins during transcription and involves a large number of splicing factors, RNA molecules, enzymes and RNA modifications. Thus, a multitude of different disturbances could underpin our findings. Whereas expression of genes encoding several core mRNA splicing factors and RNA-binding proteins was either decreased (SF3B148, SF3B5, SF3A2, U2AF2, SRSF7 and DDX4649) or increased (SNRNP27) in neutrophils from patients with SLE compared with healthy and rheumatoid arthritis neutrophils (Supplementary Fig. 6), a more specific set of RNA-binding proteins were found to be associated with sequences at cryptic splice sites in the ENCODE dataset (Supplementary Fig. 7). Downmodulation by short-hairpin RNA interference of a set of individual splice factors in the ENCODE data resulted in some of the cryptic events that we found in SLE neutrophils (Supplementary Fig. 8). Two of these splice factors, DDX24 and SF3B4, were present in both results. Another notable candidate is Ro60 (also known as TROVE2), a known target of autoantibodies in SLE. Out of the four patients with cryptic splicing events correlated with Ro60, three had SSA autoantibodies (recognizing Ro52 and Ro60). DDX24 was expressed at relatively low levels in the patient with cryptic splicing of TTC14 compared with all SLE samples (Supplementary Fig. 7c) and SF4B4 expression was very low in the patient with cryptic splicing of MON2 (Supplementary Fig. 7c). Supplementary Fig. 7d illustrates where these two latter proteins bound in the transcript in the eCLIP data. These data suggest that dysfunction of individual splice factors may be responsible for the cryptic RNA splicing in SLE neutrophils.

Aberrant mRNA splicing is common in haematological malignancies50 and solid tumours51, but the exact molecular mechanisms underlying these phenomena remain unclear except in cases of specific splicing factor mutations, such as SF3B1K700E (refs. 52,53,54) in myeloid leukaemias. Of note, SF3B1 expression was somewhat reduced (log2 fold enrichment = −0.24, adjusted P value (Padj) = 0.045) in SLE neutrophils, as were four other splicing factors (SF3A2, U2AF2, DDX41 and DDX46). However, alternative splicing is a complex process involving more than 200 proteins and U RNA components, making it challenging to identify the cause of aberrant splicing, which may not be the same in every patient with SLE.

Neutropoiesis includes a burst of proliferation in the bone marrow, during which deficiencies in epigenetic regulation could be amplified to significant levels in the mature neutrophils. Decreased DNA methylation and epigenetic gene silencing are hallmarks of SLE55,56, leading to increased transcription of many loci and genes, such as endogenous retroviruses, L1 retrotransposons, Alu elements and other transposable elements. In healthy individuals, intronic transposable elements in nascent transcripts are prevented from acting as splice donor or acceptor sites by specific RNA binding proteins encoded by HNRNPC, ELAVL157, TIA and PTBP158. SLE neutrophils express reduced levels of PTBP1 (log2 fold enrichment = −0.44, Padj = 1.75 × 10−5) and ELAVL1 (log2 fold enrichment = −0.27, Padj = 0.010). This may explain the aberrant splicing in of an inverted Alu in FCGRT (Fig. 3e), an inverted Alu in IFIT1 (Supplementary Fig. 2d), a HAL1 element in RSAD2 (Supplementary Fig. 2b) and other cases of cryptic exonization.

The importance of these cryptic-splicing-derived amino acid sequences in SLE pathogenesis can ultimately be determined only through clinical trials using agents that block their production. In support of an important role, recent work with anti-CD19 chimeric antigen receptor T cells has demonstrated that B cell depletion needs to be complete59 for an apparent cure of SLE to be achieved60. The B cells that re-emerge after treatment are newly developed naive B cells, which, consequently, are tolerant of self-epitopes, including any neoantigens that are present in the bone marrow where B cell tolerance develops and maturing neutrophils are abundant. These trials highlight the central role of B cells (rather than only dendritic cells) in neoantigen presentation to T cells and subsequent immunity against neoantigens derived from altered mRNA splicing in neutrophils.

We obtained freshly drawn blood from adult (n = 34) patients with SLE, healthy individuals (n = 20), and patients with rheumatoid arthritis (n = 15) to serve as disease controls. Study participants were recruited through the University of Washington, Division of Rheumatology Biorepository to participate in research studies at the University of Washington Medical Center, Seattle, WA. The study was approved by the institutional ethics board (STUDY00006196), the research was performed in accordance with all relevant guidelines and regulations, and informed written consent was obtained from all participants according to the Declaration of Helsinki.

The 34 patients with SLE included in our study represent the typical spectrum of SLE disease seen in an academic medical centre with standard-of-care medication (Supplementary Table 1). Eleven patients had active disease, defined as having SLEDAI ≥ 6, while 24 had inactive disease with a SLEDAI < 6 at the time of venipuncture. Based on the 95th percentile of the expression of 111 interferon-inducible genes in healthy donors, 26 were considered interferon signature positive. All healthy donors and patients with rheumatoid arthritis were interferon signature negative.

Polymorphonuclear (PMN) cells were isolated from freshly drawn venous blood (within 1 h of venipuncture) by gradient centrifugation on PolymorphPrep according to the manufacturer’s instructions. The PMN fraction was >95% CD66b+ and >85% CD15+. The cells were washed and suspended in Hanks’ buffered salt solution at 107 per ml.

Extraction of RNA was performed using Quick-RNA Whole Blood kit (Zymo Research, R1201). Cells were lysed in DNA/RNA Shield and RNAs were isolated following manufacturer’s instruction and eluted in RNase-free water. RNA was sent to the UW Northwest Genomics core for strand-specific paired-end RNA-seq at 50 million 101-bp reads per sample.

After quality control of sequencing quality, FASTQ files were aligned to the reference genome (GRCh38) using STAR (v2.7.9a)61 with two-pass mode which improves detection of reads mapping to novel splicing junctions. After post-alignment quality control, sorted and indexed BAM files were used to identify alternative splicing events by SplAdder (v3.0.3)62 which uses alignment and annotation data to create splicing graphs that are enriched with splicing events based on the provided RNA-seq data, followed by quantification of splicing events. The software filters input alignment reads based on their quality and allows four levels of confidence; we used the highest confidence setting. Additionally, this tool uses event-specific criteria to confirm splicing events based on genomic coordinates and coverage; we only included confirmed events in our analysis. Both annotated and novel splicing events were detected including six types of events: exon skip, alternative 3′ or 5′ splice site, intron retention, mutually exclusive exons, and multiple exon skip.

We detected cryptic alternative splicing in SLE, defined as splicing events with read support in SLE neutrophils and either absence or rare read support in healthy and rheumatoid arthritis disease controls. We used our established methodology (RiboSplitter24) to translate splicing events into peptide sequences to allow downstream analysis and validation. Splicing events with valid unambiguous translations were used for downstream analyses.

Because an alternative splicing event includes two isoforms, we identified cryptic splicing events (both isoforms are cryptic), as well as cryptic splicing isoforms (one of the event’s isoforms is cryptic). We used strict filtering criteria as follows: first, we required cryptic events and isoforms to have ≥10 supporting reads in at least one SLE sample and no more than 2 supporting reads in each healthy or rheumatoid arthritis sample; or ≥5 supporting reads in at least 1 SLE sample and zero supporting reads in each healthy or rheumatoid arthritis sample. Second, we excluded annotated splicing events and isoforms based on the GRCh38 reference. Third, cryptic peptides were excluded if a match existed among known annotated proteins of the gene. These filtering criteria add specificity in detecting events that are cryptic and unique to SLE neutrophils.

We consistently calculated PSI values for isoform 2, so that a higher PSI always indicates higher proportion of isoform 2, which makes it easier to interpret which group has more of which isoform.

We identified each class I and class II MHC haplotypes for each patient with SLE from RNA-seq data using arcasHLA (v0.5.0), which was shown to be highly accurate (100% accurate for class I MHC and >99.7% accurate for class II MHC)63. MHC affinity binding was predicted for cryptic SLE peptides using NetMHCpan-4.1 (mers length = 8–11) and NetMHCIIpan-4.026 (mers length = 14–16) that use neural networks trained on binding affinity as well as mass spectrometry data. Strong affinity binding was defined as percent rank of predicted affinity ≤2% (compared to a set of 100,000 random natural peptides) with predicted binding affinity <500.

Peptides that bind to class I MHC were immunoprecipitated using a method described previously64. In brief, HLA-A, HLA-B and HLA-C (W6/32) or isotype antibody was conjugated to protein A magnetic beads (Millipore-Sigma) at 1 mg ml−1. Cell lysate from 10 million cells was mixed with 100 µl of anti-HLA beads (or isotype control beads). After washing, bound peptides were eluted with 0.2% trifluoroacetic acid followed by a C-18 column clean-up and further analysed by LC–MS.

Mass spectrometry was performed at the University of Washington’s Proteomics Resource (UWPR). Peptide separation was performed on a Thermo EASY-nLC system using a 120-min gradient at 300 nl min−1. Mobile phase B was increased from 6% to 45% over 89 min, followed by a ramp to 100% B and column re-equilibration. Samples were loaded at 2.5 µl min−1. Mass spectrometric analysis was carried out on an Orbitrap Exploris 480 operated in positive ion mode. The full mass spectrometry scans were acquired at 120,000 resolution (at m/z 200) across an m/z range of 375–1575, with a normalized AGC target of 200%. Targeted parallel reaction monitoring MS/MS scans were acquired at 30,000 resolution using high-energy collisional dissociation (HCD) fragmentation with a normalized collision energy of 30%. The isolation window was set to 1.6 m/z. Scheduled acquisition windows of 0–120 min were used for targeted precursor ions listed in the inclusion list. Individual peptide was further analysed in Skyline65.

The Skyline chromatogram data were imported into and visualized with Skyline (64-bit) 24.1.0.199. Data were filtered to include only precursors with an idotp ≥0.85 and mass error <10 ppm. Then the match of peak shape and retention time of the spectra from the daughter ions to those from precursors were visually inspected and confirmed.

Selected neoantigen peptides synthesized by Shanghai RoyoBiotechnology were coated onto medium-binding EIA plates at 1 ng μl−1 in 0.1 M bicarbonate coating buffer, pH 9.5. Plates were then blocked in 2% BSA in 1× phosphate-buffered saline (PBS). Sera from patients with SLE and healthy donors were added to the blocked wells followed by anti-human IgG–horseradish peroxidase. TMB substrates were added to the wells, and the reaction was stopped by 2N sulfuric acid solution. Absorbance at 450 nm and 630 nm were measured with a BioTek Synergy 2 plate reader.

We quantified gene expression using Rsubread featureCounts66 (v2.12.3). The average expression of 111 interferon-induced genes (ISGs)67 was calculated per sample, and SLE samples were considered having high interferon signatures when the average expression of ISGs was higher than the 95% percentile of ISG expression in healthy controls.

To test whether cryptic splicing events that we discovered in SLE neutrophils were also seen in PBMCs, we used two publicly available RNA-seq datasets of PBMCs from patients with SLE. One study (GSE122459)68 included 20 patients with SLE and 6 healthy controls, and the other (GSE211700)69 included 20 patients with SLE and 10 healthy controls. We ran the same analysis pipeline as described above to align the data and detect alternative splicing events. Then we searched for neutrophil SLE cryptic splicing in the PBMC datasets.

PBMCs (2 × 106 per well) from patients with SLE were cultured in 24-well plates in RPMI 1640 medium (Gibco, 11-875-093) supplemented with 5% autologous patient serum that was syringe-filtered (0.22 μm), heat-inactivated at 56 °C for 20 min, and re-filtered (0.22 μm). Cells were stimulated with 5 μg ml−1 peptide pools containing three to six neopeptides and supplemented with IL-2 (10 U ml−1; R&D, BT-002-050) on days 4 and 9. Positive controls consisted of stimulation with phytohaemagglutinin-M (10 μg ml−1; Sigma, NC2034236) on day 1, followed by restimulation with CD3/CD28 Dynabeads (Gibco, 11131D) on day 14. Tetanus toxoid (Fisher Scientific/List Biological Labs, NC0603970) served as an additional positive control in a subset of experiments. On day 14, PBMCs were restimulated with individual peptides from each pool, and ELISPOT plates were coated with capture antibody for overnight incubation. Following 18–24 h coculture, triplicate aliquots of 3 × 105 cells were resuspended in CTL medium supplemented with 1% L-glutamine (Gibco, 2503008), plated into coated ELISPOT wells, and incubated for 4 h at 37 °C. Spots were developed using the CTL-Human IFN-γ/IL-17 Double-Color ELISPOT Kit according to the manufacturer’s instructions and quantified with a CTL S6 Universal M2 reader. The remaining cells were collected for flow cytometry analysis.

Following 14 days of stimulation, cells were transferred to a 96-well round bottom plate and.washed with 1× PBS. To prevent non-specific binding, cells were resuspended in 1× PBS with 1% bovine serum albumin (BSA) and incubated at room temperature for 20 min. Cells were then stained with a cocktail of fluorochrome-labelled monoclonal antibodies, including: CD3 conjugated to Alex Fluor 488 (Biolegend, 300320) at 1:50, CD4 BV510 (Biolegend, 317444) at 1:50, CD8 PE-CY7 (Biolegend, 344712) at 1:50 and CD69 APC (Biolegend, 985206) at 1:200 in 1× PBS with 1% BSA for 30 min at 4 °C in the dark. Flow cytometry was run on a CytoFlex Flow Cytometer (Beckman Coulter) and analysis was done with FlowJo (Becton, Dickinson and Company).

Following the 14 day T cell culture in the presence of no peptide or neoantigen peptides IFI44L-1 or IFI44L-2, 105 cryopreserved cells were sent to Adaptive Biotechnology for the ClonoSeq procedure. The resulting ~20,000 TCRB sequences were sorted by ‘template frequency’ and the top 4 TCRBs in each sample are illustrated in Fig. 5j with CDR sequences of the most enriched one.

TCR pairs were sequenced from the same T cell cultures as the TCRB sequencing but using TIRTL35.

TCR nucleotide sequences were synthesized (Twist) and cloned in the MSGV1 retrovirus backbone by Gibson Assembly (Telesis Bio). The sequence was codon-optimized for expression in human cells. The human TCR constant regions were exchanged for mouse TCR constant regions with substitutions to enhance surface expression and promote preferential pairing70,71. TCR retroviral supernatants were generated by co-transfection of 293GP cells with the MSGV1 vector containing the relevant TCR sequence and RD114 plasmid. Two days after transfection the retroviral supernatants were completed and either used fresh or frozen at −80 °C. Transductions were performed on RetroNectin-coated plates (Takara) as previously described using a modified T-FINDER35 cell line modified to express both human CD8 and CD4 coreceptors. Murine TCRβ constant region expression was assessed by flow cytometry to determine transduction efficiency.

Transduced T-FINDER cells (5 × 104) were cocultured with 1 × 105 patient B- lymphoblastoid cell lines pulsed overnight with 10 µg ml−1 of the indicated IFI44 15-mer peptides or a pool of 10-mer peptides spanning the IFI44 coding sequence in 96-well U-bottom plate. After overnight culture, the percentage of GFP+ cells within the murine TCRβ-expressing population was quantified by flow cytometry.

Neutrophils from healthy donors, and patients with rheumatoid arthritis or SLE were seeded onto glass-bottom 96-well plates and incubated at 37 °C for 30 min to adhere to the plate. Cells were then fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde for 15 min, followed by 3× PBS washes and blocked with 10% normal goat serum overnight at 4 °C. Neutrophils were incubated with perforin 4G10 antibody (1:20 dilution) overnight, washed three times with PBS, and then stained with goat anti-mouse IgG AF647-conjugated secondary antibody (ThermoFisher Scientific, A-21236; 1:1000 dilution) and DAPI (ThermoFisher Scientific, 62248) for 45 min. After three additional PBS washes, cells were resuspended in PBS. Images were captured using a Keyence BZ-X810 fluorescence microscope and analysed with Keyence Analyzer software. Control conditions included cells stained with primary antibody only and secondary antibody only in healthy, rheumatoid arthritis and SLE neutrophils.

ENCODE short hairpin RNA (shRNA)-seq datasets generated in K562 cells were used to assess potential effects of RNA-binding proteins (RBPs) on cryptic splicing72. Only paired-end, strand-specific polyadenylated mRNA libraries were included. Reads were aligned and alternative splicing events were quantified as described above. SLE-defined cryptic events were matched to ENCODE-derived splicing events using genomic coordinates. Events with at least one supporting read were retained for analysis. Each shRNA knockdown (KD) sample was paired with its matched non-targeting control samples. Control matching was performed at the sample level, and only explicitly matched control samples were used for each KD replicate. For each cryptic splicing event and RBP, knockdown effects were evaluated using a replicate-aware, read-based framework. Let KDi denote the cryptic-associated read metric for the ith KD biological replicate and let Ci denote the set of matched control samples for that replicate. A replicate-level effect size was defined as

Each biological replicate contributed one independent estimate of knockdown-induced cryptic splicing change. For each event–RBP pair, replicate-level effects were summarized by the mean effect size and assessed for directional consistency across replicates. Candidate regulatory effects were defined as those supported by at least two KD biological replicates, with consistent directionality across replicates and a mean effect size >2 reads. Event-level results were subsequently aggregated at the RBP level to summarize the number of cryptic splicing events observed following RBP knockdown.

ENCODE eCLIP peak data generated in K562 cells were used to evaluate the physical association between RBPs and cryptic splicing events73. For each RBP, biological replicates were merged to obtain a single reproducible peak set. Peaks were filtered using stringent criteria, requiring both high statistical significance and binding enrichment (−log10 P value ≥3 and log2 fold enrichment ≥3), and only peaks with valid genomic coordinates were retained.

For each alternative splicing event, event-specific binding regions were defined to capture the genomic window where RBPs are most likely to influence splice-site choice. These regions were centred on the relevant splice junctions or exon bodies depending on event type (for example, donor or acceptor sites for alternative splice sites, exon boundaries for exon skipping, intron boundaries for intron retention), using a uniform ±300 bp window.

For each RBP, the observed number of target cryptic event regions overlapping at least one filtered eCLIP peak was calculated using bedtools intersect74, counting each target region only once. To assess whether the observed overlap exceeded random expectation, a shuffle-based null model was constructed. Cryptic event regions were randomly shuffled across the genome 1,000 times using bedtools shuffle. For each shuffle iteration, the number of overlaps between shuffled target regions and the RBP’s filtered peaks was computed, generating a null distribution of overlap counts. From this null distribution, the mean and standard deviation of expected overlaps were estimated. An empirical p-value was calculated as the proportion of shuffled overlap counts greater than or equal to the observed overlap count, with a pseudocount added to avoid zero values. A z-score was computed to quantify the deviation of the observed overlap from the null expectation. To account for differences in overall binding abundance across RBPs, the total number of filtered peaks per RBP was recorded, and additional normalization metrics were derived, including peak density and a normalized enrichment score obtained by scaling the z-score by the square root of the peak count.

Empirical P values were adjusted for multiple hypothesis testing using the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure. RBPs were prioritized based on a combination of empirical significance, enrichment strength, and normalized enrichment. For enriched RBPs, event-level binding was further examined by intersecting filtered peaks with individual cryptic event regions. When multiple peaks overlapped the same event, peak-level statistics were summarized using the maximum log2 fold enrichment and maximum −log10 P value. These summaries were used for downstream visualization, event–RBP matrix construction, and network-based analyses.

We quantified differentially expressed genes and calculated gene expression normalized counts using DESeq2 (v1.36.0)75 with Wald test with correction for multiple comparisons using the Benjamini–Hochberg method. Independent categorical data were tested with the χ2 test, and nonparametric data were tested using the Wilcoxon rank sum test. Continuous data were correlated with Pearson’s test. All P values are two-sided and a cut-off of 0.05 was used for statistical significance.

#1387. Rangers midfielder Nico Raskin desperate to end his trophy drought by lifting the Premier Sports Cup

By CALUM CROWE, SCOTTISH DEPUTY CHIEF SPORTS WRITER

Published: 14:23 EDT, 1 November 2026 | Updated: 14:23 EDT, 1 November 2026

Rangers midfielder Nico Raskin insists he is desperate to finally end his own personal trophy drought after reaching the Premier Sports Cup final.

Raskin has been at Rangers for almost four years but is yet to actually lift any silverware, something which he does not seek to shy away from.

The Belgian midfielder missed the final of this competition in December 2023 due to injury as Rangers beat Aberdeen 1-0 – and therefore did not collect a winner’s medal.

After beating the Dons by the same scoreline at Hampden last night, Rangers are now through to next month’s final against Hibs as they aim to secure the first trophy of the season.

Raskin freely admits that the fact his trophy cabinet is still bare after almost four years is something which annoys him. But it is something he is determined to rectify.

‘I just want to go and win it,’ said the 25-year-old. ‘My family tell me I’ve won one (trophy), but I tell them I haven’t.

Rangers star Nico Raskin wants to make up for missing the 2023 Premier Sports Cup final

Manager Derek McInnes joins Raskin and his Rangers team-mates after their semi-final victory

Rangers striker Ryan Naderi celebrates scoring the winner against Aberdeen at Hampden

‘When we won this competition previously, I got rested for the first two games - and injured for the next two.

‘So that’s not me winning it. Yeah (it annoys me). I think I’ve been here a long time and we’ve worked so hard.

‘Not having that is difficult, but hopefully next month we’ll win one. I’m just happy to get to this final with full belief and I want to win that cup.

‘It’s top. It’s really good for the team. But now we want to win it and there’s one game to go. Now we go full force to win the cup.’

After almost leaving Rangers at various points over the past year, Raskin insists he is now fully focused on delivering success over the rest of this campaign.

He was made captain yesterday by Derek McInnes and was glad to repay the manager’s faith with a hard-fought victory.

Despite toiling to break down a stubborn Aberdeen side, Rangers finally broke through when Ryan Naderi stabbed home from close range with only seven minutes remaining.

If Rangers can go on and lift the cup in next month’s final, Raskin believes it could pave the way for further success this season.

‘Listen, it’s not going to be an easy season. It’s a long season,’ he said. ‘But the main thing is to keep focused and keep working towards the goal.

‘We need to keep believing in the manager and what we’re doing, then we’ll be there.

‘Things happen for a reason (in terms of what happened with transfer interest) and I’m looking forward to that game next month in the final.

‘Hopefully we can achieve something good this season that will lead us to a more exciting season.

‘Aberdeen gave us a difficult game. If you think you’re going to have an easy game, coming out and winning 4-0, you’re wrong.

‘The other team is coming with a plan and it’s a big game for them, also. It’s not easy to win football games. So you go out and give the best performance you can.

‘We won, so we’re very happy. In terms of the manager, he breathes Rangers and he gives that to us.

‘It’s so good to have someone like him driving us every day and on the pitch. I’m delighted for him and hopefully we can win it for him too.

‘He told us that it wasn’t going to be easy. That if we turn up and do everything we have to do, then we’d win the game.

‘We couldn’t come out with complacency and think it would be easy to score four goals. It’s a hard game that isn’t easy to win, so we have to enjoy it when we do.’

Arsenal are preparing to step up their pursuit of Bournemouth forward Eli Junior Kroupi in January, although Bayern Munich and Paris Saint-Germain are threatening to turn the race for the 20-year-old into one of the winter window’s biggest transfer battles.

Mikel Arteta wants another top-level forward as Arsenal attempt to compete for both the Premier League and Champions League, and Kroupi remains high on the club’s shortlist after an outstanding breakthrough campaign in England.

According to the Mirror, Arsenal want to make an attacking addition in January, with Kroupi among Arteta’s preferred targets.a

Bournemouth are reluctant to sell halfway through the season, while Bayern and PSG are also monitoring his situation.

Arsenal continue to admire Juventus winger Kenan Yildiz as well, but strengthening the central attacking positions is understood to be Arteta’s priority.

Kroupi scored 13 Premier League goals in his debut season, establishing himself as one of Europe’s most exciting young forwards before a serious foot injury interrupted his progress.

Bournemouth reportedly value him at around £80million, while PSG have previously shown strong interest.

Arsenal’s interest is long-standing. The Gunners regard Kroupi as a major long-term attacking target despite his injury setback, with Liverpool and Manchester United also monitoring him.

The youngster has earned major praise at Bournemouth. Former Cherries midfielder Joe Partington described him as one of “the world’s best teenage goalscorers”, while highlighting his movement, finishing technique and ability to score different types of goals.

Kroupi fits Arsenal’s recruitment model extremely well.

He is young, already proven in the Premier League and capable of operating centrally or from wider positions. His finishing ability would also give Arteta another genuine penalty-box threat without forcing the club to abandon its preference for younger players with significant development potential.

They have no urgent reason to sell, and competition from Bayern and PSG means Arsenal are unlikely to secure a bargain. Waiting until summer could make negotiations easier, but it could also allow Kroupi’s price to rise further.

That leaves Arsenal with a difficult decision.

If Arteta genuinely sees Kroupi as a long-term cornerstone of his attack, moving aggressively in January could make sense even at a premium price.

At 20, with 13 Premier League goals already behind him, Kroupi is not simply a prospect anymore. He is beginning to look like a player capable of helping Arsenal immediately while still offering enormous upside for the future.

#1385. Hearts 1 Hibs 2: Reedijk's first victory is one to remember as spirited Leith men battle back to see off rivals and reach Premier Sports Cup final

By JOHN MCGARRY, SCOTTISH CHIEF SPORTS FEATURE WRITER

Published: 13:25 EDT, 1 November 2026 | Updated: 14:33 EDT, 1 November 2026

If you are going to keep your supporters waiting until your fifth match in charge to record your first victory, best to make it a good one.

For Marink Reedijk and the Hibs fans, this pulsating triumph over their great rivals proved to be a classic case of better late than never.

By the end of a remarkable weekend, the fact the Easter Road side had dropped to the foot of the Premiership table wasn’t even so much as a mild concern.

Hibernian will return to Hampden in December 13 to face off against Rangers for the first major trophy of the season.

Just as significantly, they got there with a performance which was brave and brilliant.

After a difficult start to life in Leith, Reedijk belatedly announced his arrival with a storied victory.

McGrath fires home a rebound to put Hibs in front just before half time

Reedijk embraces goalscorer Boyle as he is substituted in the second half

Whatever happens next month against Derek McInnes’ side, Hibs have created history just by getting this far.

Their four previous jousts with Hearts at Hampden stretching back to 2006 had all ended in failure.

How those witnesses to those disappointments milked the moment at time up here as Sunshine on Leith echoed around the arena.

Reedjik’s men did not make life easy for themselves. They were behind inside four minutes when Claudio Braga struck.

Given how poor their league form has been of late, you wondered if it might get ugly. What did we know?

Hibs were scintillating until the interval, on the front foot and turning the game on its head through Martin Boyle and Jamie McGrath.

While they defended like their lives depended on it when Hearts came at them in the second half, they spurned chances to put the game to bed.

Not that they’ll care a jot about that now. Under Reedijk, they finally have lift-off.

This was a painful episode for Wouter Vrancken, the Hearts manager.

It was as if the dream start startled his players. They were never in control of the contest the minute Hibs dusted themselves down and got to work.

Braga faded from view and he was not the only one. There was an air of desperation to Hearts’ efforts long before referee David Dickinson put them out of their misery.

The truth is that all the best players on the day - Joe Newell, Owen Elding and Boyle chief among them - wore the green of Hibernian.

Accordingly, Hearts’ wait for a first League Cup since 1962 goes on.

The bookmakers had predicted a win for the Tynecastle side. The form book pointed towards it. And, after just four minutes, so did the scoreline.

Calvin Miller won and took a corner at the Hibs end which swung in viciously. Braga timed his run to perfection, ghosted into space and planted a header beyond Raphael Sallinger.

Braga gets free at a corner to head Hearts into an early lead at Hampden

After two own goals in his past two matches, Jason Kerr could have lived without the finger of blame pointing towards him.

On the sidelines, Reedijk looked on impassively. How would his side respond? In the best way imaginable, as it happened.

Rather than going into their shells, Hibs went on the attack and completely dictated the minutes up until the half-time whistle. To a man, they were simply outstanding.

Newell was at the heart of everything, demanding the ball in tight areas, finding passing angles which no one else could.

He played a cute pass to Felix Passlack. Goal-side of Malachi Fagan-Walcott, he forced Beau Reus into a low save.

Hearts’ cause certainly wasn’t helped by a couple of early withdrawals through injury.

Tomas Magnusson never recovered from a head knock he sustained in a clash with Kerr. Yan Dhanda shed his tracksuit.

Miller tried to run off a muscular injury that required treatment but was eventually replaced by Sabri Guendouz.

But there was more to the change in the game’s flow than just the personnel.

Hibs were far more secure in possession. They were more inventive. They looked more dangerous.

Adam Mayor’s pace took him to the line. His cut-back ended with Elding blazing over. But it encouraged the men in green and white.

Their equaliser on 19 minutes came after a period of control.

Newell’s pass into Elding was played with the perfect pace and direction. Elding’s flick around the corner was precise.

Running off Fagan-Walcott’s shoulder, Boyle got enough on his shot to prevent Reus’ touch keeping it out of the net.

Boyle squeezes his shot through Hearts goalkeeper Reus to bring Hibs level

Any concern among the Hibs fans that their celebrations would be cut short by VAR were ended when a still image showed Jordi Altena playing Boyle on by a couple of inches.

Hibs’ determination to stay on top extended to deserved bookings for Kerr and Josh Mulligan for taking out Dhanda and Stephen Kingsley. Altena was also carded for clipping Boyle.

Newell clipped the top of the crossbar with a drive through a packed penalty box.

Three minutes from the break, Newell was instrumental in the move which saw his side deservedly go up the tunnel ahead.

Boyle’s corner was headed clear by Jamie McCart. Newell took a brilliant touch to take Braga out of the game. His fizzing shot was blocked on the line by Fagan-Walcott. McGrath kept his nerve from four yards to stab the ball home.

Hearts had started well but completely dropped their levels. Braga did flash a header from a Josh McPake cross narrowly wide in injury time but an equaliser was ill-deserved at that point.

You sensed Vrancken would go through his players in the dressing room.

They were better after the turnaround. Laurent Mendy curled a shout just over while Braga raced clear and forced Sallinger to make a solid stop at his near post.

While Boyle did dart in from the left and force Reus to save, Hearts were asking more of the questions.

When Reedijk’s men came up for air, Elding’s hopes of nicking a third were thwarted by McCart’s slide tackle. Kerr also headed straight at Reus.

Sallinger did well to prevent Guendouz’s net-bound strike creeping in under his bar.

The Easter Road side take the acclaim of supporters after booking their spot in the final

With the game increasingly stretched, Kingsley made up the ground to deny Passlack.

What Hibs fans would have given for a third to seal the deal.

Thibault Klidje should have done so when he burst clear with seven minutes remaining. With better options to his right, he took the wrong one and fired harmlessly over. At least he worked the keeper with his next attempt.

Hibs battened down the hatches. Grant Hanley came on and, this week, there was no debate about what end of the field he’d be stationed.

When Braga headed a chance from a free-kick wide with a couple of minutes remaining, the maroon exodus began.

Wild horses couldn’t have dragged the Hibs supporters from the arena. How they savoured this.

#1384. Carrick’s United are in crisis and now spotlight is on Wilcox

Michael Carrick had urged his Manchester United players to come out and fight. But nobody could have imagined quite how Lisandro Martínez would interpret that message.

By the end of an extraordinary evening in Madrid, where United went 1-0 down inside a minute and never recovered against Atlético Madrid, Martínez had blown the lid off any pretence of all being well at the club as he launched a lacerating assault on the club’s executives.

United had come into this getting battered from all sides and when Pablo Barrios put Atlético ahead, Jamie Carragher’s pre-match assessment about how things could get “very messy, very quickly” for all involved at Old Trafford must have been ringing in the ears of the travelling supporters.

ATLETICO ARE AHEAD IN JUST 53 SECONDS! ⚡️ A nightmare start for United at the Metropolitano Stadium 😬 https://t.co/TdOwoXxopn

They certainly know how to make life difficult for themselves. Leny Yoro’s 74th-minute red card pretty much ended hopes of them taking something from the game.

Ademola Lookman scored Atlético’s second soon after and Carrick was staring at another defeat. And so they now move on to a big game at Leeds on Sunday. This was not the result Carrick would have wanted – and that is before what happened off the pitch.

Ademola Lookman PUNISHES a 10-man Man United 💥 https://t.co/GHKYIHGhNC

Another defeat intensified the pressure on Carrick but Martínez left nobody under any illusions that he felt the finger should be pointed not simply at another manager or the players, but the hierarchy above him.

It was extraordinary to see a player speaking out so publicly in this fashion against his own bosses.

But Martínez pulled no punches, even going as far as singling out Jason Wilcox, the director of football, as he criticised the club’s summer transfer business and effectively accused the club of failing Carrick and the players in the window.

To what extent Martínez’s comments mirror the views of the wider dressing room is unclear, but you have to wonder where Carrick and United go from here.

On the one hand, Martínez was providing a show of support for his manager by attacking the people above him. At the same time, he has presented Carrick with a disciplinary problem to address.

Lisandro Martínez did NOT hold back after United's loss to Atletico 😬👀 https://t.co/OGo25Pzd30

And United have enough troubles as it is without a senior member of Carrick’s dressing room turning so squarely against the club’s power brokers.

Martínez was probably only giving voice to what many fans have been saying since an underwhelming transfer window closed with more questions than answers. But for a player to talk in such blunt, excoriating terms resonated more loudly than anything a supporter or United’s most caustic critic could say.

The message was simple: you can sack all the managers you want but until you pull together a squad worthy of United’s name and give the man at the helm the tools to compete, the club will struggle to escape this cycle of mediocrity.

No one can reasonably argue United’s window was a success. They went into it with the hopes of landing Elliot Anderson and other premium midfielders but ended up going for numbers over proven quality or pedigree. Youri Tielemans, Andrey Santos and Carlos Baleba were not a trio of signings anyone expected at the start of summer, not even the club itself.

There were glaring issues to address in defence, not least at left-back, and at centre-forward but a quality alternative to Luke Shaw never materialised and no back-up was signed for Benjamin Sesko, who was missing for four months with a shin injury that has since resurfaced and which could keep him out for a while yet.

Having done so well to lead United to third and take them back into the Champions League, Carrick would have expected further backing than he got in the summer. Ever the company man, he has been too polite to criticise that lack of investment. But the cat is out of the bag now Martínez has had his say.

It now places the spotlight on Wilcox. United head to Elland Road on Sunday and that was the scene of Rúben Amorim’s final meltdown as manager. Two days after he blew up in a meeting with Wilcox at United’s Carrington training base, Amorim took aim at the director of football and others at the club, demanding they “do their job” and repeatedly declaring that he had come to Old Trafford to “be the manager, not to be the coach”.

It is remarkable to think that, 10 months on, United head back to Leeds with just as many questions as there were back then.

United’s worst start to a league season for 40 years has ensured Carrick is already under pressure, but Martínez is very much of the view that it is no longer enough for the manager and the players to keep carrying the can and that the credibility and suitability of those who recruit the players and make the decisions must now be called into question.

That Martínez picked this game to speak out was interesting. United, lost, yes, and the manner of Atlético’s opening goal from Barrios after 53 seconds was shocking. But United at least went down fighting on this occasion and had fashioned enough good chances to at least draw level before Yoro’s harsh 74th-minute red card swung a delicately poised match decisively in Atlético’s favour.

Lookman made it 2-0 soon after, but Atlético, having looked like they would run all over United in those opening 10 minutes, were made to work hard for their victory.

United cannot keep shooting themselves in the foot like they did in the first minute. Carrick had gone with a three-man midfield to shore things up and made his team more comfortable and yet they were opened up in double quick time by two passes through the middle.

Still, you only needed to look across at United’s opponents to appreciate how chaotic it had become at Old Trafford.

Diego Simeone’s reign at Atlético covers a period stretching two years longer than the post-Ferguson era and in many ways his teams have represented everything United have not been in that time: well constructed and thought through, unified, stable, organised, hungry, aggressive, uncompromising and with a flash of devilment.

If United were not in crisis before this, they are now.

Lisandro Martínez did NOT hold back after United's loss to Atletico 😬👀 https://t.co/OGo25Pzd30

[The performance] was a little bit mixed. It’s a tough enough place to come and the start we had put us in a difficult situation. I thought we grew into the game, had four big chances and [score one or more] and the game looks really different. They were really good chances.

And then the red card which I thought was a really poor one. It’s difficult after that. Disappointed that with the chances we had we didn’t [get] more [out of the game].

I haven’t seen [Martinez’s interview]. After a game like this you come here to try and get something from the game and you are disappointed and can be a little bit emotional. I have not seen it so I don’t think it is the right time for me to comment on it.

I fully know we all care and show that in different ways but now is the time to be together and work through. We have a big game on Sunday.

[What do you make of Lisandro’s comments?] I have no comment about that.

The only thing that’s going to get us back into it is to get a few wins.

It is very hard to say after a defeat that there are positives. We just have to work hard to keep working and keep trusting in our structure.

We have to keep working, keep trusting each other and be together on this.

I always wanted to be outspoken as a player but I think he’s gone too far. You can clearly see he cares and wants the club to invest more in new players but his performances have not been good enough. In some ways he’s right, the club needs to invest more. It looks like a bit of an agenda because it wasn’t a poor performance.

[How do you sum up the performance?] Really poor, Really poor. I have to control myself a lot. Sometimes it’s a mirror of the reflection of how our club is. We had a fantastic season last season but in order to compete we needed to buy more players. Many teams buy many players and Atletico Madrid did. They have an amazing team and deserved to win today.

I expected more. [Are you saying you expected more investment in the squad this summer?] Yes 100 per cent. I expect more from our technical director. I have to be honest. As players we have to do more but it is important to make a strong squad to be ready for for this kind of night.

In general, in general [should you have invested more in defence and attack given all the midfielders]. Last season we made a strong base to build an amazing team. It’s annoying and disappointing coming here and trying to get a result.

I don’t think so [was the manager backed?] He does his best. You can’t [live on] what you did last season. Every season is different. You can’t stay with what you did last season. The teams knows how you play, they know every detail, if you don’t change next season is a big problem.

It’s changing, changing, changing the manager [after a poor run]. But what about other areas? I can’t say more.

Tonight is it easy to say the coach, easy to say the players [are at fault]. But we have to look at other areas.

So far this season there have been more times when the performances have been worse than the results. This was the other way round but there is a sizeable quality gap between Carrick’s squad and the company they are keeping. They can point to a soft red card but they still shot themselves in the foot with their doziness in the first minute and squandering the good chances they created.

Manchester United have had their chances but they have lacked an elite or even merely decent finisher.

This feels a big moment for Carrick and United’s players to answer some of their critics. They have been getting battered from all sides in the last couple of days. Nicky Butt suggested on his podcast that Carrick told him before he got the United job that management “not for me” and “my head’s all over the shop” and that United was the only job he would take. At the very least, those comments are unhelpful and they are thought to have been dimly received internally.

Jamie Carragher offered a lacerating analysis of United’s performance against Spurs on Saturday on Sky Sports on Monday night and suggested things could get “very messy, very quickly” for all involved if there is not marked improvement. Steven Gerrard questioned why United opted to invest £50m of their summer budget in Andrey Santos, an unused substitute in the last three league games, insisted the back four was not good enough and questioned the work ethic.

And it was interesting to see Carrick alongside his mate Wayne Rooney just now pitchside. Rooney told the Stick to United podcast that captain Bruno Fernandes looks “fed up” and ready to explode at any moment.

It would have been pretty unthinkable for Carrick not to run with a three-man midfield here, not just because of the wide open spaces opponents have exploited this season but when you look at the back line United are fielding. Dalot at left back, two youngsters in Lenny Yoro and Ayden Heaven and a horribly out of form Lisandro Maríinez.

Nor has Senne Lammens looked convincing this term. Matheus Cunha has been dropped – not before time – and I expect to see Fernandes playing off the right. There’s going to a big onus on Rashford on the left. I’m not sure if he is fully fit but he’s going to be important.

It’s fantastic. It’s where we want to be, these games, these competitions. It’s as tough a place as you can come to. They’ve got a really good history in this competition and it’s where we want to come to challenge and test ourselves. We have put ourselves in this position, got a good start at home and now this is our first away game.

We want a reaction, of course. A positive reaction [to Saturday’s poor performance]. It hasn’t gone how we wanted, how we expected so far but it’s been fine margins in some of those games. It can go both ways but the reality is where we are at now.

It’s a fresh night and we’ve got to adapt, we’ve got to adjust in a positive way.

We want a little more control in the game [with three central midfielders]. At times we have been too open. We wanted to make a difference in that way. We’ve made other changes, certain spaces, certain positions.

To be honest it’s not really a big change of shape, personnel maybe but a lot of it is similar. We want more control, a little bit without the ball and a lot more with it. We’re happy with the way we set up.

Look at the last three goals we’ve conceded. They’re a mixed bag, simple goals you can something about. We need to defend better as a whole team .

Good evening and welcome to live coverage of the Champions League tie between Atlético Madrid and Manchester United from the Metropolitano. The two sides had contrasting fortunes in their opening fixtures in this competition, Man Utd beating Azerbaijan’s Sabah 4-0 at Old Trafford a month ago while Atléti were defeated by Liverpool who came back from 1-0 down to win 2-1.

But domestically it is the other way round – Michael Carrick’s side have made the club’s worst start in the league for 40 years with one win, three draws and two defeats and have been knocked out of the League Cup. Those of us who watch them regularly – purely because of occupational obligations in this instance – have been surprised by how poor they have been. The results have been bad but the performances even worse.

They seem to lack players who can play on the front foot, who have the athletic dynamism required in this league and too many self-indulgent forward players who either can’t be bothered to help out their team-mates or cannot concentrate long enough to do so. Spooked by their lack of pace in defence and midfield, they are hidebound by caution, dropping ever deeper, ever more reliant on counter-attacking despite the blatant disconnect between the front four and back six. If they drift through this match and Sunday’s trip to Elland Road, Carrick may join the long list of Ineos-driven managerial mis-steps.

Atlético have won six of eight in La Liga and have been defeated only once. They are five points behind Barcelona in second and have score 18 goals and let in eight, which may seem a curious thing to include in a preview but it is done to emphasise that many fans’ perception of Diego Simeone’s team are out of date. Back in the days of Diego Godín, Gabi, Juanfran et all, six wins a draw and a defeat would have had goals for of about 10 and goals against of maybe three.

Simeone is a martinet about attitude not systems or styles and his team have evolved, with the World Cup-winner Alex Baena, who has scored four goals so far, driving them on. He has reintegrated Julián Alvarez, too, after his brazen attempt to force a move to Barcelona so incensed Atléti fans that it seemed they would drive him out of the club. Simeone refused to let Alvarez get his own way and he is now buckling down. Ten years ago Simeone would have bitten his head off.

The one surviving veteran in the squad from that first of El Cholo’s Liga winning sides and the two Champions League finals, victory in which would represent Simeone’s crowning achievement, is the midfielder Koke. Remarkably, if he features today, the 34-year-old midfielder will be making his 750th first-team appearance as an Atlético player.

Manchester United have stepped up their preparations for 2027 by sending scouts to watch four Borussia Dortmund players, with Serhou Guirassy, Jobe Bellingham, Felix Nmecha and Daniel Svensson all emerging on their recruitment radar.

The quartet cover three areas United are assessing closely, centre-forward, central midfield and left-back, suggesting the club are already planning beyond the immediate January window rather than focusing on one position alone.

According to TEAMtalk, United scouts attended Dortmund’s 2-2 Bundesliga draw with Bayern Munich to monitor Guirassy, Bellingham, Nmecha and Svensson.

Guirassy, Bellingham and Nmecha are described as longer-term targets, while Svensson has more recently joined United’s shortlist as they search for additional options at left-back.

Guirassy remains particularly attractive because of United’s need for another reliable goalscorer. The 30-year-old has scored eight goals this season, although Dortmund are considered extremely reluctant to lose him midway through a title challenge.

Svensson, meanwhile, could provide a younger alternative on the left. The Sweden international has contributed two goals and one assist in 14 appearances this season and is under contract until 2029. Any move is currently viewed as more realistic next summer than in January.

Nmecha may be the most expensive of the four. Dortmund reportedly value him at around €100million in January, although an €80m release clause is expected to become active next summer.

CaughtOffside report on United’s interest in Nmecha also confirms that Liverpool are competing with United for the Germany international.

Watching four Dortmund players does not necessarily mean United intend to sign all of them. Instead, it shows how broadly the recruitment department is working.

Guirassy would offer an experienced striker capable of making an immediate impact, while Svensson could address a position United have repeatedly tried to strengthen.

Bellingham and Nmecha are exciting midfield options, but both would likely require enormous investment and United already have significant numbers in that area. That makes the other two particularly interesting.

Svensson fits the age profile of a long-term signing, while Guirassy could provide the short-term reliability United need in attack.

The key point is that this scouting mission appears to be about building options rather than preparing one imminent transfer.

With Dortmund challenging for major honours and under little pressure to sell, January deals will be difficult. But United’s presence in Munich shows the club are already laying the groundwork for what could become an important summer 2027 rebuild.

#1382. Derek McInnes will need to do more than 'win ugly' if he is to thrive as Rangers manager

By CALUM CROWE, SCOTTISH DEPUTY CHIEF SPORTS WRITER

Published: 13:55 EDT, 1 November 2026 | Updated: 14:39 EDT, 1 November 2026

There have been several Rangers managers over the past ten years or so who never quite seemed to grasp the most basic and fundamental parameters of the job.

You either win matches and win trophies, or you are deemed a failure. If you do not fulfil that remit, there is no mitigation that can be offered. No extra points for artistic merit.

It is a reality which never felt like it sat all that comfortably with the likes of Mark Warburton, Michael Beale, Philippe Clement, Russell Martin or Danny Rohl.

Derek McInnes has spoken repeatedly this season about the fact that winning matches is ultimately what underpins everything else.

Unlike many of his predecessors, McInnes knows what is expected of him, and he knows what will and will not be tolerated by supporters.

Even on days when his team do not play overly well and it turns into a grind, as was the case in this Premier Sports Cup semi-final against Aberdeen at Hampden yesterday, getting the win is all that matters.

Rangers boss Derek McInnes enjoys his team's Premier Sports Cup victory over Aberdeen

Rangers fans have never demanded silky free-flowing football. Even Walter Smith’s nine-in-a-row team would never be mistaken for prime Barcelona. But they were efficient, effective and relentless.

But here’s the rub. Rangers are too often a tough watch at the moment. Winning ugly is a valuable and necessary trait to have for any manager in the Ibrox hotseat, no question.

When it starts to become the default method, however, it becomes more of a concern. This is where McInnes is still searching for the right balance in this Rangers team.

In the early part of the season, he flip-flopped between various different systems: 4-3-3, 4-2-3-1, 3-5-2, before eventually settling on 4-4-2.

Perhaps it was the back-to-back victories over Celtic in September that cemented in his own mind the belief that 4-4-2 would be the way forward.

But there have been times recently when it has looked an awkward fit. It didn’t work at all against Hearts at Tynecastle last week as Rangers scraped a 2-2 draw.

And, despite eventually grinding Aberdeen into submission courtesy of a late winner from Ryan Naderi, it didn’t really work yesterday.

Aberdeen arrived short-handed, with five defenders missing through injury or suspension, and set up to make the evening as awkward as possible for Rangers.

By and large, Stephen Robinson’s side succeeded in doing exactly that. It was a performance which offered some signs of life despite their woeful form in the league.

But the reality for Robinson heading into next weekend’s home clash with Hibs is that he probably needs a win in order to save his job.

Aberdeen will also rue a massive opportunity that was squandered by Kevin Nisbet on 76 minutes when the score was locked at 0-0.

After Stuart Armstrong fed a pass into his path, Nisbet hesitated when the situation demanded that he hit it first time.

Striker Ryan Naderi celebrates with supporters after scoring the only goal of the semi-final

Rangers dominated possession and had 25 shots at goal, although the fact that only five of those were on target was described as ‘embarrassing’ by McInnes.

But it was often slow and disjointed. As was the case at Tynecastle, they completely bypassed midfield and went long to Naderi and his strike partner Kevin Kelsy, looking to then play off second balls.

You wonder what might be possible from this Rangers team if they were to go with three in midfield and really control games properly and play through the lines.

It’s not like they don’t have the personnel. Nico Raskin and Dan Neil are more than capable of getting the ball down and playing football.

But the overall balance of the midfield just doesn’t look right at present. Perhaps this was why McInnes tried to shake things up by dropping Neil and playing James Penrice in the middle of the pitch at Hampden.

RANGERS (4-4-2): Pandur 6.5; Sterling 5, Fernandez 6.5 (Godfrey 89), Makhanya 7.5, Rommens 6 (Neil 65); BOUANANI 7.5 (Curtis 89), Penrice 7, Raskin 6, Min-su 6 (Gassama 65); Naderi 7.5, Kelsy 6.5 (Chukwuani 89).

ABERDEEN (3-5-2): Muller 7; Devlin 6.5 (Marshall 89), Molloy 6.5, Milne 6.5; Gyamfi 3 (Armstrong 14), Ronan 6 (Smith 89), Lyons 6.5, Aremu 7 (Yogane 89), Guinness-Walker 7.5; Nisbet 4, Mouloua 5 (Ntelo 56).

Penrice, a left-back by trade, didn’t have a poor game by any stretch. After eventually reverting to his normal position when Neil came off the bench, he teed up the winner for Naderi.

But, playing him in midfield was a change that never really worked. It was a square peg in a round hole – and actually highlighted the lack of faith that McInnes has in some players.

Tochi Chukwuani and Vanja Dragojevic were signed for a total outlay of almost £9million. Chukwuani hasn’t started a game since the defeat to Jablonec and has been limited to substitute appearances.

Dragojevic also hasn’t featured from the start since the Jablonec game – and has made only one substitute appearance since then.

The word from Rangers is that the 20-year-old midfielder, who captained Partizan Belgrade, is a talent but still very raw. That’s fine. But he is not going to develop if he doesn’t play any football.

Chukwuani and Dragojevic were both signed for good money. The current system has cast them as bystanders. It is incumbent on McInnes as manager to nurture that talent.

All in all, this was an exercise in winning ugly for Rangers. There is, of course, a lot to be said for that. Especially in cup semi-finals, getting the job done is all that matters.

But when winning ugly starts to become the norm rather than a fallback, it is only natural that fans will start to question the style of play.

Badredine Bouanani was Rangers’ best player against Aberdeen. He was a constant menace to them, cutting in from the right on to his left foot.

Aberdeen striker Kevin Nisbet could not come up with the goal his team needed at Hampden

Minsu Kim probably had his poorest game yet in a Rangers jersey. But there’s no doubting his talent and the fact he’s a player around whom things should be built this season.

Ultimately, McInnes is still searching for the right balance. That search is visible in the selections and in the way the team plays.

A midfield that can control the tempo, progress the ball cleanly through pressure, and offer both defensive cover and creative outlets remains a work in progress.

This victory at Hampden demonstrated the progress being made in terms of a team who can grind it out, but also highlighted some of the limitations that remain in this Rangers team.

Winning ugly is a useful habit. Whether it can evolve into something more fluent on a consistent basis remains to be seen.

Whether midfielders purchased at considerable expense can be integrated rather than left on the periphery, and whether the long-ball tendency becomes a Plan B to fall back on or merely the default style of play – these are the issues that will define how this Rangers team develops under McInnes.
