with A = 4π2/Δk2. The screening of the Coulomb interaction is given by the dielectric function \({\epsilon }(q)=1+{v}_{{\rm{c}}}(q)D({\varepsilon }_{{\rm{F}}})\mathop{\Pi }\limits^{ \sim }(q)\)57,58, in which:

and rS is the Wigner–Seitz radius of graphene, kF = εF/(ħvF) the Fermi wavevector and D(ε) the density of states close to the Dirac point. This approximation holds for n ≥ nth = 1012 cm−2, thus if εF ≥ 37.14 meV, as in our case.

In this form, the scattering rate for electron–electron interaction is computationally extremely expensive. Therefore, we assume that the electron distribution for the second particle can be approximated by the equilibrium Fermi–Dirac distribution of the carriers:

This allows us to write a simplified expression for the electron–electron scattering rate:

in which we use that \({S}_{{\rm{ee}}}({\bf{k}},{{\bf{k}}}_{\ast },{{\bf{k}}}^{{\prime} },{{\bf{k}}}_{\ast }^{{\prime} })={S}_{{\rm{ee}}}({{\bf{k}}}^{{\prime} },{{\bf{k}}}_{\ast }^{{\prime} },{\bf{k}},{{\bf{k}}}_{\ast })\) and define:

In our simulations, we only focus on a small momentum space region around one of the six equivalent K points. In doing so, we neglect intervalley electron–phonon and electron–electron scattering processes, which are not expected to contribute notably in these conditions34. However, for electron–electron scattering, it is possible that an electron scatters from one state to another within the same valley by interacting with a charge carrier in a different one. For this reason, we effectively account for these processes by multiplying \({S}_{{\rm{ee}},\beta \beta {\rm{{\prime} }}}^{{\rm{eff}},1}\) and \({S}_{{\rm{ee}},\beta \beta {\rm{{\prime} }}}^{{\rm{eff}},2}\) by the number of equivalent K valleys, that is, six. To reproduce the experimental data, we assumed Veff = 4.386. It is important to notice that the dependence on the relative angle between k, k′, \({{\bf{k}}}_{\ast }\) and \({{\bf{k}}}_{\ast }^{{\prime} }\) determines the characteristic angular dependence of electron–electron scattering in graphene47, also termed collinear scattering41. Notably, at variance with the relaxation time approximation, our approach does not enforce any specific electron distribution at any time instant, while matching our experimental results.

To reduce the computational costs when relating the phase delay to an effective scattering time, a customary approach when solving the SBEs is to invoke the relaxation time approximation6,20,55,56. In this context, the scattering rate \({\varGamma }_{{\bf{k}}}^{\alpha }\) is assumed to be inversely proportional to a time constant, T1, associated with the mean free time between scattering events. Defining \({f}_{\alpha }^{(0)}({\bf{k}})\) as the equilibrium electron distribution in the α band, we obtain:

It is important to notice that, even though this approach allows us to extract an effective time constant, it is not enough to reproduce the experimental data. In fact, in this approximation, the scattering rate at a given point k in momentum space will only depend on the instantaneous electron distribution at that point and not on any other point in momentum space. This makes it impossible to reproduce any carrier redistribution dynamics in momentum space owing to, for example, the interaction with optical phonons.

The original works of Landau22, Zener23, Majorana24 and Stückelberg36 considered a two-state quantum system with an energy separation Δε = ε1(t) − ε2(t) = αt that changes linearly with time and undergoes an avoided crossing with a half gap energy δ. The diabatic transition probability is then given by26

with the diabaticity parameter \(\varGamma =\frac{{\delta }^{2}}{\hbar \alpha }\). This simple formula can be used to estimate the region in momentum space in which transitions occur in our experiment. The model is applicable under the condition that the characteristic sweep time through the transition, τ = 2δ/ε, is short compared with the oscillation period T = 2π/ω of the driving electric field. In this case, the field can be considered quasistatic during the transition and we simply have \(\alpha =2{v}_{{\rm{F}}}\hbar |{k}_{x}-K|=2{v}_{{\rm{F}}}|e|{E}_{0}\). With δ = vFħ|kx − K|, we obtain \(\tau =\frac{\hbar | {k}_{x}-K|}{|e|{E}_{0}}=\frac{\gamma }{\omega }\). Because γ ≈ 0.1, the crossing indeed occurs very fast (τ < 1 fs). For the peak electric field E0 = 1.57 MV cm−1, the diabaticity parameter \(\varGamma =\frac{\hslash {v}_{{\rm{F}}}}{2|e|{E}_{0}}{|{k}_{x}-K|}^{2}\,\cong \) \(210\,{{\rm{\mathring{\rm A} }}}^{2}{|{k}_{x}-K|}^{2}\) becomes smaller than 1/π for |kx − K| < 0.04 Å−2. In this region around the Dirac point, 1 − e−2 = 86% of the transitions from the valence band to the conductions band are expected to take place as long as Pauli blocking can be neglected. This region roughly coincides with the momentum area in which the conduction band of our doped graphene samples is occupied. This shows that transitions can only take place after the electrons have been accelerated away from the Dirac point. After several driving cycles, the observed dynamics of the doped and a hypothetical undoped sample are expected to be similar (Extended Data Fig. 8).

For an empty upper Dirac cone, we expect the carrier injection rate owing to LZM tunnelling to closely follow the magnitude of the electric field and the electron population to increase stepwise, with the highest injection rates occurring at the largest absolute field values. In an n-doped system and for high injection rates, as in the present experiment, Pauli blocking modifies this simple picture (Extended Data Fig. 5a). Electrons can only be injected when there is sufficient empty space in the conduction band near the K point. Consequently, intraband transport plays a decisive role in determining the injection timing. Carrier injection happens most efficiently during the intervals between the extrema of the electric field and the carrier displacement. Our simulations clearly show that this results in a phase delay between the population jumps and the field, which grows as more population has been transferred. Beyond the effects of Pauli blocking and scattering, the injection dynamics can be strongly influenced by quantum interference59. Here we find that they can cause a deviation of a step-like increase in the conduction band population (or electron distribution width) by transforming the plateau regions, following a strong injection phase, into local minima through destructive interference of electron wavepackets (Extended Data Fig. 9). Although the signal-to-noise ratio of the measured conduction band population does not allow us to resolve the jumps in the population during carrier injection experimentally, the dynamics of the increase of the carrier density can be well reproduced with the theory.

The simulations also show that the elongation of the conduction band electron distribution in momentum space is closely tied to the carrier population (Extended Data Fig. 5b). Notably, the weak oscillations in the width of the electron distribution, which are superimposed on the stepwise increase, become more pronounced with scattering (Fig. 4c). This effect is probably caused by a shortening of the effective injection time window. In the absence of scattering, the electron displacement follows the vector potential and is therefore phase-shifted by π/2 relative to the electric field. With scattering, the phase shift between the electric field and the displacement of the electrons shrinks, such that periods of rapid population increase occur only a few femtoseconds before an extremum in the displacement (Extended Data Fig. 5). Experimentally, the oscillation of the width of the electron distribution at twice the frequency of the driving field is clearly visible during the first three cycles of the electric field, that is, at times when there is still substantial carrier injection (Fig. 3c). The observed relative phase with respect to the electric field transient and the COM displacement agrees well with the simulations that include scattering. The data thus support the picture of a well that is periodically driven by the electric field and opened and closed by the oscillating carriers in the conduction band.

The new experimental platform presented here was developed to give direct access to strongly driven electron dynamics without relying heavily on theory or models. This philosophy also translates to data processing: our conclusions only rely on features present in the raw data. The previously described streaking compensation is the first and only step in the data analysis pipeline that is required to ensure that the observed dynamics can be attributed to processes that are happening in the solid and not the vacuum. Following that, the general strategy is that filtering is only used to remove technical noise and signals related to the matrix elements before the data are analysed or to enhance visibility in the figures. To ensure full transparency, the following contains a summary of all notable data processing steps for the presented figures.

The raw data from the delay line detector are binned with a spacing of 0.084 eV × 0.022 Å−1 × 0.022 Å−1 for the data in Fig. 1 and with a spacing of 0.084 eV × 0.011 Å−1 × 0.011 Å−1 for all other photoemission data.

The 3D data in Fig. 1c are symmetrized to remove the decrease in photoemission intensity caused by the angle of incidence of the XUV pulse.

The 2D momentum maps in Fig. 2a are obtained by integrating the 3D data within an energy window of 0.33 eV around distinct energy levels (0.25 eV, −0.25 eV, −0.75 eV, −1.25 eV, −1.75 eV). Before plotting, the data are further processed to enhance the visibility in the figure. First, a 1D simple moving average along both momentum axes (window size: 0.08 Å−1) is applied to the data four times. The filtered data are further processed by a 2D curvature filter described by equation (11) of ref. 60 with C0 = 0.2. Finally, a 2D median filter with window size 0.045 eV × 0.045 Å−1 is applied three times to clean up numerical noise.

The band structure cuts in Fig. 2b are obtained by integrating the 3D data within a momentum window of 0.08 Å−1 around kx − K = 0. Before plotting, the data are further processed to enhance the visibility in the figure. First, a 1D simple moving average along the energy and momentum axes with window sizes of 0.59 eV and 0.08 Å−1, respectively, is applied four times. The filtered data are subject to a 2D curvature filter with C0 = 0.2. Finally, a 2D median filter with window size 0.34 eV × 0.045 Å−1 is applied three times. The raw data are shown in Extended Data Fig. 2b.

The applied field transient and current in Fig. 2c are extracted from the raw data as laid out in Methods sections ‘Electric field waveform reconstruction and streaking compensation’ and ‘Current extraction and Fourier analysis of the phase delay’. Before plotting, a 4-THz high-pass filter is applied to the data to remove slowly varying offsets. The data showing the increase of the carrier population in the conduction band were acquired under almost identical experimental conditions in which special care has been taken to align the MIR polarization such that the electric field exhibits no perpendicular component leading to coherent oscillations of the integrated photoemission intensity.

The 2D momentum maps in Fig. 3a are obtained by integrating the 3D data for energies higher than 170 meV. This energy level is chosen to minimize contributions of the valence band caused by the limited energy resolution of the setup. Before extracting the COM displacement and width, a Gaussian filter with a small window size 0.02 Å−1 × 0.02 Å−1 has been applied to the 2D data. We applied the same filter to the experimental 2D data for a better comparison between experiment and theory. For the theory data, this is necessary to reduce numerical or binning artefacts. Owing to its small window size, the filter does not change or remove any of the features retrieved for data analysis.

To extract the COM motion and change of the width of the carrier distribution shown in Fig. 3b,c, the plotted 2D maps are integrated along kx and ky. For the data along ky, a Gaussian distribution with a constant offset (accounting for the background) is fitted to the integrated distribution. For the data along kx, the previously constant offset is modified with a linear decrease for growing kx values to account for the decrease in background caused by the photoemission matrix element. The mean of the extracted fit for the ky distribution is used to characterize the COM motion. Before plotting, a 15-THz high-pass filter is applied to these data to remove a slowly varying offset. The change of the standard deviation, Δσ, of the extracted fits is used to characterize the change of the width of the carrier distribution along kx and ky.

The 2D momentum maps in Fig. 4a are obtained by integrating the simulated population of the conduction band and applying a Gaussian filter with a small window size of 0.02 Å−1 × 0.02 Å−1 to the 2D data, as described above for the data shown in Fig. 3a.

The extraction of the simulated current density and change of the width of the carrier distribution shown in Fig. 4b,c follows the procedures outlined for the experimental data.

a, A Yb:KGW oscillator seeds two Yb:KGW amplifiers, each providing a pulse energy of 1.5 mJ at a repetition rate of 50 kHz. Half of the output of one amplifier is upconverted to 400-nm pulses with a pulse duration of 20 fs, which are then used to generate sub-10-fs XUV pulses by high-harmonic generation in argon (left side). In parallel, widely tunable, intense, few-cycle and CEP-stable MIR pulses are generated by difference frequency generation (DFG) of the outputs of a dual-branch OPA, which is supplied with the remaining half of the output of the first amplifiers (middle). The output of the second amplifier is used to almost exclusively pump the last amplification stage in the dual-branch OPA. Furthermore, a NOPA generates 10-fs-long NIR pulses (right side), which can be used to detect the MIR waveforms (EOS). Finally, all beams are guided into the UHV chamber of the momentum microscope, in which they are spatially overlapped. b, Generated XUV spectrum. The intense seventh harmonic order centred around 57 nm is selected by multilayer mirrors (grey shaded area) and is used as a probe pulse in the subcycle momentum microscopy experiments. c, Typical MIR waveform measured by EOS.

a, Photoemission spectra in different streaking conditions. The first two panels show a band-structure snapshot taken in equilibrium (left panel) and a snapshot with strong streaking along ky by the s-polarized MIR field (middle panel). The electric field is reconstructed by matching the streaked band structures to the equilibrium case. Once the electric field is known, the streaking effects can be compensated (right panel). The dashed black lines are a guide to the eye representing the equilibrium band structure. Applying the calculated shifts along energy and momentum, according to the extracted field from the middle panel, to the dashed black line yields the solid black line. b, Unfiltered version of the data shown in Fig. 2, showing the raw photoemission data after streaking compensation.

Simulations based on the SBEs in relaxation time approximation reveal how the phase delay between an applied waveform (central frequency, 30 THz) and the lightwave-driven current scales with the scattering time. For very small scattering times, the phase difference converges to zero, whereas for longer scattering times, it converges to π/2. The strongest change in the phase delay can be observed for scattering times on the order of a half-cycle of the driving waveform.

Simulated 2D carrier distribution in the conduction band for selected delay times without scattering. a, Interband coupling switched off. b, Interband coupling switched on. It causes a large elongation of the carrier distribution along the polarization of the driving light field, filling the gap between the displaced electrons distribution and the K point.

a, Normalized carrier density in the conduction band extracted from our theory model with electron–phonon and electron–electron scattering (black curve) and from experimental data (grey curve). The observed difference in the number of extra carriers between theory and experiment is to be expected, as the theory does not account for inherent constraints of the measurement itself, such as matrix element effects. The population rises fastest during the time window between a maximum of the field (red curve) and the COM displacement (green curve). b, During the first few cycles, the evolution of the width of the electron distribution (green curve) closely follows the population dynamics (black curve).

Simulated 2D carrier distribution in the conduction band for selected delay times without scattering in the weak-field and strong-field regimes. The interaction regime is defined by means of the Keldysh parameter for an energy gap corresponding to single-photon absorption. a, The weak-field regime is reached by using fields that are 200 times weaker than in the experiment. Here the interaction is dominated by perturbative absorption, which is strongly affected by the selection rules owing to the pseudospin texture of graphene. By removing the doping, the first row highlights how this leads to a population increase in regions perpendicular to the polarization of the light pulse. The second row depicts the situation with the same doping level as in the experiment. Here no change in the population can be resolved, even when exaggerating the colour map by a factor of 2,500. b, In the strong-field regime, the interaction with light is characterized by a unidirectional elongation of the electron distribution parallel to the electric field as well as a displacement of the Fermi surface.

a, Illustration of the distribution of bandgaps Δ and the varying Keldysh parameter γ in graphene. b, Simulated 2D change of the population in the conduction band (blue curve) and aspect ratio of the carrier distribution (red curve) after interacting with the electric field for different field strengths in an undoped sample without scattering. For Keldysh parameters γ ≫ 1, the number of excited carriers scales quadratically with the field (grey curve), indicative of single carrier absorption. At the same time, the aspect ratio of the carrier distribution shows that the distribution is broader along the momentum direction perpendicular to the light field (left inset). In the strong-field regime (γ ≪ 1), the number of excited carriers is trending towards saturation, indicative of light-field-induced tunnelling as the transition mechanism. Simultaneously, the aspect ratio of the carrier distribution inverts, resulting in the elliptical distribution observed in the experiment with broadening in the direction parallel to the applied field (right inset). The extracted sub-quadratic scaling of the excited carrier density for the field strength used in the experiment (grey shaded area) indicates that perturbative single-photon or multiphoton absorption does not play a substantial role in the interaction.

Simulated 2D carrier distribution in the conduction band for selected delay times without scattering and different doping levels. a, No doping. b, Moderate doping. c, High doping. Intrinsic (a) and the moderately doped graphene (b, Fermi level 200 meV) closely resemble each other. Higher doping levels (c) reveal the difference between the intraband and interband signatures.

Simulated 2D carrier distribution in the conduction band for different dephasing times. a, T2 = 0.1 fs. b, T2 = 1 fs c, T2 = 5 fs. d, T2 = 500 fs. The 2D carrier distribution is shown after the first (left panel) and second (middle panel) cycles. For very fast dephasing, the efficiency for LZM transitions decreases substantially, manifesting in a lack of additional carriers in the second panel of a. For very slow dephasing, signatures of LZSM interference emerge after the second cycle (fishbone pattern in the second panel of d). They manifest in a modulation at the second harmonic of the driving field in the elongation of the electron distribution along the direction parallel to the electric field (right panel), as highlighted in the inset by its Fourier transform during the first half-cycles of the driving field (grey area). The scale of the vertical axis is fixed across the insets.

Simulated 2D carrier distribution in the conduction band for selected delay times with different scattering contributions. a, No scattering. b, Only electron–electron scattering. c, Only scattering with optical phonons. d, Combination of electron–electron scattering and scattering with optical phonons.

Lightwave-driven dynamics in graphene. The video shows the subcycle dynamics of lightwave-driven graphene in the vicinity of the K point. On the left side, the electron population in the conduction band is shown, whereas the right panel shows a cut through the band structure at the K point. The field-induced asymmetry in the number of carriers with positive or negative momenta testifies to a macroscopic lightwave-driven current. Meanwhile, the emerging elliptical shape of the electron distribution in momentum space highlights the presence of LZM tunnelling into the conduction band. For late delay times, the electron distribution becomes circular again and relaxes back to its original shape by scattering.

#1374. Man City dismantled by PSG in breathless Champions League battle

When Manchester City play like this what a loss their football will be to the Premier League – and the Champions League – if they are heavily sanctioned later this season.

In what turned out to be a match for the ages, a night of brilliant, unbridled attack, we were treated to the ultimate game of two halves as the back-to-back European champions Paris St-Germain took City apart for 45 minutes. And then were left holding on.

City will hope this is a sign of what is to come in their Premier League fight. But with a different result. After suffering a resounding defeat at the hands of the Premier League’s independent commission, with 114 of the 115 charges against them proven, they maintain their innocence and are mounting an appeal.

Could they make a comeback? It would be incredible and highly improbable if they did so but, out on the pitch, and 3-0 down after a first half in which they were in danger of being humiliated by PSG, they created enough opportunities to save themselves.

The data backed that. City’s expected goals (xG) was 2.57 while PSG’s was 1.83. City had 27 shots to 15 and had more possession and more passes. Enzo Maresca made a triple substitution to devastating effect, especially with the introduction of new signings Ayyoub Bouaddi and Iliman Ndiaye.

In the end they clawed back two goals, both scored by Erling Haaland, who now has 61 in 60 games in this competition – seventh outright in the all-time list, before Ruud van Nistelrooy. And 37 of those for City, overtaking Sergio Agüero’s club record.

Erling Haaland gets his second of the night, and the game could be back on 🔥 📺 Stream on TNT Sports & HBO Max https://t.co/sFZ0eT2Egz

It could have been a hat-trick. It could even have been four as Haaland, taking the captain’s armband as Rúben Dias was withdrawn during the interval, clipped the top of the crossbar with a header and then was denied by goalkeeper Matvei Safonov as the striker slid in.

“Even with 3-0 in the first half, with the amount of chances we created in the second half, we deserved more. Luis [Enrique, PSG’s coach] said at the end of the game that they were quite lucky,” Maresca claimed before being asked whether he would relish facing PSG again, later in this competition. “My feeling is we are there. We are close,” he added.

Did City deserve a draw? No one was predicting that at half-time as they were suffering as comprehensive a defeat as was inflicted by the commission. Accused of “sham” contracts to inflate income, this was a sham of a performance, made all the more emphatic because of how brilliant PSG, and their exceptional 21-year-old winger Désiré Doué, were.

Désiré Doué with a brilliant finish from range to give PSG an early lead in Manchester 😮‍💨 📺 Stream on TNT Sports & HBO Max https://t.co/Uwilx7I37H

There is a certain irony that it was PSG who inflicted this defeat, ending City’s run of eight wins from eight in all competitions under Maresca.

It was a meeting of two clubs empowered more than any other by the riches of Gulf states: Abu Dhabi versus Qatar. Both have also had their run-ins over money. Both were sanctioned, but escaped full bans by Uefa for breaching financial fair play rules.

The question, also, was: would the eighth meeting of these clubs in the Champions League in the last 11 seasons be the last for some time?

So we should savour it and we did. That included Pep Guardiola on his first return to the Etihad – in a sign of solidarity – after quitting at the end of last season. Not that he savoured much of what he saw as PSG dominated City to such an extent that their fans adopted the “Poznan” celebration and the home supporters were silenced.

City could have gone in front before they conceded with the erratic Safonov – who was Gianluigi Donnarumma’s understudy and has become his unlikely replacement – punching a corner against his own crossbar before Antoine Semenyo shot the rebound over.

Then PSG ran all over City. They broke far too easily and scored far too easily. Not once, but twice, to go 2-0 up.

For the first, PSG countered, with City struggling to cover, and Doué caught out Donnarumma with a low shot inside his right-hand post from 22 yards.

Then PSG sliced through City’s defence with Ousmane Dembélé scooping the ball across the area to Doué who returned it back. Dembélé stooped to head home.

Ousmane Dembélé doubles PSG's lead just 2 minutes after they scored the first 🤯 📺 Stream on TNT Sports & HBO Max https://t.co/MxhJ3oCWpC

After Achraf Hakimi headed against the inside of a post and City could not clear, the ball came back with Warren Zaïre-Emery flicking on Maghnes Akliouche’s cut-back. It ran to Vitinha who slammed in a first-time shot. It was the first time City had ever conceded three goals at home in the first half of this competition.

Vitinha with a BEAUTY to put PSG three up after just 30 minutes 🥵 📺 Stream on TNT Sports & HBO Max https://t.co/vgqkI6kI3h

Maybe it was too easy. Maybe City could not continue to be so dominated but it was as if a switch was flicked when the teams returned. The chances came for City. Enzo Fernández should have scored from a close-range header and Haaland did, glancing in an inswinging Ndiaye cross.

Finally the City fans found their voices but then they were silenced. What a calamity for Donnarumma as he got a hand to Akliouche’s shot on the turn, but only palmed the ball up in the air before it bounced into the net.

But City did not stop. Nuno Mendes headed Josko Gvardiol’s flick off the line, Fernández hit a post before Bouaddi set up Haaland and he swept the ball past Safonov.

There was time for PSG to miss a penalty, with Donnarumma comfortably saving Ferran Torres’s weak effort as City bravely continued to push. They lost, but it did not quite feel like that.

Pep Guardiola, wearing a flat cap, has taken his seat in the Manchester City directors’ box, directly behind chief executive Ferran Soriano and director of football Hugo Viana. It is of course his first game back at the club after quitting as manager in the summer. It is also a declared show of solidarity after the guilty verdict.

It’s a special night against the best team in Europe, I hope it’s a special game. Pep is here but was not at the training ground. I have not spoken with him.

Under normal circumstances there would be a high level of anticipation around this game, even though it is the eighth time in 11 seasons that City and PSG have faced each other in the Champions League. But given the backdrop of City guilty verdict and it being the first home fixture since that announcement it is even more fascinating. There will also be, of course, Pep Guardiola back “in his house”, as his successor, Enzo Maresca. put it. The atmosphere will be interesting.

If the verdicts are upheld, of course, it wasn’t their penthouse and it wasn’t their caviar.

We got to live in a penthouse and eat caviar for 15 years and if we have to go back to a semi in the suburbs, well, fine.

When Manchester City endured their first major sanction over financial fair play in 2014, the biggest club accused alongside them that summer were Paris St-Germain, another Champions League arriviste who had been raised from mediocrity to the elite by some frantic spending from a Middle East fossil fuel dynasty.

Then, 12 years ago, both sides bitterly opposed the Uefa sanctions imposed on them – although they eventually agreed to the terms. Now, they face one another in Manchester with PSG aiming for a third consecutive Champions League title, and City fighting for their lives in the face of an overwhelming guilty verdict for nine years of Premier League rule-breaking.

Both clubs are transformed from the entities that their current owners acquired. While PSG now find themselves at the centre of the new order in European football, City are once again on the outside.

Whatever the outcome of this process, I won’t forget the connection and relationships I had here. It will never be erased.

Good evening, and welcome to live coverage of the Champions League tie between Manchester City and Paris St-Germain, champions in 2025 and 2026 and favourites to become only the fourth club, after Real Madrid (who have done it twice), Ajax and Bayern Munich to win a hat-trick of European Cups.

After Manchester City’s conviction by an independent commission on 114 charges of financial malpractice in contravention of Premier League rules, finding the right tone to use to cover their matches during their appeal is difficult. While they are in limbo, the rest of English football is in purgatory and although Gary Neville, the Pope of Pilsworth, in unsurprisingly hyperbolic fashion has said he would prefer not to cover City’s games in future, that is not an indulgence a serious news organisation would countenance. They have to be covered and the issues addressed.

Having said that, in this format of a rolling report on the old minute-by-minute template, I think we have to cover the controversy and its implications in the whole during the build-up and keep an eye on reaction and references to it during the run of play. But I don’t think it would serve anyone to take the stance during the live coverage that anything that is happening on the field is unimportant, redundant and ultimately void because of the guilty verdicts, and hence adopt a flippant tone. I propose once the match starts to treat it as a match while not ignoring the context.

Right, let’s get stuck into the Gulf State sovereign wealth fund derby… sorry, imposible to resist.

PSG have made a slow start to their Ligue 1 campaign, their worst since Luis Enrique’s first season in charge. Starting with two draws and a defeat, they have rallied with three successive victories to climb up to sixth as the head coach, as he tends to do in the league, rotates his midfielders and forwards like crazy, to whose ranks he has added the World Cup-winner Ferran Torres. The summer signing scored a hat-trick in his Champions League debut for the club, a 6-1 mauling of Slovan Bratislava.

City, too, started their European campaign with a win, Erling Haaland scoring both goals in the 2-0 victory over Porto at the Dragao and you won’t need me to remind you that they have won all six of their Premier League games to lead Arsenal by three points at the top of the table.

#1373. After Robbie Fowler claimed the moon landing is 'bulls***' and dubious Joe Cole said he has 'questions' for Neil Armstrong... who makes our ultimate XI of football conspiracy theorists?

Published: 02:00 EDT, 1 November 2026 | Updated: 15:15 EDT, 1 November 2026

Robbie Fowler certainly helped to draw attention to his new podcast with his former Liverpool and England team-mate Steve McManaman this week by airing his views on the 1969 moon landing.

After answering fan questions ranging from favourite films, comedians and useless talents, Fowler responded to McManaman's prompt of the moon landing as a conspiracy theory.

'I think the moon landing is bulls*** to be fair,' with an excited McManaman declaring 'that is a massive one,' before declaring his subsequent reasoning made 'perfect sense'.

He is far from the only footballer to have doubts, with another ex-England international Joe Cole declaring he would like to sit down with Neil Armstrong – who died in 2012 – to get to the bottom of it.

Fowler later quipped he is 'not a flat earther' having been up on a plane. However, some former footballers are, while others have raised a wide range of conspiracies, ranging from the small scale to the more wild.

Here, Daily Mail Sport puts together our ultimate XI of football's conspiracy theorists.

Former Liverpool forward Robbie Fowler admitted this week he believes the moon landing is 'bulls***' Source: YouTube - We'll have a look podcast

For many, David Icke is football's original conspiracy theorist – so entrenched in his off-the-wall beliefs and so willing to share them publicly that he is more widely known as a crackpot than a goalkeeper.

Nevertheless, Icke turned out for Coventry City's youth set-up between the sticks in the late 1960s, and later played for semi-professional outfit Hereford United before hanging up his boots and pivoting to sports journalism.

While his playing career might have been small-fry, his commitment to conspiracy theories is Premier League. Among his often-cited beliefs is the idea that an inter-dimensional race of reptile-like shape-shifters – the 'Babylon Brotherhood' have infiltrated the upper echelons of global society.

Among the accused are the late Queen Mother, the Rockefeller and Rothschild families, and former Prime Minister Edward Heath, whose eyes, Icke alleged, he saw turn 'jet black' when the pair met in 1989.

Icke also believes that the 'Illuminati' at the top of the global food chain organised world events including Dunblane, 9/11, the assassination of John F Kennedy, the death of Princess Diana to prompt their subsequent responses. Less laughable is the thick seam of anti-Semitism which critics believe runs through his thinking, although Icke has denied this.

For many, David Icke is football's original conspiracy theorist, with one of his cited beliefs is the idea that reptile-like shape-shifters have infiltrated the upper echelons of global society

Javi Poves endured a similarly unmemorable professional playing career in Spain, but did at least register one La Liga appearance with Sporting Gijon. Then, he quit. It was a matter of principle: he had grown to believe that 'professional football is only money and corruption'. Not an unreasonable view point, from some perspectives, but years on from his 2011 resignation things become somewhat more surreal.

Poves joined lower-division Madrid club Mostoles Balompie in 2016 and later became the club's president. In 2019, he renamed the club Flat Earth FC, to draw attention to his primary cause.

'Football is the most popular sport and has the most impact worldwide, so creating a club dedicated to the flat earth movement is the best way to have a constant presence in the media,' he said that year.

'Flat Earth FC is the first football club whose followers are united by the most important thing, which is an idea.'

Although Poves has since moved to fellow amateur side CDC Moscardo, he remains passionately committed to the idea that the earth is flat and not round, and other environmentally-rooted conspiracy theories. These include viewing 'chemtrails' as a deployment of toxic chemicals, and refusing to believe that suncream can help prevent skin cancer.

One thread which runs through a number of players included in the XI is a scepticism of Covid-19. Some, like Sol Campbell, have suggested that the pandemic was in some way man-made. Icke is in the camp which believes that the lockdown and vaccination scheme was akin to governmental 'facism'.

Lovren was firmly in team Icke during the lockdown years, posting a number of his videos on social media. He also used social media to attack Microsoft billionaire Bill Gates, implying some kind of conspiracy with his comment: 'Game over Bill. People are not blind' on Gates's online tribute to health workers.

The Croatian defender seemed particularly swayed by Icke's theories around the links between Covid-19 and 5G technology in 'controlling' populations, with Lovren resharing clips with the caption 'we will not be censored'.

Dejan Lovren supported Icke's views during the pandemic and hit out at Bill Gates

Lovren took to Instagram to promote an interview with Icke during the pandemic

As mentioned in Lovren's section, Campbell also had his suspicions during the Covid-19 pandemic. Then managing Southend United, in May 2020, Campbell appeared to suggest that he believed the disease was made deliberately and designed to target certain population groups.

'Was this virus a natural mistake or a designed mistake...?' he posted on social media. 'I wonder does this virus deliberately attacks a certain blood type.....?'

Campbell shared his idea alongside a screenshot of an article citing an ONS report that showed Black people were four times more likely to die from Covid-19 than any other ethnic group. He later was widely derided for having no scientific evidence to support his argument.

Sol Campbell appeared to suggest in 2020 he believed Covid-`9 was made deliberately and designed to target certain population groups

Campbell shared his idea alongside a screenshot of an article citing an ONS report that showed Black people were four times more likely to die from Covid-19 than any other ethnic group

The former Manchester City defender has previously admitted to a conspiracy theory that has more sympathetic readers nodding in approval: he believes in ghosts.

Delph admitted in 2016 that he sees ghosts 'all the time', adding that 'genuinely' he had seen about 'four'.

'When I first signed for (Aston) Villa I stayed in a hotel there was lots of things moving in the room, a lot of bangs,' he told Man City's official YouTube channel.

'And about four months ago I saw, in my house in God's country (Yorkshire), I saw two ghosts in my bedroom.'

'I don't think they're there to harm me. But I've definitely seen them. It was just a split second and then they were gone.

'The one four months ago, that actually was carrying a body, it went out onto my balcony, then disappeared.'

Joe Cole admitted he is open to having his head turnedabout the moon landings and would be keen to sit down with Neil Armstrong to 'get to the bottom of things'

Compared to how some of the other members of Daily Mail Sport's XI have at times risked public safety or aired unpleasant and divisive views, Cole's position on the 1969 Moon Landings feels somewhat milquetoast.

Additionally, unlike many, he admitted that he is open to having his head turned, with Cole keen to sit down with Neil Armstrong, the first man on the moon, to 'get to the bottom' of things.

'I'm not sold either way and I need some convincing. I want to believe it, honestly,' Cole told FourFourTwo. 'But I've heard too much about it being fake - things like the flag waving and the footprints and all the rest of it.

'I would love to sit down with a man who actually went there and be convinced. I want him to tell me exactly how it all went down and some of the science behind my questions.

'I just want to put it to bed. If anyone could convince me, it's the first man to have apparently visited the moon. I don't mind being talked round to new ideas which is why I'd be more than happy for him to tell me how silly I'm being.

'That's what makes you evolve as a human being. You have to be open to different ideas in life.'

If Pove represents a distinctly Spanish-style conspiracy theorist, Marcos Llorente treads the well-beaten path, with his primary focus the benefits of sunlight – to the extent of snubbing suncream – and a suspicion of 'chemtrails'.

Llorente takes his theories on natural light and the sun to the extreme, however. A staunch advocate of the blue light-blocking sunglasses also favoured by stars including Erling Haaland, the Atletico Madrid midfielder also eschews unnatural light sources in his house after dark. Instead, Llorente works on soaking up as much red light as possible.

In the sun, Llorente takes it one step further, frequently sharing incorrect views on suncream's impact on Vitamin D and dismissing the connection between skin cancer and unprotected skin.

Marcos Llorente is a committed wearer of blue light-blocking glasses in a bid to boost his melatonin

Llorente has frequently endorsed the repeatedly debunked theory that 'chemtrails' are the result of government or corporate intervention

Llorente often does so in a tongue-in-cheek way: in April, he dressed up as a bottle of suncream, but with a twist. Written on the bottle in Spanish were messages reading: 'Protect against your biology' and 'Blocking Vitamin D since 1985'.

On the back of the bottle costume in lieu of ingredients, Llorente drew a graph of rising skin cancer rates and an accompanying message.

'Get in the shade when your body tells you, 'That's enough'. Get sun exposure year-round, not just three days in August,' the 'warning label' read. 'Use clothing as sun protection. Start in the morning and work your way up (don't start at 1pm).

'Build melanin gradually. Eat a balanced diet so your skin responds better. Stay hydrated and connect with nature.'

More recently Llorente, a bon viveur and lover of rare steak, 'bulletproof' butter coffee and good wine, has intensified his stance on other medical theories, including alleging that high cholesterol or 'bad' cholesterol does not have an impact on health.

Matt Le Tissier is no single-issue conspiracy theorist, with the Southampton icon borderline indiscriminate about the wide range of his causes.

Like many, his outpourings amplified amid the pandemic, with Le Tissier frequently opining on the efficacy of vaccines and painting 'big pharma' as a bogeyman. Then, in 2022, he was stood down from his role as Saints ambassador after peddling Russian lies that the massacre at Bucha, in Ukraine, had been fabricated. This came despite the fact that there was video, satellite, and photographic evidence that Russia had murdered over 320 people in the town.

Earlier this year, Le Tissier found himself in a spat with Grok, X's AI chatbot, over 'chemtrails', asking: 'Hey (Grok), why do some plane trails disperse quickly while others hang around and spread out to form grey blanket clouds?'

The bot had responded that the contrails lingered or didn't due to atmospheric conditions, much to Le Tissier's displeasure, with the former midfielder grumbling that Grok was 'spouting government propaganda'.

Matt Le Tissier, pictured taking a selfie at a Southampton game in February, has frequently raised conspiracy theories over social media

Former Wales international David Cotterill sparked widespread backlash in 2022 when he referred to 'false flag events' using 'crisis actors' at the whim of 'controllers' within hours of a fatal school shooting in Texas.

Cotterill said in the incendiary post that 'false flag events are one of their go to methods of manipulating the public opinion to bring about change'.

He also alleged: 'America is the last major country that allows it's [sic] citizens to arm themselves. Which they can't really have with what they're planning to do in the coming months and years.'

Cotterill later stressed that the post had not been related to the Texas massacre, instead stating that his post was 'just about recent articles when you see some of the stuff about the pandemic'.

He similarly received intense criticism when he suggested that the retirement of Brighton's 24-year-old Enock Mwepu due to cardiac issues was linked to side effect of the Covid-19 vaccine.

Cotterill remains unrepentant however, recently appearing on a podcast where he admitted that he supports 'everything' Le Tissier says, and revealed his belief in 2016's discredited Pizzagate conspiracy, among other conspiracy theories.

'I've gone into so many rabbit holes. If you see lots of things happening in the world with the number 33, which is obviously massive for Freemasonry and symbolism,' he told Made in Brum Podcast. 'If you see a lot of things that happen in the world, 33 is not far from that. Some people think I'm f***ing nuts.

David Cotterill sparked widespread backlash in 2022 when he referred to 'false flag events' using 'crisis actors' at the whim of 'controllers' within hours of a fatal school shooting in Texas

Former Liverpool and Southampton star Rickie Lambert is among this cohort's Covid-19 conspiracy theorists, starting off on social media as a staunch vaccine sceptic - only to fall deeper into more fringe views.

Unusually, in 2023, Lambert claimed that he believed that one can change the molecular structure of water based on speaking to a glass of the substance positively or negatively.

'The one word where water responds in the most beautiful way, with the most beautiful crystals, is showing gratitude to water,' Lambert said.

More recently, Lambert has been an active supporter of the campaign against '15-minute cities', whose detractors believe is a government scheme to control the movement and rights of people, rather than an attempt to provide walkable goods and services.

Ahead of attending a protest in Liverpool in September 2023, Lambert's call to arms to publicise the event stressed that the scheme was 'a controlled tactic being implemented across this country' and that Merseyside was set to be put under permanent surveillance.

Rickie Lambert has claimed talking positively to water makes it clean

Like Cole, Fowler appears to have merely dipped a toe into the world of conspiratorial thinking, and has similarly alighted on the Moon Landing as the target of his suspicion.

Unlike the former Chelsea star however, there seemed to be little that would change his mind when he discussed the topic with his We'll Have A Look podcast with co-host Steve McManaman.

'I think the Moon Landing is bulls***, to be fair,' Fowler said. 'Because there was a race in the Sixties, between the Americans and the USSR.

'All of a sudden, the USSR were ahead of the Americans (after Yuri Gagarin became the first man in space) and all of a sudden, the Americans got there first.

'I think it's a bit far-fetched. I don't know, that is the general gist of what I'm saying - I just don't think it was real.'

Manchester United captain Bruno Fernandes is once again at the centre of transfer speculation, with a fresh claim suggesting the Portugal international would prefer to leave Old Trafford for another major European club.

The report should be treated cautiously because it originates from an unverified source on X, but it arrives at a time when Fernandes’ long-term future is genuinely uncertain.

His current deal expires in June 2027, although United hold an option to extend it by another year.

A source on X has claimed that that Fernandes hopes to leave Man United and join another top European side.

There is, however, no firm evidence yet that Fernandes has formally asked to leave.

In fact, Michael Carrick recently insisted the 32-year-old remains fully committed to United following clear-the-air talks after their disagreement over tactics. Carrick also confirmed Fernandes would remain captain.

What is undeniable is that the contract situation is becoming increasingly important.

United are considering whether to extend Fernandes’ deal or sell him next summer rather than risk losing a valuable asset for nothing.

European interest also exists. Atlético Madrid, Juventus, AC Milan and Galatasaray have all been linked with Fernandes, although some of those possibilities appear more realistic than others.

Portuguese journalist Pedro Sepulveda recently argued that Fernandes may be better suited to another elite European project, suggesting his United spell could be approaching its natural conclusion.

If Fernandes genuinely wants to stay in Europe, that could make United’s decision more complicated.

Saudi clubs can comfortably meet his wage demands and potentially offer United a substantial transfer fee. European giants, on the other hand, may be less willing to match those numbers for a player who is now 32.

That makes activating the one-year extension increasingly logical.

It would protect United’s negotiating position and give the club time to decide whether Fernandes should remain central to the next rebuild or be sold while his value is still significant.

The X claim alone is not enough to conclude that Fernandes wants out. But combined with stalled contract talks, public frustration, growing transfer interest and United already assessing potential replacements, it adds another layer to a situation that is becoming harder to ignore.

#1371. Molecular underpinnings of rheumatic diseases and emerging therapeutic concepts

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature volume 658, pages 1141–1152 (2026) Cite this article

Inflammatory rheumatic diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis and systemic lupus erythematosus represent chronic inflammatory disorders that are caused by dysregulation of innate and adaptive immune responses. Here we review current advances in our understanding of the molecular underpinnings of these diseases and discuss consequences with respect to emerging targets and treatment strategies, which are increasingly enabling more robust disease control and the first prospects of a cure for previously chronic inflammatory rheumatic diseases.

#1370. Hibs boss insists his improving team are ready to upset the odds against Rangers in cup final

By JOHN MCGARRY, SCOTTISH CHIEF SPORTS FEATURE WRITER

Published: 14:00 EDT, 1 November 2026 | Updated: 15:31 EDT, 1 November 2026

Marink Reedijk warned Rangers that they'll face an ever-improving Hibs team when they meet in the Premier Sports Cup Final next month.

The Dutchman created history by becoming the first manager of the Easter Road club to taste a Hampden victory over Hearts when they came from behind to win 2-1.

After recording just one draw in his four opening league games, Reedijk was starting to feel the heat ahead of the semi-final.

But having secured a date against Rangers on December 13, the Leith boss feels his side are now in a different place.

Asked what gave him the confidence that his side can now upset the odds and win the cup for the first time since 2007, Reedijk said: 'The performance of today and the performance we showed the week before.

'And if we have more progression, we can make every opponent's lives a little bit difficult or very difficult.

Hibs boss Marink Reedijk celebrates his team's 2-1 win over Hearts with Josh Mulligan

'And no matter which team it is, it's always another match to play.

'Finals are, again, special matches, but also finals are not only based on these special moments.

'It's also about teams with a plan and teams with an idea.

'And I think if we build on what we are doing now, keep on going - it will have ups and downs - I know I have a really good belief that we also can do something in the final.'

Behind when Claudio Braga struck on four minutes, Hibs responded brilliantly and deservedly went in ahead at the break thanks to goals from Martin Boyle and Jamie McGrath.

Reedijk was effusive in his praise for the way his players bounced back from the early blow to dominate the game.

'In the first half, I really enjoyed how we played football, how we dominated the game on the ball, how we made sure that we created chances and gave Hearts a big problem in defence,' he reflected.

'And in the second half, I really enjoyed the togetherness, the work rate, the energy, the desire.

The Hibs players start the party after reaching League Cup final by beating Hearts

'This is where we made a big step today. And also I'm so happy for the staff, the players, because they worked so hard for this. And that's really important.

'Not only those people, like the staff and the players, but also for the fans who kept on supporting us, not only during the match, but especially those matches where we didn't have the result like it was today. And that's really important to me.

Reedijk was asked if his first victory at the fifth attempt was the first real sign that the players had bought into what he was trying to do.

'Not the first sign,' he stressed. 'For me, I already saw glimpses and signs in the last matches, starting at Falkirk, where you see that we dominated the game, but we didn't bring the game home and lost by individual errors and moments.

'And then against Celtic and St Mirren also you saw that we can dominate matches, that we can make our way of playing a challenge for the opponent. That didn't lead to the result we wanted.

'However, today it did. So, it is not the first sign, but it is the first performance with a result.'

Jamie McGrath soaks up the acclaim after putting Hibernian in front at Hampden

At full time, the entire Hibs squad lapped up the rendition of Sunshine on Leith which was sung by their supporters.

Reedijk admitted that he felt more emotional at the scenes than his impassive demeanour suggested.

'I'm not always showing my emotions, but it's really touching,' he said.

'Maybe it looks like I'm an ice king, so to say.

'Normally in Holland we say ice queen, but therefore an ice king because I'm not a woman.

'But for me, it is really important that this happens and it comes close to my heart because this is what football is about.

'Guys who inspire people on the pitch with something people off the pitch and in the stands love to see.

#1369. Pioli: ‘Milan have four or five top players, Leao needs to be encouraged in a certain way’

Stefano Pioli believes that Milan currently have ‘four or five’ top-class players and has explained how he used to get the best out of former Rossoneri star Rafael Leao: ‘He has incredible quality.”

Pioli discussed his time with Milan in an appearance on Sky Sport Italia during Sunday’s Serie A match between Juventus and Napoli.

The 2021-22 Scudetto winner has been out of work since leaving Fiorentina early into the 2025-26 season, but says that a sabbatical has been exactly what he needed.

“I’m fine but I do miss it. I needed to take a break,” said Pioli.

“I really wanted to succeed with Fiorentina, I had other offers from abroad, but I didn’t take them into consideration. I think I made a mistake by trying to raise the bar too much. I put pressure on a team when there wasn’t a need to. Some results could have gone differently, but the pressure didn’t allow us to express ourselves properly.”

Pioli would go on to discuss his time with Milan and his relationship with Leao, who was sold to Galatasaray for a fee of just €38m over the summer, not including bonuses and sell-on clauses.

Leao was one of Milan’s star players when they last won the Scudetto and was also named as the division’s MVP that year.

“He was devastating in the year of the Scudetto, I’ve rarely seen players like that,” Pioli recalled.

“The work that Maldini, Massara and I did with him was important, he has incredible quality, but we weren’t as good at raising the bar for him, though.

“A coach has to understand his players. Rafa is a good player and a good person on the inside, but needs to be encouraged in a certain way. We had Kessie and Tonali, who did the job of three or four players. It’s not that Rafa can’t mark a full-back, it’s that he wasn’t supposed to. He would follow a centre-back and a midfielder would go wide. You need to find the right place for him.”

Pioli feels that current Milan star Diego Moreira has a bit of the Leao factor about him. He also went on to discuss Milan’s current squad and their need for more strength in depth.

“I watched him against Sassuolo and he impressed me. He and Rabiot have been very important players. Maignan made a great save [against Inter]. They’re a really strong team with their top 11 players, but they started to struggle a bit more when Amorim made a few more changes.

“It’s taken them a while to get to this point because when certain players arrived, they probably arrived with a few issues and needed time to settle in and find their rhythm. Now we’re seeing the results.

“Luka Modric is still an important player, Goncalo Ramos is doing a great job for the team as well.”

On Maignan, one of the few surviving Milan players from their 2021-22 Scudetto victory, Pioli said: “He’s the best in an absolute sense: The way he participates in games and the saves that he makes. Milan have four of five top players. Modric still has the legs in him, Rabiot, Pavlovic is a top defender, De Winter is growing as well. Ramos is an excellent striker and you can’t look past Pulisic either.”

Peter Young is a Senior Reporter with Football Italia.

#1368. Pierre Sage’s Lyon return ends in disappointment for Crystal Palace

Pierre Sage felt Crystal Palace were “really far off” his expectations after suffering a 3-2 away Europa League defeat by his former side Lyon.

Corentin Tolisso opened the scoring for the hosts and Ernest Nuamah doubled Lyon’s advantage late in a first half devoid of any shots on target for the visitors.

Yéremy Pino halved the deficit five minutes after the break, before Pavel Sulc restored the two-goal lead, and substitute Daichi Kamada’s late goal proved a mere consolation.

“At the end, we were frustrated by the result, but in the first half we have to be frustrated in the way we play,” said Sage, speaking to PalaceTV.

“I think we didn’t play this first half. We are really far off our standards in the mental side of the play, in the tactical side of the play, because the players are too high between our lines and we really struggled a lot with that.

“When you give back the ball to your opponent, you suffer a lot and we were better in the second half. You cannot win this kind of game by playing only one half.”

Sage’s side got the better of his predecessor, Oliver Glasner, after they bounced back to beat Nottingham Forest 3-1 at Selhurst Park on Sunday.

After that victory, the Frenchman called for more consistency from his team, but on Thursday night was left ruing missed opportunities and goals conceded too easily by last season’s Conference League winners.

Sage was sacked by Lyon in January 2025 after a 14-month spell with the Ligue 1 outfit. Like Glasner’s, his own reunion ended in disappointment.

He told Uefa: “It’s a very disappointing return because we lost. I can’t take satisfaction from coming back home or seeing familiar faces when the result isn’t there.

“The scoreline may have been close, but there was a big difference in the way the two teams played.

“We improved considerably after the break and gave ourselves a chance, but conceding that third goal made things difficult.

“I think our second-half efforts deserved an equaliser, although winning would have been a generous reward given that we only really played [to our level] for one half.”

The veteran captain said: “It has been a long time coming. The fans were up for it, the players were up for it so we’re very happy with the performance.”

When asked about Evanilson’s header, which Smith supplied the assist for, he replied: “It wasn’t my best cross but I put it in an area, what a finish from him and I think we deserved that little bit of luck.

“From there on we went on to win the game but in the second half we got a little bit tired but the quality that came off the bench is great and we look forward to Sunday now.

“It’s a great header, he deserved it because he has worked very hard this season and many more to come from him.”

Brighton reached the Conference League after brushing Tromso aside in the play-offs with a 4-0 aggregate victory and enter the competition as one of the favourites.

Fabian Hurzeler’s side have made an excellent start to the Premier League season, sitting third with 18 goals scored in six matches, and will hope to replicate their domestic form in this European encounter against Lithuanian minnows Kauno Zalgiris.

English clubs have won the Conference League in three of the five seasons since the competition’s creation, with Brighton’s bitter rivals Crystal Palace previously lifting the trophy in May.

Hurzeler has made eight changes to the team which beat Sunderland last Saturday, with Jack Hinshelwood notably returning to the line-up.

Good evening and welcome to our live coverage of Thursday night’s European football with Crystal Palace, Sunderland and Bournemouth in Europa League action, and Brighton hosting Kauno Zalgiris in the Uefa Conference League.

Palace manager Pierre Sage managed Lyon between November 2023 and January 2025, and another sub-plot is American businessman John Textor’s involvement with the French club. The former Palace shareholder was the reason the club missed out on Europa League participation last season because Lyon were in the same competition and thus Palace were considered in breach of multi-club ownership rules. Textor sold his stake in Palace, but despite the club’s best efforts they had to settle for the Conference League, a competition they subsequently won.

Palace could have been three or four down against Nottingham Forest at the weekend but fought back for a much-needed Premier League victory. They made a winning start in Europe, beating Lech Poznan 4-0 at Selhurst Park in their opening Europa League game.

Bournemouth and Sunderland also made winning starts, despite both teams’ poor form domestically. Sunderland travel to Portuguese side Torreense, while Sturm Graz are the opposition for Bournemouth’s first ever European game at the Vitality Stadium (or Dean Court if you prefer). Bournemouth continue to be without Justin Kluivert, Eli Junior Kroupi and Alex Scott because of injury.

Brighton are favourites to win the Conference League and play their first game in the competition against Lithuanian club Kauno Zalgiris. Lifting the trophy in Istanbul at the end of the season would assure Brighton of a place in next season’s Europa League, though given their Premier League form and Manchester City’s predicament, Champions League qualification could be a realistic aspiration. Brighton won with 10 men at Sunderland on Saturday, and were successful in their appeal against Pascal Struijk’s red card.

#1367. Hearts boss Wouter Vrancken says the loss of two more players to injury was costly in semi-final defeat

By JOHN MCGARRY, SCOTTISH CHIEF SPORTS FEATURE WRITER

Published: 15:31 EDT, 1 November 2026 | Updated: 15:31 EDT, 1 November 2026

Wouter Vrancken claimed Hearts were unable to cope with the double blow of losing Tomas Magnusson and Calvin Miller as their hopes of lifting the Premier Sports Cup ended with a 2-1 defeat by Hibs.

Already missing eight first-team players, the Tynecastle men were further depleted when the pair left the field inside the opening 38 minutes of their semi-final at Hampden.

Vrancken felt the loss of two more key players was instrumental in his side failing to build on the early lead handed to them by Claudio Braga.

Instead, Hibs hit back with goals by Martin Boyle and Jamie McGrath to secure a place in next month's final against Rangers.

'I'm really sore and disappointed, of course, especially when you see how the game was going,' said Vrancken.

'It didn't have to go that way because we had control with how we started.

Wouter Vrancken insists Hearts had control until two key players left the field with injuries

Tomas Magnusson is treated for a head knock that led to his substitution early in the semi-final

Calvin Miller uses crutches after going off with what appeared to be a knee injury at Hampden

'But it changed the moment Tomas was injured, that's clear. And then afterwards with Cal.

'I'm not pointing out the guys who came out, but those changes took us out of our rhythm.

'We lost some connections and weren't top in the duels. At first, we were picking up second balls and finding the right spaces.

'But then we lost those profiles and we were searching again. There were hesitations and that gave Hibs too much space.

'You lose the game in that 20 minutes. At half-time, we tried to make adjustments, be clear and try to take those hesitations out.

'It was much better and we dominated the game again.

'Unfortunately, we didn't get rewarded. The players have taken a lot of knocks mentally and emotionally so you just hope they get rewarded for fighting hard.

'It's a pity they didn't especially in such a game.'

Magnusson came off with a head-knock while Miller succumbed to what appeared to be a knee injury.

'I haven't seen Tomas because he's at hospital,' Vrancken explained.

'Calvin is in a brace, but it's difficult to say. We have to wait for a scan tomorrow.

'With Tomas, the medical staff did a concussion test on the pitch at that moment.

'He passed it but when he came to me, he was going from left to right and couldn't stand on his legs any more.

'When I saw that, there was no doubt in my head about letting him back on the pitch. He said, I can't do it.'

Vrancken now faces serious selection issues for the Conference League match away to Swiss side Thun on Thursday.

'I don't know how I make changes. We'll see how it goes and who's fit,' he said.

'Players will have to play out of position, so we'll see who has the quality to play in certain ones.

'We have to make the puzzle on Monday or Tuesday.

'And we have to keep pushing the guys because when you go on the pitch, there can be no excuses, you have to take responsibility, go for it and try to win the game.

'We have 10 out. When you have those 10, you have a really good squad in the Premiership.

'The players have taken responsibility in difficult moments, like dominating parts of the game today.

'When they do that, you just hope they reward themselves like they did today in the second half. It's just a pity the last 20 minutes of the first half which killed the game.

'Everyone is disappointed, no matter the situation we're in.

'When you see the second half, you know there was something in the game today even with the knocks we got.

'So, the disappointment is really big, not about losing players, but missing the chance to beat your rivals and go to the final.'

#1366. 35 Greatest Central Midfielders Since 1990 (Ranked)

There's always huge debate surrounding the greatest midfielders of all time, with many differing opinions among fans. It will always be a subjective matter - as is the case with almost everything in football - but certain factors can be taken into consideration.

The likes of Zinedine Zidane, Andrea Pirlo, Xavi Hernandez and Lothar Matthaus are all viable options. But there are also plenty of Premier League legends to be considered, spearheaded by the likes of Steven Gerrard and Frank Lampard and Paul Scholes.

It's relatively easy to go through and simply name the best. However, when it comes to actually sorting the finest of the lot, well, that's when things become challenging. But here at GiveMeSport, we've had a go at ranking the 35 of the greatest central midfielders in recent history.

Given how incredibly divisive this list is, several ranking factors will be taken into account. These include:

Federico Valverde has established himself as one of the best central midfielders in the world since joining Real Madrid from his boyhood club Penarol in 2016. During his time so far at the Spanish giants, he has won the Champions League twice and La Liga on three occasions. Still very much in his prime, Valverde will be hopeful of more silverware in the future. Joshua Kimmich is three years older, but he has also won the Champions League and is renowned as one of the best midfielders in the world due to his versatility and tactical awareness.

Bruno Fernandes, Kevin De Bruyne and Jude Bellingham make the rankings for best midfield player in world football right now.

More understated stars like Ilkay Gundogan and Fernandinho also deserve a spot on the list. Both midfielders are experienced professionals who won multiple domestic titles with Manchester City under the management of coaching legend Pep Guardiola.

Jude Bellingham is still in his early 20s, but it feels like he's been around for decades. Since making his debut for Birmingham City in 2019, his career trajectory has been nothing short of remarkable. In the 2023/24 season, he won La Liga and the Champions League, scoring 23 goals in the process – he has maintained impressive form ever since. Showing just how special he is, the Englishman surpassed Zinedine Zidane's goal tally for Real Madrid (49), scoring 50 goals for Los Blancos in 73 fewer games.

Paul Pogba has been somewhat inconsistent during his career, but there have been times when he's looked almost unplayable. The former Manchester United man, whose four-year sporting ban ended early in March 2025, just before his 32nd birthday – having been reduced to 18 months – is arguably talented enough to have finished higher on this list with his passing range and all-round confidence something to be admired, but let himself down when it came to doing it regularly. Bastian Schweinsteiger was once a leading midfielder in Germany before injuries, which have also plagued Pogba, blighted his twilight years.

By comparison, Roy Keane, Claude Makelele and Michael Essien are all defined by their consistency as dependable holding midfielders. Xabi Alonso, Cesc Fabregas and Mesut Ozil make up three of the finest passers of a football the world has ever seen. The trio were all sensational when it came to keeping possession for their respective sides and were the best in the business at controlling games from the centre of the pitch. Ozil's unerring creativity is reflected by his status as one of the players with the most international assists in the 21st century.

Toni Kroos was an integral part of the all-conquering Real Madrid side for many years before retiring at the age of 34. Moving at the same spell-binding but pedestrian pace as the German, Juan Roman Riquelme is often overlooked and underrated in the modern day, but the Argentine was sublime to watch at the peak of his powers and is rightfully placed high on the list.

Spain conductor Rodri also features in this section and is rightly regarded as one of the best central midfield players in Premier League history. The defensive midfielder won the 2024 Ballon d'Or - and rightly so. Before his injury, the Spaniard was the most important player in an all-conquering Manchester City team. Instrumental for his country, too, Rodri deservedly won the Player of the Tournament award after Spain beat England in the Euro 2024 final, and then picked up the same award two years later at the 2026 World Cup.

Sergio Busquets and Yaya Toure became two of the most influential figures ever seen in the middle of the park with wildly different attributes. They shared the same lofty footballing intelligence, but Toure was a powerful force that couldn't be stopped when he got into full flow, while Busquets at his best let the ball do most of the work.

Frank Lampard and Paul Scholes all place high on the list. The two English midfielders have certain advantages over each other, with Lampard being the better goalscorer and finisher of the duo, while Scholes dictated play almost at ease in the middle of the park for the best team in Premier League history with an unrivalled technical ability and passing range. This leaves just Steven Gerrard left from one of the most heated debates in English game, as he ranks inside the top 10 for his extraordinary performances for club and country.

GIVEMESPORT Key Statistic: Despite playing exclusively in midfield, Frank Lampard is Chelsea's all-time top scorer with 212 goals.

Entering the top 10 is the timeless Kaka. The elusive attacking midfielder lifted the Ballon d'Or in 2007, just before the Lionel Messi and Cristiano Ronaldo era set in. He goes down as one of Brazil's greatest-ever players after playing a starring role in the dominant AC Milan team of the 2000s. Also joining him is his former teammate, Clarence Seedorf. The Dutchman remains the only player to lift the Champions League with three separate clubs, which is quite an astonishing achievement itself. He did so once with Ajax in 1995, once with Real Madrid in 1998, and twice with AC Milan in 2003 and 2007.

Kevin De Bruyne and the aforementioned Steven Gerrard make the list as world-leading players throughout Premier League history. The former is up there with the very best technicians we have ever seen in world football and would hold his own with anyone in that regard. Left foot, right foot - it doesn't matter for the majestic Belgian playmaker, as he has consistently served up chances for his teammates.

Michael Laudrup just missed out on a place in the top five. He won an impressive 16 trophies throughout his illustrious career, including Barcelona's first European Cup and five La Liga titles, four with the Blaugrana and one with their fierce rivals, Real Madrid. Laudrup is placed seventh on Denmark's all-time goalscorer list with 37 strikes from midfield - just three goals shy of a place in the top four.

Lothar Matthaus lifted the Ballon d'Or in 1990 and is one of Germany's greatest-ever players. He won the FIFA World Cup with his country in the same year and has an incredible 20 trophies to his name. Among those pieces of silverware are seven Bundesliga titles with Bayern Munich and a Serie A crown at Inter Milan.

Matthaus also claimed the European Championship with Germany in 1980 at the start of his glittering career. The former international captain is arguably overlooked when it comes to discussing the greatest players in the game. This is perhaps due to recency bias, but there is no doubting just how good Matthaus was for his respective clubs and on the international stage with Germany.

World Cup, Euros, Champions League, Bundesliga (x7), Serie A

Ballon d'Or, FIFA World Player of the Year,

Andres Iniesta formed a formidable partnership with Xavi Hernandez for Barcelona and Spain. They complemented each other perfectly and were arguably the best midfield duo in the world for several years. Iniesta is still going strong at the age of 39 and is currently plying his trade in the United Arab Emirates.

The former Barcelona star has won a staggering 40 trophies during an exceptional career, 32 of which were in the Catalan capital. Iniesta also had great success with Spain during the nation's golden era. The diminutive playmaker was a fixture of the side that won three consecutive major international tournaments between 2008 and 2012, scoring the decisive goal in the 2010 World Cup final to overcome the Netherlands.

World Cup, Euros (x2), Champions League (x4), La Liga (x9)

Alongside Iniesta, Xavi was a mainstay in those legendary Barcelona and Spain sides. His understanding of the game, when to pass the ball, when to keep it and his positioning were all exquisite. The midfield maestro, like Iniesta, won an incredible number of trophies throughout his fantastic career.

Xavi won 25 of his 32 trophies with Barcelona, including four Champions League titles and eight La Liga crowns. His influence on the sport has been huge, and numerous players have looked at how the proud Catalan played and tried to incorporate it into their own game. Xavi is rightly regarded as a Barcelona and Spain legend, and he deservedly has a place in the top three.

World Cup, Euros (x2), Champions League (x4), La Liga (x8)

World Soccer Player of the Year, La Liga Best Midfielder of the Year (x3)

Luka Modric can consider himself the greatest ever Croatian player. Given the superb players they’ve had over the years, that is quite an accolade. His longevity and desire to remain at the top are evident in his 1000+ appearances over the last 24 years for club and country.

From Cristiano Ronaldo's work ethic to make it to the top to N'Golo Kante covering every blade of grass, these are the most hardworking players.

The midfield master won six European titles with Real Madrid, but it was his performances for Croatia at the 2018 World Cup - in which his side finished as runners-up - that ended the Messi-Ronaldo dominance of the Ballon d'Or, when he was crowned the world's best footballer in the same year. Now in his 40s, Modric is still playing at the highest level of European football with Italian heavyweights AC Milan.

When it comes to the greatest central midfield player of all time, there can only be one and that right is reserved for a very special player, Zinedine Zidane. The Frenchman - considered to be one of the footballers who retired too early - was more of an artist than an athlete, gracefully gliding about the pitch in a seemingly gravity-defying manner when you consider his towering 6ft 2in frame.

Zidane won everything there was to win in the game, both individually and with his teams. He even scored two winning goals in the 1998 World Cup final to defeat Brazil, as well as arguably the greatest Champions League goal of all time in the 2002 final against Bayer Leverkusen. The ultimate big game player, there was no stage he wouldn't thrive on, and is rightfully regarded as the best in the world in his position.

World Cup, Euros, Champions League, Serie A (x2), La Liga

Ballon d'Or, FIFA World Player of the Year (x3),

Serie A Footballer of the Year, Ligue 1 Player of the Year

All statistics from Transfermarkt - correct as of 02/10/26.
