#1365. Inter recover one player ahead of Champions League test but still without Lautaro

Benjamin Pavard is back in training with Inter and will be available to face Feyenoord in the Champions League on Tuesday night, but the Nerazzurri are still expected to be without captain and leading goalscorer Lautaro Martinez.

Inter are hoping to bounce back from a disappointing Derby della Madonnina against rivals Milan, losing 3-1 in San Siro over the weekend, as they prepare to take on Feyenoord in Rotterdam in the Champions League at 20.00 GMT on Tuesday night.

According to reports from Gianluca Di Marzio, centre-back Pavard was able to rejoin his teammates for the full training session on Monday.

The 30-year-old, who spent the 2025-26 season on loan with Marseille, had worked his way back into Chivu’s first-team plans before suffering an adductor injury in mid-October and has not featured since then.

The Nerazzurri are still without a handful of key players heading into Tuesday’s game against Feyenoord, most notably captain Lautaro Martinez.

He has missed the last four league games with a hamstring injury, and with just two games to go before the next international break, it is becoming increasingly likely that he does not return until the end of November.

Curtis Jones, John Stones and Luis Henrique are also expected to miss the Feyenoord match through injury.

Peter Young is a Senior Reporter with Football Italia.

#1364. Narrow carbon pentaheptite nanoribbon as a covalent metal

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature volume 658, pages 1176–1182 (2026) Cite this article

Metallic carbon-based nanoribbons are sought after1,2 as atomically defined one-dimensional conductors with potential relevance to future carbon-based electrodes and interconnects3, ideally with quantum-limited conductance comparable to metallic carbon nanotubes4. Metallic graphene nanoribbons have been realized by band engineering, notably through zero-mode superlattices1. However, atomically precise metallic nanoribbons of fully non-benzenoid carbon allotropes, such as the theorized metallic carbon pentaheptites5,6, remain unexplored. The realization of these nanoribbons could enable bottom-up fabrication of all-carbon electronics7,8 compatible with semiconducting graphene nanoribbons9,10,11,12,13 and nanographenes14,15, along with their fascinating properties16,17,18,19,20. Here we report a hierarchical approach for the on-surface synthesis of planar carbon pentaheptite nanoribbons (CPHNs) by laterally fusing well-aligned polypentalene chains transformed from pre-synthesized polycyclooctadiene chains. Two distinct types of narrow pentaheptite nanoribbon share a similar basal structure consisting of a central heptagon chain flanked by either identically (CPHN 1) or differently (CPHN 2) oriented polypentalene chains on opposite lateral edges. CPHN 1 is an intrinsic metal, whereas CPHN 2 is a narrow-bandgap semiconductor. The CPHN 1 ribbon exhibits near-ballistic conductance approaching one conductance quantum, comparable to metallic carbon nanotubes4. This highlights CPHN 1 as a promising planar carbon metal and suggests a possible route towards carbon quantum wires, although further synthetic optimization will be required for device integration.

For the Br adlayer, a coverage of 1/3 monolayer of Br atoms adsorbed at the hollow sites of Ag(111) was adopted by considering the observed Br adatom structure on Ag(111) (Supplementary Fig. 21f). Bader charge analysis shows negligible charge transfer from the Br/Ag(111) substrate to CPHN 1 and CPHN 2, compared to the nearly identical charge transfer of 0.56 electrons per unit from the Ag(111) substrate to CPHN 1 and CPHN 2.

#1363. Bradley Lowery's mum issues heartbreaking statement to condemn 'cruel' Coventry fan who used her late son's photo to taunt Sunderland fans as 14-year-old boy hands himself into police

Published: 10:02 EDT, 1 November 2026 | Updated: 18:17 EDT, 1 November 2026

Bradley Lowery's mum has released a heartbreaking statement after a Coventry fan appeared to use his photograph to taunt Sunderland supporters.

The deplorable behaviour came during the Premier League clash between the two sides on Saturday, which the Sky Blues won 3-1.

A video on social media showed a supporter holding up a picture of Bradley - who tragically died from a rare form of childhood cancer at the age of six in 2017 - smiling in the direction of Sunderland fans, with the individual pointing at it and seen smirking at the same time.

A 14-year-old boy 'handed himself in' to West Midlands Police on Sunday.

In a statement on Sunday morning after the behaviour of the Coventry fan went viral, Bradley's mum Gemma shared a heartbreaking message.

'My beautiful boy deserves to be remembered with love, not hate,' she wrote. 'Yesterday, a Coventry fan used a photograph of Bradley to taunt Sunderland supporters. As Bradley’s mam, this is heartbreaking, especially as it’s one of my favourite photographs of him. Just look at that smile.

A Coventry fan appeared to use a photograph of Bradley Lowery to taunt Sunderland fans

A fan held up a photo of Bradley, the Sunderland fan who tragically passed away aged six from a rare form of childhood cancer, and was seen smirking and pointing

'I remember that day like it was yesterday. He was so happy, having so much fun. Those moments were precious because they were few and far between. So much of Bradley’s short life was spent battling cancer and enduring treatments no child should ever face. To see such a beautiful memory used in such a cruel way really does make my heart hurt.

'We are a football-loving family who follow Sunderland home and away. I’m all for football banter, but surely mocking a child who died from cancer is not banter? I hope the club takes appropriate action and the young lad’s family help him understand how hurtful his actions were.

'I don’t want hatred directed towards him, so please please don't, just for him to learn from this. Behind that photograph is a little boy who was loved beyond measure and a family who miss him every day. Thank you to everyone who has defended Bradley and shown us so much love. It means more than you know.'

Gemma continued: 'What some people don’t realise is that Bradley’s story didn’t end when his life did. Because of Bradley, children’s lives are being saved, hundreds of families have received vital support, and children facing unimaginable battles are being given hope.

'Through Super Brad’s Pad, families can escape hospital life, spend precious time together and make memories that last forever. That is Bradley’s legacy. The difference my little boy continues to make in this world. No amount of cruelty will ever take that away.

'So rather than let this photograph be remembered for hatred, I want it remembered for what it truly represents. My beautiful little boy, enjoying one of the happiest days of his life, with the biggest smile on his face. That is how I want the world to remember him. #CancerHasNoColours.'

Bradley touched the hearts of football fans across the UK during his battle with neuroblastoma, and formed a touching relationship with then Sunderland striker Jermain Defoe

Confirming that a teenager had handed himself in to authorities on Sunday, West Midlands Police said in a statement: 'We are aware of a video circulating on social media showing an incident at Coventry City's Premier League match with Sunderland.

'A thorough investigation has been launched, and a 14-year-old boy has since handed himself in and will be spoken with in due course.

'We understand the upset and outrage this video has caused in the community and to the victim's family, and our officers are keeping them up to date with the progress of our investigation and working closely alongside both football clubs.'

Coventry condemned the shameful behaviour in a strongly-worded statement on Saturday.

It read: 'Coventry City FC is aware of footage circulating on social media in connection with an incident during our Premier League fixture against Sunderland.

'The club does not tolerate offensive behaviour and will liaise with the relevant authorities to determine the appropriate course of action.'

Since Saturday's clash, more than £1,000 has been donated to the The Bradley Lowery Foundation by Coventry City fans, with many supporters leaving heartfelt messages as they refused to let the actions of one person define them.

Bradley was previously used by a fan as a taunt back in 2023 when Sheffield Wednesday supporter Dale Houghton was seen holding up a picture of him at a match against Sunderland and laughing.

Houghton was subsequently handed a 12-week suspended prison sentence and ordered to do 200 hours unpaid work.

Bradley pictured with his mum Gemma at his sixth birthday party back in May 2017

Bradley touched the hearts of football fans across the UK during his battle with neuroblastoma, a rare form of childhood cancer, before he tragically passed away aged just six in 2017.

The Bradley Lowery Foundation was set up in his honour, with the charity aiming to help families who are fundraising for treatment or equipment that is not readily available or covered by the NHS, while it also supports research into various childhood cancers, including neuroblastoma.

Bradley, who was diagnosed with neuroblastoma when he was just 18 months old, also built up a touching relationship with Jermain Defoe, who later called him his 'best mate'.

Defoe played for Sunderland at the time, and speaking in 2023, he said: 'He will always be in my heart, for the rest of my life. There's not a day that goes past where I don't wake up and think about little Bradley, because his love is genuine.'

#1362. Ethan Nwaneri’s Career Takes Fresh Twist After 9 Games For Borussia Dortmund

Arsenal wonderkid Ethan Nwaneri's career has taken an interesting turn in recent weeks, having now made nine appearances for Borussia Dortmund while on loan for the 2026/27 Bundesliga campaign.

The England Under-21 star initially hit the ground running in the red and black of the German giants, seemingly proving to be the all-action, tireless attacking midfielder that Niko Kovac's unbeaten side had desperately needed.

It also appeared likely that he would return to Arsenal next summer with a new lease of life, ready to prove he remains one of the Hale End academy's finest graduates and give the likes of Martin Odegaard a run for their money for a place in the starting XI.

While that may still be the case, not everything has been plain sailing for the teenager in recent weeks, although some eye-opening developments could soon be coming to fruition.

Since his last start for Dortmund on October 17, the 19-year-old has found himself relegated to a bench role, with his impact seemingly beginning to wane as matches wore on.

That was also the game in which he was mistakenly shown a red card, only for the decision to be overturned later. He has only been involved for 42 minutes of playing time since.

Nwaneri came on in injury time during the Champions League clash against Sabah FK before playing 22 minutes of the second half in the 1-0 win over Frankfurt.

He then made another 19-minute cameo in the German Cup victory over Werder Bremen, before being left as an unused substitute against Bayern Munich this past weekend. Watch his highlights from October 14 against Bodo/Glimt below:

There are, however, some positives to take from his spell in Germany so far. Nwaneri has already racked up more minutes than he managed throughout the entirety of the 2025/26 season, when he was on loan at Marseille. That said, he is still waiting to get off the mark in black and yellow, having seen an audacious bicycle kick ruled out for a foul earlier in October.

The biggest development in Nwaneri's career, however, has to be the speculation surrounding his possible switch away from England national team commitments.

He was born in Islington, England, to a Nigerian father and an English-French mother, making him eligible to represent England, Nigeria, or France internationally.

The Borussia Dortmund player was involved in a very strangest incident.

Nwaneri won the Under-21s European Championship with the Young Lions last summer, but after only recently following Nigeria's Super Eagles on social media, rumours have begun to swirl around the potential for him to turn out for the African nation.

He has reportedly since unfollowed them after fans caught on to his social media activity, while the Nigeria boss has downplayed any suggestions that he's close to changing national sides. Although, indeed, talks have taken place.

#1361. Steely Chelsea triumph despite losing Martinez to head injury

This was the afternoon when Xabi Alonso’s Chelsea went from swashbuckling to stoic, thrilling to tenacious.

For all Alonso’s attacking vigour at the start of his reign, there can have been no more symbolically satisfying victory under the new coach than this resolute win at Everton – the most vivid example of an increasingly impressive transformation.

This was what Alonso described as “winning in a different way”. A triumph amid the adversity of losing goalkeeper Emiliano Martínez to what appears to be a serious injury after a head collision with Jarrad Branthwaite is just one facet of why the joyous visiting supporters might consider this an early turning point.

Where recently they wilted, on Saturday they thrived in securing a first Premier League clean sheet for nine months.

Much more of this and the adjectives which were splattered across Chelsea during the golden years of José Mourinho – solid, robust and dogged – will be part of the Stamford Bridge lexicon once more.

“Just one day,” Alonso warned, both acclaiming the importance of the win while wisely preaching caution. “It will be key when we manage 10 clean sheets, even though this one feels good. We need to repeat it again and again, but the mentality was very good. Sometimes it is not to play nice, it is to play good – to win second balls, and to be efficient. We needed one of these: a clean sheet and a win.”

Asked about Martinez’s condition, Alonso said: “It was a concussion, but beyond that I do not know. I have only seen one clip of the incident, so we need to wait.

“What we know is that he left the stadium conscious and is now in hospital undergoing precautionary tests.

“We need to wait. Hopefully it will not be too serious, but at the moment we just have to wait.”

Alonso is speedily shifting perceptions of this previously underperforming bunch, the Stamford Bridge culture on and off the pitch already unrecognisable from a few months ago.

It was Chelsea’s trip to Everton last season which facilitated the endgame of Liam Rosenior’s short, but generally hideous reign.

For those who tried to banish memories, it was a darkly comical period when Chelsea’s players were paying their respect to stationary footballs, seemingly finding new ways to stand in front of travelling fans to apologise for meek and rancid performances.

How different the scenes after Pedro Neto’s double on Merseyside – a success built on those old-fashioned and too often underestimated qualities of character and application before the artists had the final say. These are the wins that build connections and trust between players and supporters, especially during the getting-to-know-you period of a managerial tenure. While neutrals mutter about a generally disappointing spectacle, the players and supporters return home clutching three points believing they have fought together in the trenches.

#1360. Carrick reflects on Man United 7-1 Roma and has four injury doubts ahead of UCL test

Michael Carrick looked back fondly upon Manchester United’s 7-1 victory over Roma in the Champions League almost 20 years ago ahead of the meeting of the two sides at Old Trafford on Tuesday night, and confirmed that four of his players are likely to miss the test against the in-form Giallorossi.

Manchester United will host Roma at Old Trafford in the Champions League at 20.00 GMT on Tuesday evening. Carrick, joined by midfielder Kobbie Mainoo, sat down for their pre-match press conference on Monday.

Despite the upcoming test against Roma, most of the questions that went Carrick’s way were about United and the difficulty that they have faced over the last few weeks. They have lost three games in a row, a run that started with a 4-1 Champions League defeat away against Como, and have now gone nine matches without a win across all competitions.

Roma, meanwhile, remain unbeaten in Serie A after 10 matches. They have four points after three matches in the Champions League this season with one win, one draw and one loss on their record.

The first question that came Carrick’s way was about the availability of former Lecce winger Patrick Dorgu, who is just back from injury but is unlikely to feature against Roma.

“Yeah, it was his first day with the group, great to have him back, but he won’t be involved tomorrow. We’ll see how he progresses during the week,” Carrick confirmed.

The United boss did not want to get into a further war of words with centre-back Lisandro Martinez, but dismissed suggestions that the Argentine is not in the right headspace at the moment: “Nah, I’ve got no concerns about commitment at all. Things happen in football, sometimes you make mistakes, sometimes it goes well for you, but commitment is not an issue, for sure.”

Carrick also insists that he is not feeling the pressure despite a dismal run of results heading into the Roma clash.

“No, not at all,” he said. “You never know what is going to happen in the future, but that doesn’t change the way I feel. I can’t wait for the game tomorrow. You might think I’m crazy with the results we’ve had, but I can’t wait for it.”

Despite a turbulent few weeks, Carrick insists that the United squad is united and determined.

“The dressing room is in a good place. Perception is a funny thing, you can make things look in different ways. The commitment from the players, to the club and each other, I don’t question that at all.”

Carrick faced just one question about Roma, and that was about their 7-1 defeat against United in the 2006-07 Champions League quarter-finals. Carrick, not typically remembered for his goalscoring prowess, netted a brace on that occasion.

“It’s a long time ago, eh? It was a magical night, one of the best nights and atmospheres I’ve been fortunate enough to witness. The fact that I scored a couple, and that was unusual, gives me great memories,” he recalled.

Lastly, Carrick confirmed that Luke Shaw will not be available to face Roma and that Leny Yoro and Maruc Rashford are big doubts.

“Leny has a bit of tendon (pain), but he’s been managing it. Luke definitely won’t be around this week. He won’t be fit, and Marcus, we’ll have to see day by day how he keeps improving.”

#1358. Former Liverpool defender Stephen Warnock reveals he hid seizures from club because he was 'petrified' of being released as youngster

Published: 19:09 EDT, 1 November 2026 | Updated: 19:15 EDT, 1 November 2026

Former Liverpool defender Stephen Warnock has revealed he hid seizures from the club out of fear that the Reds would axe him.

Warnock, 44, played 67 times for Liverpool and has transitioned into broadcasting since retiring from playing in 2018.

He suffered from a number of epileptic fits as a youngster - a condition that affects around one in every 100 people.

Warnock never understood what was causing his seizures and told 5 Live: 'I was petrified of telling Liverpool because I was worried about being released. Because I was thinking "if they think I've got a condition they will release me".

'I was worried about being on the pitch and it happens. There were no triggers for me, I never knew what triggered it. That was what petrified me.'

Warnock experienced the seizures for around three years and underwent a number of tests including a CT and MRI scan.

Stephen Warnock, pictured working as a broadcaster, revealed he suffered from seizures

The former Liverpool defender, pictured in action for the Reds back in 2005, said he was terrified of telling the club about his health issue

'I was at a computer and then I woke up in a hospital bed,' he went on. 'And I was like "wow, how have I got here?". I didn't remember anything, I completely blacked out.

'My friends told me I started having a seizure. Obviously an ambulance was called and I was taken to a hospital bed.

'I was embarrassed to be honest, because no-one else had it, no-one knew about it, I didn't know about it until it happened.'

The risk of having a seizure can be reduced with medication and Warnock has not experienced one since he was 14.

'I was in a fortunate position where I grew out of it,' he said.

'I didn't have to go on medication or worry about driving a car or things like that. It's the first time I've ever really spoken about it.'

Warnock, a left-back, departed Liverpool in 2007 and went on to play for Aston Villa, Leeds and Derby among other sides.

He has appeared on a number of television channels while working as a pundit, including the BBC, Sky Sports, BT Sport, NBC and DAZN.

Manchester Untied and England midfielder Kobbie Mainoo insists that ‘it feels like we’re one win away’ from turning things around after a difficult period for the Premier League side heading into Tuesday’s Champions League test against Roma.

Mainoo joined United head coach Michael Carrick for a pre-match press conference on Monday afternoon ahead of their visit from Roma in the Champions League, which kicks off at 20.00 GMT on Tuesday evening.

Despite the upcoming test against Roma, most of the questions that went Mainoo and Carrick’s way were about United and the difficulty that they have faced over the last few weeks. They have lost three games in a row, a run that started with a 4-1 Champions League defeat away against Como, and have now gone nine matches without a win across all competitions.

Roma, meanwhile, remain unbeaten in Serie A after 10 matches. They have four points after three matches in the Champions League this season with one win, one draw and one loss on their record.

“It’s been a tough season, we haven’t got the results we wanted, but we need to look forward now. It feels like we’re one win away from changing it,” said Mainoo at the beginning of his pre-match press conference on Monday.

“I’ve been at this club for a long time and know there will be ups and down. You expect bumps, but the best thing about them is you’re to bounce back from them.

#1356. Harry Kane Names the Major Trophy He'd Happily 'Trade' His Ballon d'Or For

It's been a fantastic few seasons for Harry Kane, culminating in his 2026 Ballon d'Or win.

The English striker scored goal after goal for Tottenham Hotspur, but never managed to get his hands on a major trophy with Spurs. In the pursuit of glory, he made the move to Bayern Munich in 2023, and that has proved to be a sensible transfer.

The 33-year-old, one of the oldest Ballon d'Or winners, has now won two Bundesliga titles and the DFB-Pokal, while continuing to score at an electrifying rate. Indeed, Kane scored 73 goals for club and country in 2025/26, which helped him win the 2026 Ballon d'Or.

Lamine Yamal may have won, but some former Ballon d'Or winners didn't even include him in their top three.

Having been named the world's best player, the Englishman could not hide his delight, saying he was 'speechless' as he claimed the award in London. However, in the short time since that historic night, Kane has revealed that he would swap the Ballon d'Or for one major honour.

Speaking to reporters via Goal, he claimed that he'd happily 'trade' his prize if it meant winning the Champions League with Bayern. Kane explained:

"Team trophies are why we play football. The team aspect of our sport is really, really important. The Ballon d'Or last week was one of the best feelings I've had in my life and my career... but to have moments with the team, celebrations with the club, to be able to lift the Champions League with Bayern would be an incredible feeling.

"Of course the Ballon d'Or is a highlight, it puts me on an even bigger level, but you want to have these big finals, the Champions League, having that feeling of emotion with your teammates as well. I would choose the Champions League, but I have the opportunity to do both, let's see what happens."

That's not to say Kane isn't appreciating the value of his award, as he went on to add: "Winning the Ballon d'Or was a huge achievement for me. I've had to overcome many challenges in my career, some people didn't think I'd get this far..."

Kane most notably made it all the way to the Champions League final with Spurs in 2018/19, but was unable to get across the line, as his team lost 2-0 to Liverpool. At the time, he dejectedly said:

“It was a tough one to take. It’s probably one of the biggest games we’ll ever play in our careers and to let it slide by is always a tough one to take. It’s an experience we need to learn from."

At Bayern, Kane then made it to the semis twice, and the quarters once, but still hasn't been able to make another final. He's also suffered more disappointment in cup competitions with England.

Once again, his goalscoring record at that level has never been questioned – he is the Three Lions' all-time top scorer after all – but he's lost two finals with his country, suffering defeat at both Euro 2020 and Euro 2024. He also made it to the semis with England this summer at the 2026 World Cup, but once again fell short when it came to pushing for glory.

With all that disappointment in mind, it's little wonder Kane would happily give up his Ballon d'Or if it meant finally getting his hands on a major team honour such as the Champions League.

#1355. Invincibles beware! Mikel Arteta might just be assembling Arsenal's greatest EVER defence, writes ISAAN KHAN

Published: 21:00 EDT, 1 November 2026 | Updated: 03:48 EDT, 2 November 2026

Within seconds of the full-time whistle, Gabriel Heinze had lifted an elated Mikel Arteta off the turf.

The Argentine knew why this result brought his colleague a certain catharsis, which had eluded him for over a decade.

Arteta had previously opened up about the psychological difficulties of playing at Anfield, describing the experience akin to a cyclist suddenly running out of energy. A mental paralysis of sorts.

The game in question was in February 2014, having experienced a 5-1 defeat as a Gunners player. Arsenal’s previous victory against Liverpool away dated back to September 2012, a 14-year wait to banish these demons which he was duly reminded of in Friday’s press conference and in the minutes before kick-off.

Instead, it’s now getting scary for Arsenal’s Premier League title rivals. The prospect of Arteta's side opening up a gap from the chasing pack by Christmas is becoming a real possibility — and it’s all because of their defence.

A William Saliba-less backline reducing the Reds to zero shots on target at Anfield is a moment worth digesting.

Mikel Arteta and Gabriel Heinze jubilantly embrace as the final whistle blows at Anfield

Arsenal ended their 14-year wait for a Premier League victory at Anfield with a superb display

Winning on opposition territory after an abysmal record lasting over a decade is an achievement in itself. But to ensure a frontline featuring Alexander Isak, Florian Wirtz and Bradley Barcola aren't given so much as a sniff in front of goal is a further statement.

For all the focus around the fragilities of their frontline — the weaknesses are still very much in the open, as seen by the shock Carabao Cup defeat to Fleetwood Town — it’s Arsenal’s defence which underpins everything.

Since the start of last season, Arsenal have not lost a league game when leading the scoreline at half-time. Just like how Arsenal’s (previously) woeful record at Anfield would be used as a reminder, this statistic is a menacing one for future opponents.

It raises the question: how does this backline compare to the best Premier League defences who came before them?

If the team carry on in this vein towards a consecutive league title, the Arsenal Invincibles set-up from the historic 2003-04 season of Sol Campbell, Kolo Toure, Ashley Cole and Lauren, with Jens Lehmann in goal, could soon be superseded.

The current collection of defenders, backed up by David Raya, create a defensive structure which is proving so hard to break down, even with the lack of a sole regular scorer in the side.

Gabriel, despite his embarrassing attempt at pretending Isak struck him in the face yesterday, stayed strong in physical duels and didn’t relent in periods when Liverpool piled the pressure on.

By the 42nd minute, the Reds had whipped in 17 crosses, many of which were cleared by Gabriel or Konsa.

Riccardo Calafiori is a wonderfully-gifted footballer who finds himself in some unorthodox positions which are difficult to track. The Italian’s menacing runs inverting from the left flank caused Liverpool many a problem.

Kai Havertz tapped home from a low cross early on to give Arsenal a crucial lead to defend

Even Jurrien Timber, who didn’t have his best game in the final third, helped ensure solidity at right back up against Cody Gakpo.

It’s Ezri Konsa, though, who reflects a shrewdness typifying Arsenal and Arteta. As soon as it emerged that Saliba would be sidelined for months with a back injury, a right-sided centre back became the priority.

The 29-year-old has slotted in seamlessly and again shone against the Reds, mirroring the ‘blessed’ tattoo he has inscribed on his left hand.

The versatile defender won 100 per cent of his ground duels, made 14 defensive contributions and completed eight clearances. He ranked No1 in all these categories yesterday.

An Arteta team starts from a rock-solid base with multiple, versatile defenders, often at the cost of fewer frontline options (Arsenal struck just two more league goals than third-placed Manchester United last season, for example).

It ultimately worked in the previous campaign, their defence propelling Arsenal to a first Premier League title in 22 years.

Another title appears to be well on track. And: watch out Campbell and Co. The moniker for Arsenal’s best defence in modern history is at risk.

GUNNERS GAINING FROM MIKEL'S RUTHLESS STREAK

Arteta’s ruthlessness is well-documented. Just ask Aaron Ramsdale or Jakub Kiwior, who were eased out after being surplus to requirements in recent years.

Or the cold treatment of Pierre-Emerick Aubameyang and Mesut Ozil earlier in the Spaniard’s reign over their behaviours.

Arteta's ruthlessness with team selection is continuing to pay dividends for the Gunners

The current squad is brimming with talent — and spades of uncertainty.

Eberechi Eze performed well off the bench against Bayern Munich after Bukayo Saka’s thigh injury on 10 minutes, followed up by a start against Everton — and didn’t get a minute against Liverpool.

While Viktor Gyokeres was given his first league start of the season against Everton, where he played well — only to be dropped for this match.

As seen by Christos Tzolis’ dash to make yesterday’s squad ahead of schedule, influenced by Max Dowman’s three-match suspension, no one’s place is really secure.

That makes for a truly competitive environment.

The fiery serial-winner, drafted in by Arteta in July 2025, was always going to demand high standards and bring a ferocity which can turn some the wrong way. At Argentine side Newell’s Old Boys, for example, he would weigh the players twice a day.

Heinze's arrival in July 2025 has added a steeliness to the defence and paid off in spades

So the appointment was attached with risks, even if Arteta had grown close to his ex-team-mate from his Paris Saint-Germain.

It’s turned out to be a clever addition, which has added a steeliness to the defence and paid off in spades.

Sources say that Heinze, who has managed five teams, is well-respected by the players, but is also seen as someone who does not mince his words. They know he’s not here to mess around.

#1354. Connectome simulations identify a central pattern generator for fly walking

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Animal locomotion relies on rhythmic body movements driven by central pattern generators (CPGs): neural circuits that produce oscillating output without oscillating input. However, the circuit structure of a CPG for walking is not known in any animal1,2. To identify the cells and synapses that underlie rhythmic leg movement in walking flies, we developed dynamic simulations of the Drosophila ventral nerve cord connectomes3,4,5,6. A computational activation screen of descending neurons from the central brain identified DNg100—a known command neuron for walking—as the strongest driver of rhythmic leg motor activity. Simulated network pruning isolated a minimal rhythm-generating circuit consisting of one inhibitory and two excitatory interneurons; this three-neuron circuit was necessary and sufficient for motor rhythms across all six legs and in four connectome datasets. Simulations also predicted that a separate descending pathway (DNb08) drives rhythmic leg movements, which we confirmed experimentally using optogenetics in behaving flies. Our results reveal the cellular identity and synaptic structure of a putative CPG circuit for walking and other rhythmic leg movements in flies.

#1353. City of Milan honors legendary Baresi with Famedio inscription

Legendary former Milan captain Franco Baresi was among the individuals to be honoured with an inscription in the Famedio at the city’s Cimiterio Monumental on Monday: ‘One of the city’s highest honors’.

Baresi, considered one of the greatest defenders in the history of the sport and an icon of Milan and the Italy national team, died at the age of 66 earlier this year following a battle with illness.

On Monday, Baresi was one of 14 individuals to be have their name inscribed in the Famedio in the Cimiterio Monumental, one of the two largest and most prestigious cemeteries in the city of Milan. This has been described as ‘one of the highest honors’ by the club in a statement that was released on Monday afternoon.

“The City of Milano today honored Franco Baresi, AC Milan’s legendary Captain, by inscribing his name in the Famedio at the Monumental Cemetery, a memorial dedicated to the figures who have shaped the city’s history and identity,” AC Milan wrote.

Monday’s ceremony was conducted in the presence of Baresi’s family, mayor Giuseppe Sala and AC Milan ambassador Daniele Massaro.

“This city holds extraordinary reserves of passion, creativity and industry,” said the mayor at the ceremony on Monday. “This energy is rooted in centuries of experience, restoring confidence in Italy and the ability to look to the future with optimism. Gathering here today at the Famedio means rediscovering a pride in what Milan has been able to achieve in so many different fields thanks to the contributions of these irreplaceable individuals.”

Among the others to be honored on Monday were Ornella Vanoni, Don Antonio Mazzi, Gianni Cervetti, Ulrico Carlo Gustavo Hoepli, Gioia Marchi Falck, Bruno Pizzul, Vera Vigevani Jarach, Luisa Muraro, Laura Hoesch, Giovanni Gastel, Giancarlo Consonni, Giovanni Barbareschi and Rosellina Archinto Marconi.

The City of Milan honored Franco Baresi, our legendary Captain, with an inscription in the Famedio at the Monumental Cemetery. #1352. Liverpool’s £400m front line clicks but win at Brentford turns on red card

Only time will tell if Liverpool’s £400m front line can ever justify the extraordinary amount of money that was spent on them, but this was at least a significant step in the right direction. In a gritty victory away to Brentford, all four of Alexander Isak, Florian Wirtz, Bradley Barcola and Victor Muñoz either scored or assisted goals.

Admittedly, the task was made significantly easier by the major turning point of this game: a red card for Brentford’s Yehor Yarmoliuk. At the time of Yarmoliuk’s “headbutting action” towards Liverpool defender Jeremy Jacquet, the visitors were trailing 1-0 and looking worryingly short of ideas in attack.

But as the context of the match changed, so did the level of threat from the visitors. Against 10 men, with more space in which to operate, Liverpool’s forwards looked increasingly dangerous. Wirtz began to pull the strings, Barcola started to cause problems, Muñoz stretched the Brentford defence and Isak became a lurking menace.

For Andoni Iraola, who had failed to beat Brentford in six attempts as manager of Bournemouth, it would have made for an immensely pleasing sight. After last weekend’s thrashing by Manchester City, Liverpool have responded with a 6-3 Champions League win over LASK and this victory against a previously unbeaten Brentford. Iraola will know, however, that his team’s numerical advantage was the fundamental reason for the dramatic shift in the flow of this game.

The Gtech Community Stadium simmered with outrage following Yarmoliuk’s red card, which came in the eighth minute of first-half stoppage time, and the home fans probably had a point. Yes, there was a movement of the midfielder’s head towards Jacquet, but it was hardly an act of violence. Jacquet’s reaction, collapsing to the turf in mock agony, was embarrassing but predictably effective. Cynics would say the Frenchman changed the game for his team. Purists would argue this is no way in which to influence a match.

Keith Andrews, the Brentford head coach, chose against complaining too aggressively. But he did make it clear what he thought of Jacquet’s behaviour. “I do think they were cute and clever,” Andrews said. “He is walking into Yarmo. But we need to look at ourselves and I understand why it was a red. Yarmo is an amazing young man and he will learn from this.”

Brentford had been the better team before this decisive incident and they deserved their lead, given to them by a majestic header by Keane Lewis-Potter, from Igor Thiago’s cross. It was a moment of attacking quality that Iraola’s glitzy attackers had looked unlikely to replicate, especially when Barcola fluffed a one-versus-one showdown with Brentford goalkeeper Caoimhin Kelleher.

To play an entire half of Premier League football with only 10 men is a brutal examination, though, and Brentford were unable to pass the test. Wirtz unleashed Muñoz after an hour, allowing the Spaniard to fire home with his left foot, before Barcola’s header found Isak in the box with 20 minutes remaining.

It was Isak’s fifth goal of the campaign, which means he has now beaten last season’s tally of four. He has scored in all five of his Premier League appearances against Brentford. “I didn’t have too many chances,” Isak said. “I was waiting for my moment.”

Any hopes of a Brentford comeback evaporated in stoppage time, when the home side lost another man to a red card. This time it was Vitaly Janelt, who received his second yellow for fouling Rio Ngumoha, Liverpool’s sparkling teenage winger. From there, Liverpool’s attempts to score a third were comically poor. “We lacked some composure,” admitted Iraola. “But it was a good battle today, and very important points for us. To take three points here is very valuable.”

An encouraging result for Liverpool, then, but this was not an afternoon without concerns. The first-half showing was worrying, and there were also injuries to Dominik Szoboszlai and Jeremie Frimpong. Both players limped off, and Iraola said they will now be out “for some time”.

The loss of Szoboszlai will be a particular concern, as he was rushed back from a hamstring injury for this game but then felt the same muscle again after only 32 minutes of action. “It’s a very delicate situation,” said Iraola.

The injury to Frimpong meant that Muñoz, a winger, played most of the second half as an attack-minded right-back. He did so excellently, and took his goal with impressive composure after Wirtz had pushed the ball into his path. Liverpool’s second was similarly clinical, as Isak pounced on Barcola’s knock-down in a congested penalty area. These, clearly, are the moments of game-changing quality that Liverpool expect from their big-money forwards. Iraola will hope it was a sign of things to come.

Speaking to Sky Sports after his first Premier League win as Fulham head coach, Arbeloa said: “I’m so happy, happy for my players, happy for my supporters, happy for everyone at the club that they deserve this victory. We [waited] a lot of time and some many games that I think we deserved this victory before, but today we did a very good game and yes, I can’t believe that the game finished just 1-0.”

One of the advantages of Iraola’s Anfield appointment was his Premier League experience with Bournemouth. The Basque well knows the division and has plenty of positive memories from which to borrow.

However, there will also be some scar tissue, and that certainly is the case with Brentford. Iraola never beat the Bees in seven attempts (five draws, two defeats), a run which included a 4-1 thrashing at the Gtech Community Stadium in his final season at Bournemouth.

It’s back-to-back wins for Chelsea and a rare clean sheet, their first since January. But all thoughts will be with Emi Martinez after his clash of heads with Branthwaite. Hopefully we get some good news on that front soon. Follow the latest updates here.

Enzo Maresca has been looking for opportunities for rest his key players - but Erling Haaland is a player that is impossible to rest. He has scored in his last seven matches and leads Manchester City’s attack again.

But Maresca has changed half of his team from the line-up defeated by Paris St-Germain in the week. Jeremy Doku and City’s first-choice centre-backs are the others to keep their place. The rest are drafted in to face Ipswich, with Matheus Nunes, Nico O’Reilly, Ayyoub Bouaddi, Iliman Ndiaye and Mateo Kovačić are drafted in.

There is also a place for Phil Foden after serving his three-match ban for getting dismissed in the Manchester derby.

Keith Andrews has established a clearly defined, direct style of play which speaks to Brentford’s strengths. His side are third in the Premier League for percentage of passes forward (39.2 per cent) and, coupled with the second-most high turnovers which end in a goal, Brentford have thrived off passages of organised chaos.

To play this way requires quality when you do have the ball, and full-backs Keane Lewis-Potter and Michael Kayode deserve particular praise. They have contributed materially to Brentford’s attacks, helping their side to league-high successful crosses (26) and expected goals from set-pieces (4.03).

Manchester City’s claim to have “irrefutable evidence” that will overturn their guilty verdict on appeal is based on a trove of emails, letters and bank statements.

A re-examination of Abu Dhabi government documents, receipts and testimony from 24 witnesses – all of which the club believe were wrongly dismissed at the original hearing – will be central in attempts to force a full or partial acquittal or retrial, according to people familiar with the case.

City’s legal team will attempt to demonstrate “fundamental errors” in tests applied by an independent commission to the Premier League’s case that commercial revenue was artificially inflated by £920m. Sources with understanding of City’s case have told Telegraph Sport the club are bullish about their appeal, based on:

Shahid Khan, Fulham’s owner, insists that his team are on a “positive path” despite remaining winless in the Premier League after six matches.

In his programme notes, he wrote: “I want to reflect on our recent form. Prior to the international break, we were trending upward… That momentum carried us through most of Saturday’s match at Ipswich Town, but we all know how that ended. The result was devastating for all of us, and I won’t pretend otherwise.

“And yet, I am reminded of the positive path we have been on and the genuine potential of this team. Our squad is strong, while still coming together. We have been in every match, missing only the opportunities we’ve had to complete the task. I believe those opportunities will soon be seized.”

This feels like an extremely treacherous trip for Liverpool and for Andoni Iraola, who has a poor record against Brentford. With Bournemouth, he did not win any of his six matches against today’s opponents.

The good news for Liverpool is that Alexander Isak and Dominik Szoboszlai are fit enough to start the game, and that Brentford top scorer Kevin Schade is not. Schade is on the bench after picking up a shoulder injury against Aston Villa last weekend.

Barcola opened his Liverpool account on Wednesday and he will look to continue his goal-scoring form at the Gtech Community Stadium.

Speaking of the France winger, head coach Andoni Iraola said: “I think it’s still very early, especially for him who hasn’t played any minutes in pre-season, he’s kind of been doing pre-season in the first games with us almost [in] official games.

“It’s remarkable because to score three goals in a Champions League game is … not a lot of players can say they have done it.

“It’s something nice for him but I think the best thing is we can feel him, he seems with confidence on the ball [away] from the goals, straight away you could feel he was confident going in one-to-one situations, attacking the spaces and [those] are his strengths.”

Good afternoon and welcome to our live coverage of the 3pm kick-offs. Manchester City burst the Anfield bubble last weekend but were defeated by Paris St-Germain in a Champions League thriller on Wednesday, and Enzo Maresca will have to manage his leading cast members’ workload. Before Ipswich Town’s visit to the Etihad he floated the idea of resting some of his players at some point.

“We are thinking about this not just with Erling [Haaland] because we have players, unfortunately or fortunately, they are playing all the games with us and all the games with the international teams,” Maresca said in his pre-match press conference.”

“Elliot [Anderson], Enzo [Fernández], Marc [Guéhi], Erling, Rúben [Dias] – so at some point we probably need to give them some rest.”

Ipswich’s spirited start to the season was characterised by a stunning late turnaround against Fulham last weekend. Gary O’Neil’s side have accrued three wins in their first six top-flight matches for the first time since 1993 and may consider today’s match as something of a free hit.

Elsewhere, Liverpool’s confidence-building midweek win in Austria was underlined by Bradley Barcola’s first, second and third goals for the club. It was exactly what the France winger needed, and with Alexander Isak and Cody Gakpo emerging as doubts for this afternoon’s trip to Brentford, the attacking burden may fall on Barcola and Florian Wirtz’s shoulders once more.

Breaking down fourth-placed Brentford, who are one of only three teams to remain undefeated this season, will be a tall task. Keith Andrews’ stock has never been higher, but the same cannot be said for Álvaro Arbeloa, whose winless Fulham are bottom of the league.

Pressure was already mounting before Fulham’s three-game run against the promoted teams, and the late collapse at Portman Road will not have helped the Spaniard’s cause. Defeat by Hull City will not be seen kindly by the club’s hierarchy.

#1351. Exclusive: Nick Montgomery On Managing In China And Working Under Postecoglou

Beijing Guoan are unbeaten in 21 games in all competitions, and last month's trip to Henan showed exactly why. Three goals down at half-time, Nick Montgomery’s side scored four times after the break. Zhang Yuning got the 81st-minute winner. It was the first time in Guoan's 33-year history they had ever won from three goals down.

It caps a superb first season in China for 44-year-old head coach Nick Montgomery. He won the Chinese FA Super Cup – China’s version of the Community Shield – in his first competitive game in March, and Guoan are also unbeaten through three games in the AFC Champions League Elite tournament. Thai side Port FC are up next on Tuesday.

Only a five-point deduction for historical breaches, handed down after Montgomery arrived, has kept Guoan out of the title race. Without it, they would go into the final-day fixture on November 8 against Chongqing Tonglianglong top of the table, ahead of current leaders Chengdu Rongcheng on goal difference. Instead, they are third, two points behind Dalian Yingbo, with a Chinese FA Cup semi-final against Shanghai Port to come on November 20.

A former Sheffield United midfielder, Montgomery won the A-League as a head coach with Central Coast Mariners and the Europa League as Postecoglou’s assistant at Tottenham. Now he is making his name in China.

Montgomery did not need much convincing. He had played in Beijing with the Mariners, and the memory never left him.

“If we’re talking about Beijing Guoan, we’re talking about one of the biggest clubs in Asian football, and it’s a club I know well because of my time playing in the A-League,” he told GIVEMESPORT. “I played in the Asian Champions League, and I remember, I think it was a Wednesday night, playing in Beijing. There were 40,000 fans, and that always stuck in my mind.”

After leaving Nottingham Forest, where he was Ange Postecoglou's assistant, Montgomery had plenty of offers but was waiting for the right one. It came from Matthias Brosamer, the German who had just been appointed Guoan’s new sporting director.

"He is a great guy, very intelligent. He speaks fluent Chinese, and we had some amazing football conversations," said Montgomery, who was appointed on 8 January. “He told me about the project. He was looking for a head coach with experience in Asia, and he really loved my profile. Things moved forward quickly, and probably within a week or two we’d agreed to take on the project. I was landing in Beijing in wintertime – I think it was minus 20 when I arrived – and that was the start of such an exciting journey.”

Working largely through translators, Montgomery knew his first job was to win people over. It didn't take him long.

“When you come into a new country, you’ve got to be brave to start with,” he said. “You’ve got to know there’s a period where you’ll have to get everybody to buy in – to you as a person, forget the football – because you’re coming into their culture. If they see you’re committed and believe in your style of football, then they’re going to support you. I have created a real family environment, which is important.”

The start could hardly have gone better. Guoan’s Super Cup triumph came against Shanghai Port, winners of the last three Chinese Super League titles, who were beaten 2-0 in Nanjing.

“We beat Shanghai Port, who were the benchmark team. They had players picking up ridiculous salaries over the years, the best squads,” said Montgomery, who knows Port boss Kevin Muscat from their days in Australia. “That was the first real game, so to win a trophy was a great start.”

Injuries soon took their toll, though, and Guoan won just four of their first 14 league games, the last of those a 2-1 home defeat by Henan on 23 May. They have not lost since.

“People said you can’t play like this in China, that the players are not resilient enough, and I never believed that,” he said. “The players showed me on the training ground every day. We don’t speak about being 21 games unbeaten. We just focus on the process.”

The biggest change has come up front, where Montgomery has paired China captain Zhang Yuning with Angola international Fábio Abreu.

“I always played in Australia with two strikers, and I play in China with two strikers, which I was told no one did before,” he said. “I was told they couldn’t play together. The previous season, only one of them played and the other was on the bench. Now they’re both top scorers in the team.”

Unfortunately, Guoan lost Abreu in mid-October after he broke his leg in a 1-0 win against Qingdao West Coast.

"We were very sad," said Montgomery. "He will miss the rest of the season. Most of our injuries have been contact ones, which is very unlucky. We have had to deal with many challenges this season, and that makes our form even more satisfying."

Guoan's numbers speak for themselves. They are also at or near the top of the league for possession, forward passes and touches in the opposition box.

“If the players don’t want to run for you, you’re never going to have those statistics,” Montgomery said. “That tells you Chinese players are honest. If they believe in you, they’ll do everything you ask.”

It is all the more impressive given Guoan started on minus five points – a deduction neither Montgomery nor Brosamer knew about when they took over.

“It was a bit of a shock to everybody. You’re on minus points before you even get to zero,” he said. “If we’d started on a level playing field, we’d be top of the league."

The title may be out of reach, but Montgomery will feel encouraged that, without the deduction, Beijing Guoan would be top. Second place is still possible if Guoan win their last league game againstChongqing Tonglianglong and Dalian Yingbo lose or draw. And there is the chance to defend the Chinese FA Cup, which Gooan won for the sixth time last season when they beat Henan 3-0 under former coach Quique Setien.

“We can’t win the league because of what happened, which is a shame, but we can still finish second,” Montgomery said. “In the cup, we’ve got a difficult game against Shanghai Port. They were the Galácticos of the Chinese Super League for the last couple of years. Players like Oscar and Hulk – all the big names – loved playing in China.”

In the AFC Champions League, Guoan beat Pohang Steelers 3-1 in the first Asian Champions League game at the Workers’ Stadium for seven years, before winning 1-0 at Buriram United – “a very difficult place to go”, according to Montgomery. They drew 2-2 with Jeonbuk Hyundai Motors on October 27 and are currently fifth in the league phase.

Montgomery is clearly relishing life in China, where Guoan have drawn crowds of more than 60,000 at the rebuilt Workers’ Stadium this season.

“What the Western world thinks of China is the total opposite of the reality. It’s so advanced,” he said. “The infrastructure in football is unbelievable. Our home games get 50,000 to 65,000 on a weekly basis. There aren’t many Premier League teams that can match that attendance. It is one of the best stadiums in the world – very similar to the Tottenham stadium, which I know very well.

“And there is the belief, moving forward, that the club can bring a championship back to Beijing for the first time since 2009, which is a long time ago.”

Montgomery made the decision that he wanted to return to work as a No.1 again after spending time as Ange Postecoglou's assistant at both Tottenham Hotspur (2024-2025) and Nottingham Forest (2025).

“It’s not like I would be an assistant for any manager,” he said. “I did get asked about being an assistant to another manager, but it wasn’t for me. I knew I was waiting for the right opportunity to get back into management.”

His route to Tottenham began with a message from Postecoglou, who was among the first to congratulate him when the Mariners won the A-League in 2023. A year later, Postecoglou’s assistant Chris Davies left to become Birmingham City manager.

“As with anything in life, it’s about timing,” Montgomery said. “Ange contacted me, we jumped on a call, and he said, ‘I’m going to win a trophy at Tottenham. I want you to come and help me.’ To be honest, I didn’t really need to think about it much. It was a pretty quick decision, and one I definitely don’t regret. Seeing the Tottenham fans at the parade with the trophy was something you can never forget.”

That parade followed Brennan Johnson’s winner against Manchester United in the Europa League final in Bilbao in May 2025, which ended Spurs’ 17-year wait for a trophy – even as an injury-ravaged side finished 17th in the Premier League.

“There was an unbelievable amount of injuries, and the squad was very, very thin,” said Montgomery, who joined in June 2024 with his long-time assistant Sergio Raimundo. “We had some big results, beating Man City 4-0 away and Man United 3-0, but after the injuries came, it was difficult. Winning the Europa League would get the club Champions League football, so you put all your eggs in one basket. As a staff, that’s what we all did. We believed we could win it, and that’s what we did.

“I think only now, or years after, will people look back and think what an amazing achievement that was, because it’s been a difficult ride since then – when you look at the amount of money they’ve spent.”

Even that was not enough to save Postecoglou, who was sacked 16 days after the final. Montgomery admits the staff saw it coming.

“Ange came out and said it in an interview, so for sure – everyone knew there was going to be a change no matter what happened,” he said. “So you have that laser focus on what you can control, and that was winning the Europa League. It was amazing for the club to get Champions League football the following season – it’s just a shame they didn’t give Ange and us that chance. But that’s football. You move on.”

When Postecoglou took over at Nottingham Forest in September 2025, Montgomery went with him, alongside Raimundo and fellow Spurs assistant Mile Jedinak. The Australian was sacked after 39 days and eight games without a win.

Asked what went wrong, Montgomery chose his words carefully.

“Probably the least I say, the better on that one,” he said. “It’s a club with a passionate owner [Evangelos Marinakis] that wants instant success, and it’s a club that is renowned for making changes – a lot of changes, as we’ve seen. So you’re never going to go in thinking, ‘This is a stable environment.’

“I was literally about to take an offer of a head coach role, and Ange said: ‘I think it’s a young squad, we can play good football, and I’d love you to come in with me again.’ It was a big boost, because we’d just come off the back of winning the Europa League. We all went in there wanting to do something, but there wasn’t much time.”

Forest have since been through Sean Dyche and Vítor Pereira, with Oliver Glasner appointed in July as their fifth head coach in less than a year.

“A lot of the performances were very good, but the results didn’t match them,” Montgomery added. “These type of projects depend on how much time people are willing to give you, and in the end, you’re not in control of that.”

One player he loved briefly working with was Elliot Anderson, who joined Manchester City for a reported £116m this summer.

“Elliot is a magnificent player, and I still keep in touch with him now. He literally never stops running and is brave on the ball – he just wants it all the time,” said Montgomery. “I think he’s definitely one of the best English midfielders I’ve seen, because he can do everything.”

Before Tottenham came Hibernian. Montgomery left Central Coast for Easter Road in September 2023, taking over a side who had lost their opening three league games.

“I had a lot of offers to go to Japan and other places, but I’ve got Scottish heritage in my family, and Hibs is a big club that hasn't had much success in a long time,” he said. “I was promised a rebuild. The club was bottom of the league and in a bit of a mess. I started well and took the team into the top three at one point. Then there was the Africa Cup of Nations and the Asian Cup, and we lost half the starting players.

“I felt I was building something really good, but we just missed out on the top six with the last kick of the ball. Then I had differences of opinion with the club over what had been promised in terms of the rebuild. You have the owner who wants his way, and in the end we chose to part ways. I moved on, went to Tottenham and won the Europa League. Everything happens for a reason.”

That last kick was Shane Blaney’s stoppage-time equaliser for Motherwell in April 2024, which let Dundee pip Hibs to the final top-six place. Hibs finished eighth, and Montgomery departed the following month – but he holds no grudges.

“I always believe every experience is a good experience – good, bad or indifferent,” he said. “Trust is a big thing for me. If you lose that trust, it’s difficult. But you grow from every experience.”

Montgomery’s methods were forged down under. After 12 years at Sheffield United, he joined Central Coast Mariners in 2012 and helped them win their first A-League Championship a year later. He made 133 appearances in all competitions and captained the club, then coached its academy side before stepping up to the top job in 2021. Two years later, he delivered the Mariners’ first title since his playing days.

“There were big teams spending a lot of money, like Sydney FC, Melbourne Victory and Melbourne City, and we were, comparatively, a small club,” he said. “As a coach, the club had suffered a lot of bottom-of-the-table finishes, with no budget compared to the other teams. I always believed I would take over the youth team, develop the players and push them into the first team when I got the opportunity for the job, and that came within two years.

“In my second season, we brought a lot more young players through and recruited some good foreign players. Jason Cummings, who many people will know in Scotland, was our top scorer. We beat Melbourne City 6-1 in the final with the youngest squad and lowest budget in history to win the championship, which was a massive achievement, and it made me really believe in myself as a coach.”

Cummings, the former Hibs striker, scored a hat-trick in that 2023 Grand Final, delivering the Mariners’ first title since Montgomery’s playing days a decade earlier.

“I never look too far ahead. One thing I remember Ange saying is: ‘They’ll only ever remember the people who win silverware.’ I think that’s true,” he said. “If you don’t win silverware, nobody really remembers your stint there. So making history with the three trophies I’ve been involved in, in such a short period of time as a young manager, makes you cherish those moments, because a lot of players and coaches go through their whole career without ever winning a trophy."

The excellent job Montgomery is currently doing is sure to catch the eye of other clubs around the world, including back in England. He is settled, and solely focused on some big games ahead to close this season with Guoan. Yet in the long run, the chance to manage in the Premier League would be hard to turn down.

“For me, I just take each day as it comes," he said. "For sure, maybe one day I would love to manage in the Premier League. But for now, being China is huge for me. I can't think of a better job right now for me, to be honest. I have a great sporting director [Brosamer] and president, Zhou Jinhui. They both support me and really believe in what I am doing.”

Once the domestic campaign ends, the AFC Champions League continues and will run on into next season. Should Guoan go deep, the finals are due to be held in Saudi Arabia next spring – where Postecoglou’s Al Nassr could be waiting.

“For me to represent Beijing, the capital of China, and get through to the knockout stage would be a huge moment for Chinese football,” he said. “There’s a long way to go, but who knows? It would definitely be good to see Ange if that happened.”

Almost two years on from Bilbao, it would be quite the reunion.

#1350. 'I have something unresolved': Ole Gunnar Solskjaer piles more pressure on old pal Michael Carrick as he says he WOULD manage Man United again - despite trying to back him to succeed

By LUKE AUGUSTUS, ASSISTANT SPORTS EDITOR

Published: 03:52 EDT, 2 November 2026 | Updated: 05:42 EDT, 2 November 2026

Ole Gunnar Solskjaer has admitted that he would be interested in returning as Manchester United manager in the future as he has 'something unresolved'.

Pressure is mounting on current head coach Michael Carrick as the Red Devils' dismal season continues to go from bad to worse.

After losing 2-0 at Chelsea on Saturday afternoon, United sit 17th in the Premier League - only above 18th-placed Crystal Palace on goal difference and just two points ahead of bottom side Sunderland.

Solskjaer has been in the Old Trafford hotseat before with his own path mirroring Carrick's from being an interim manager initially to becoming a permanent appointment.

The Norwegian had Carrick among his backroom staff before he was sacked as United boss in November 2021. When Ruben Amorim was sacked in January, both were interviewed as interim successors before Carrick was chosen.

And speaking about taking the reins at United in the future, Solskjaer revealed he would accept it.

Ole Gunnar Solskjaer (left) has revealed he would like to manage Manchester United in the future but backs current head coach Michael Carrick (right) to overturn the club's fortunes

Pressure is growing on Carrick which increased following Saturday's 2-0 defeat at Chelsea

Solskjaer was sacked as United manager in November 2021 after nearly three years in charge

'Going back to what has been is not always as good,' he told Norwegian outfit TV2.

'Yes, I had lined up [as Manchester United's interim manager last season], but I didn't think it would last longer than the summer. It was probably time for someone else to try.

'I also feel like I have something unresolved. Of course it would have been nice to have the opportunity again.'

Elaborating further, Solskjaer was keen to stress that he is not looking to oust his former United team-mate and friend Carrick.

'If Michael does well for 10 years and decides to quit, and they ask me if I can take them for two months, of course I wouldn't say no. I've been at that club for 18-19 years, so it's part of the family. But it's not something I'm thinking about.'

Despite growing scrutiny on Carrick, Solskjaer is adamant that the under-fire head coach can turn around the club's fortunes.

'Michael has what it takes to take that club forward. I think he's the right man. He understands the club, understands the fans and knows what's needed.'

Proof will be in the pudding with Carrick preparing his side for Tuesday's Champions League clash with Roma and then Sunday's Premier League encounter versus Aston Villa, both at Old Trafford, before the international break.

#1348. De Zerbi Loves Him: Nobody is Talking About Tottenham Star in Williams-Barnett’s Way

Tottenham Hotspur are flying high currently in the Premier League after finding their feet with three consecutive victories, and Roberto De Zerbi can do no wrong.

Spurs claimed a dominant 2-0 win over ten-man Crystal Palace this past weekend thanks to goals from Archie Gray and Jan Paul van Hecke in either half, moving them up to eighth in the table, and a win in the next game against Leeds could see them move up to fifth ahead of other games taking place over the weekend.

The north London club are even finding themselves in a position to hand young talents some minutes, with the Italian boss able to hand 18-year-old winger Luca Williams-Barnett an opportunity in the win over Palace.

The talented forward made an immediate impression too, beating his opposition full-back with ease on a number of occasions, and his dribbling leading to a huge opportunity for Mohammed Kudus to add a third goal, only for the Ghana international to miss the target from two yards out.

Savio has been dealing with injury issues so far during his time at the club, while Omar Marmoush has struggled massively with his form playing across the forward line, and Dominic Solanke seemingly doesn't fit the way the manager wants to play too well.

That has seen many people clamour for the teenage sensation to be handed a rare start against Leeds, with the short cameo he had in the most recent game enough to ignite the excitement among the fan base.

It would be a huge opportunity for the youngster, but it's also worth noting that he is getting these opportunities because of injury issues within the squad currently.

Savio remains sidelined until after the international break, while James Maddison and Dejan Kulusevski continue to deal with their own fitness issues following long-term injury problems. But another forgotten member of the squad is Chelsea loanee Mykhailo Mudryk, who is yet to feature after suffering a muscle problem back in September, and played for just 16 minutes prior to that issue.

De Zerbi has recently confirmed that he expects the Ukraine international to return to contention after the international break, and that could be a major issue for Williams-Barnett's chances of becoming a regular in the team.

While injuries mean that Williams-Barnett is getting a chance, good performances should see him keep his place in and around the team. But with the way De Zerbi has managed things so far, that seems unlikely.

Mudryk is someone that De Zerbi has been a huge fan of for a long time, having worked with him previously at Shakhtar, and even declaring that he could one day win the Ballon d'Or.

"We spent a very particular season together in Shakhtar," De Zerbi told a news conference in September.

"When the war started, we were together. And when I spoke about the Ballon d'Or, I was very clear. Maybe my English is not so good, but I was very clear because I was speaking about the potential of the player. The potential of the player can be the same and can respect the prediction or not.

"Until now, he has had many problems. The last problem, the suspension for whatever was the problem, but the [outcome] is clear. And now his challenge is to respect all his qualities because he's a great player. He has to leave this season in a right way, not too [much] pressure, but it is the right moment for him to show [his ability] because if Chelsea paid €100m four years ago ... I think they brought a lot of big, big players and to spend €100m, I think they thought very well about the qualities of Mudryk."

Having brought him into the club to strengthen the attack, it seems highly unlikely that when he's fit he won't be involved in the first-team picture more often than the teenager.

That may halt his development and also anger fans who want to see one of their own come through, especially ahead of a Chelsea player who didn't cut it at Stamford Bridge. It's something that De Zerbi will have to juggle with once the decision needs to be made, and the youngster may have the chance to ensure the decision is a difficult one against Leeds.

#1347. Liverpool's anonymous attackers cost them the chance of beating Arsenal despite dominant display... the gap to the champions is narrowing - but the Reds still aren't close enough, writes LEWIS STEELE

Published: 21:00 EDT, 1 November 2026 | Updated: 06:06 EDT, 2 November 2026

As disheartened fans spilled out of Anfield, nearly all conversations were about the referee and questions over why he did not point to the penalty spot in the first half when Jurrien Timber pulled back Alexander Isak.

They had a point and this game would have been completely different had Andy Madley – or VAR Stuart Attwell – seen what everyone else saw when Isak was an inch short of connecting with a header and possible goal because he was pulled back by his marker.

It was a similar situation to Liverpool’s only other defeat under new boss Andoni Iraola, where supporters were left aggrieved at the incorrect call to send off Ryan Gravenberch against Manchester City.

In both cases they were unlucky to be on the wrong side of refereeing mistakes and would have cursed the fine margins. But in both cases Reds fans will also realise their team just did not do enough to win too.

Just like against City, Liverpool dominated Arsenal for large parts of this match. It felt as though they were one magic moment or opposition mistake away from scoring and lfiting off the Anfield roof.

But in both cases, that moment never materialised. It felt like the Liverpool attackers were looking around waiting for somebody else to step up and be the man to start the pendulum swinging in Liverpool’s favour.

Alexander Isak and Liverpool's attackers struggled against Arsenal's defence

They had zero shots on target, according to Opta, and that is the only statistic that Iraola will be mulling over in the coming days.

Bradley Barcola, Florian Wirtz and Alexander Isak have all been frighteningly good in recent weeks but in this game, especially the second half, Liverpool’s big-money forwards looked like they had run out of ideas.

Arsenal defended like their lives depended on it and their away fans, who barely saw the ball down their end of the pitch after half-time, celebrated every Gabriel header or David Raya catch like a goal.

The home team, meanwhile, were left throwing long balls forward to Virgil van Dijk – the only player who could aerially compete with Arsenal’s team of giants. It felt like several Hail Mary passes but no one could answer Iraola’s prayers.

Liverpool’s two defeats to City and now Arsenal both demonstrate the gap between Iraola’s outfit and a genuine title contender. There is definitely a small level between Liverpool and Arsenal – but Reds fans can take solace in knowing it is not a chasm like last season.

A referee decision here, a better final ball there and Liverpool may be still unbeaten under Iraola and the whole country would consider them a title contender.

Iraola has closed the gap on the top teams but knows several tweaks are still needed to take that next step. Can they do it this season? It is far from impossible but seems a tall order.

The upcoming fixture list is kinder to them, at least. Of the current top eight, Liverpool have played all of them – two in the Carabao Cup – and won each test apart from City and Arsenal. The next two league games are against teams in 18th and 17th.

Florian Wirtz has improved recently but was unable to provide cutting edge on Sunday

But right now, Liverpool are a team with too many ‘ifs’, ‘buts’ and ‘maybes’. If Alexis Mac Allister did not get under a first-half header that looked like a certain goal… if the referee had given a clear foul on Isak… if the forwards packed their shooting boots.

As it was, for all of the nail-biting moments for Mikel Arteta on the touchline as Liverpool had lots of the ball in the final third, his goalkeeper David Raya could have had a cigar in and read the papers for most of the second half.

That is what will bother Iraola the most.

As for being a complete team able to compete for the league title again, Liverpool seem so close yet so far.

Trey Nyoni made his first Premier League start and it will not be his last after he put in a solid shift.

Though he misplaced some passes and was probably lucky to escape an early yellow card after two late challenges, the 19-year-old presents Iraola with an interesting tactical quirk.

The Englishman always wants the ball and drops into the back line to start attacks, with a maturity beyond his years.

He sits deep which allows Alexis Mac Allister to play as more of a box-to-box midfielder, undoubtedly his best position.

So where does this leave Ryan Gravenberch, who spent the afternoon on the bench? Given the amount of games Liverpool have across competitions, the Dutchman will still play many minutes — but he is currently at risk of falling down the pecking order thanks to the exciting talent of Nyoni.

There is also a conversation to be had about how Liverpool’s balance and control was lost when Nyoni was replaced by Dominik Szoboszlai.

Trey Nyoni excelled for the Reds and helped the home side control the tempo

Casual football fans who maybe only tune in for the big games have never seen Wirtz play well.

They must wonder what all the fuss is about.

The German has been on fine form in recent weeks but has been like a ghost — no Halloween pun intended — in the two biggest matches against City and Arsenal.

It is all well and good performing against teams like LASK in the Champions League but Wirtz, at £116million, was signed to make a difference in these blockbuster clashes.

Instead, his national team colleague Kai Havertz continued his record of impacting the games that really matter come May. How Wirtz could do with some of that killer instinct.
