#1331. Gabriel and Mac Allister's cheating is not just embarrassing, it's malevolent and wicked... players need the threat of red cards for such dishonesty and - if that fails - punishments after review, writes IAN LADYMAN

Published: 18:05 EDT, 1 November 2026 | Updated: 06:37 EDT, 2 November 2026

Football’s lawmakers like to meddle. The problem is they do it in areas that tend not to need any meddling. Like around handball and offside and other places that were doing just fine as they were.

So here’s a tip for the meddlers at the International Football Association Board. Meddle somewhere that needs it. Meddle in a way that would be meaningful and important and in a way that would actually help the game.

Please meddle with cheating. Please do something that would spare us from the embarrassment of grown men behaving like children in a bid to get other players booked and sent off. Yes, please meddle there.

Because football at the top level really needs it.

It needs a route through which players such as Alexis Mac Allister and Gabriel Magalhaes can be properly punished, shamed and embarrassed for what they did during Sunday’s otherwise fabulous Premier League game between Liverpool and Arsenal at Anfield.

It needs a deterrent. It needs greater power to match referees and greater leeway for retrospective punishment.

Alexis Mac Allister drops to the floor holding his face after his forehead is slightly brushed

The Liverpool man tried to get Noni Madueke sent off during Arsenal's 1-0 victory at Anfield

In a way, it is handy that there was one from each team this time. That way, we can be spared the usual accusations of bias that tend to come when footballers are called out for their sins.

Here, live on TV, Gabriel and Mac Allister were both as bad as each other. One in each half, clear as day.

Arsenal defender Gabriel was poked in the chest early on by Aleksandar Isak and went down holding his face. Then, much later, Liverpool’s Mac Allister was brushed by the forehead of Noni Madueke and did likewise.

Neither fooled referee Andy Madley. Both were told to get up and get on with the game. On TV, Sky Sports analysts Gary Neville and Jamie Carragher didn’t hold back.

‘Embarrassing’ was the word they both chose. Neville to describe Gabriel and Carragher as a way of calling out Mac Allister.

But this type of chicanery is more than that. We see it from lots of players and we see it all the time. It’s not just embarrassing. It goes much deeper. It’s malevolent. It’s low. It’s pre-meditated. It’s wicked.

Short of dark subjects such as spitting and leg-breaking tackles, I can’t think of much worse things on a football field than pretending to have a head or facial injury when you actually haven’t.

So where IFAB need to get involved – where they need to ‘meddle’ – is simple. They must increase football’s powers to punish.

On the field and in the moment, referees can issue yellow cards for simulation and for cheating. Players can be booked for exaggerating contact (Mac Allister) or pretending contact has been made with a certain area of the body when it hasn’t (Gabriel).

Arsenal defender Gabriel Magalhaes performed a similar act of cheating in the first half

The Brazilian fell down clutching his face after Alexander Isak brushed his neck and chest

But why is there no power – at least in occasional and exceptional circumstances - to issue a red card?

Gabriel and Mac Allister appeared to be trying to get their opponents sent off. Would they do it if they knew the match referee at least had the option of showing them the red card instead?

Retrospectively, meanwhile, we need greater leeway for action.

Under a law passed a decade ago, a player can theoretically be banned by a review panel for two-games for ‘successful deception of a match official’. However the reality is that the initiative has largely been superseded by VAR and was only really used for players diving to try and win penalties anyway.

In terms of the nonsense we witnessed at Anfield on Sunday – and indeed see on a reasonably regular basis around the country – there is very little recourse once the game is over so once again a possible deterrent has been removed from the equation.

Cheating of this nature currently looks and feels like a risk worth taking and that is what must change.

Alexander Isak was not given a penalty despite being blatantly pulled back by Jurrien Timber

Here, it was interesting to hear Liverpool manager Andoni Iraola suggest afterwards that he must start telling his players to go down under contact. He was talking about Isak’s refusal to buckle under a clear penalty area shirt tug from Jurrien Timber.

That’s an important issue, too. Players should not be punished for their honesty. A foul is a foul, regardless of the reaction. VAR should have awarded a penalty.

But here on an otherwise fine day for the Premier League, another known and rather ugly blot on the landscape grew larger.

The threat of red cards for cheating and – if that fails - punishments handed down by review. That’s the kind of meddling we should all be on board with.

#1330. Official: Udinese sack Runjaic with Zanetti lined up

Udinese have officially sacked Kosta Runjaic, with Paolo Zanetti set to take over as head coach.

According to Calciomercato.com, the club announced the decision on Monday after days of reflection, and only Zanetti’s signature is needed to complete his appointment.

Runjaic paid the price for a dreadful run. Udinese have gone eight matches without a win, and their only league victory came against Monza on 29 August. Saturday’s 5-2 home defeat to Roma was the final straw. It left the Bianconeri on five points from 10 games, just above the relegation zone on goal difference.

The club released the following statement:

“Udinese Calcio has announced that Kosta Runjaic has been relieved of his duties as first team head coach.

“The club and the coach part ways, having worked together for over two years and achieved important objectives.

“Udinese Calcio would like to give its sincere thanks to Kosta and his staff members, Przemyslaw Małecki and Alexander Trukan, and wishes them the very best in their future professional endeavours.”

Zanetti has been out of work since Verona sacked him in February. According to Sky Sport Italia, Udinese have set strict terms for the new coach: a contract only until June, and a limit of two members of his own staff.

His first game is likely to be a crucial relegation clash away to bottom side Venezia on Friday.

#1329. Tandem repeat variation shapes immune cell type-specific gene expression

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Tandem repeats (TRs)—highly polymorphic, repetitive sequences across the human genome—are important regulators of gene expression but remain underexplored due to challenges in accurate genotyping and analysis1. Here we generate whole-genome and single-cell RNA sequencing from more than 5.4 million blood-derived cells across 1,925 individuals in two cohorts2, and perform meta-analysis to characterize the impact of variation in more than 1.7 million TR loci on immune cell type-specific gene expression. We identify more than 69,000 single-cell expression quantitative trait loci, 30.7% of which are specific to 1 of 28 immune cell types, and reveal dynamic regulatory effects using cell-state inference. Matched single-cell assay for transposase-accessible chromatin with high-throughput sequencing profiles from more than 3.4 million nuclei in 922 individuals3 uncover chromatin accessibility quantitative trait loci for nearly one-third of expression-associated TRs, supporting coordinated effects on cis-regulatory architecture. Fine-mapping implicates 1,490 TRs as candidate causal drivers of gene expression in 6.1% of tested genes, and colocalization analyses highlight more than 200 genes in which TRs likely mediate genetic associations with immune and haematological traits. Together, these results provide a genome-wide, multiomic view of TR-mediated regulation in the human immune system, establishing TRs as key contributors to cell type-specific regulatory variation and complex trait architecture.

a, Distribution of number of distinct alleles per locus. b, Distribution of mode allele per locus. c, Distribution of summed alleles (of a diploid genotype). X-axis truncated at 100 repeats. Overall, 13.7% of alleles represented expansions relative to the locus-specific mode, 9.3% were contractions, and the remainder matched the mode allele exactly. The median summed dosage across all loci was 14 repeat units. Following stringent filtering for call quality and locus-level metrics (Methods), the resulting high-confidence callset had a median of 6 distinct alleles per locus and a median mode allele length of 9 repeats.

Bulk eTR catalogs were based on GTEx11,36 (bulk RNA-seq of whole blood; FDR < 10% for STRs and <5% for VNTRs) and gEUVADIS96 (bulk RNA-seq of HapMap lymphoblastoid cell lines; FDR < 5%) datasets. Differences in cell type/tissue resolution, TR genotyping methods, and analysis pipelines limit interpretability of direct comparisons. In particular, cell type-specific signals discovered in TenK10K Phase 1 may be diluted in bulk tissue, and TR catalogs used in prior studies may not capture loci genotyped in TenK10K Phase 1.

Distributions of sc-eTR effect sizes stratified by MANE gene annotation (a), ENCODE candidate cis-regulatory element (cCRE) annotation (b), and motif length (c). Violin plots show the distribution; centre lines indicate medians, boxes indicate interquartile ranges (IQRs), and whiskers extend to 1.5 × IQR. MANE annotations: 5′ untranslated region (5′ UTR), coding sequence (CDS), and 3′ untranslated region (3′ UTR). Unadjusted P values were calculated using two-sided Mann–Whitney U tests (n = 112,100 sc-eTRs). In a, **P = 3.4 × 10−7 and *P = 1.6 × 10−4; in b, **P = 2.5 × 10−3 and *P = 3.1 × 10−3; in c, ***P = 6.1 × 10−9, **P = 2.6 × 10−7, and *P = 5.0 × 10−6.

UMAP plots of B cells (n = 539,820 cells) first labeled by cell identity, then subsequently labeled by low (15th percentile), medium (between 15th and 85th percentile) and high (above 85th percentile) activity scores for cell functions of natural killer cell activation, response to multicellular organisms, and protein localization to membrane. Swarmplots demonstrate a cell state-specific poly(TTTG) sc-eTR associating with SYNGR1 expression across the natural killer cell activation axis in n = 1,925 individuals. Horizontal bars indicate the first quartile, median, and third quartile. P values were calculated using two-sided Wald tests of the regression coefficient (β) and are uncorrected for multiple testing.

For each scenario, from left to right: brief description of the scenario, association swarm plots for the lead TR in each of the two cell types (n = 1,925 individuals; horizontal bars indicate the first quartile, median, and third quartile), association plots of all tested variants around the gene, with signals for both cell types overlaid. P values were calculated using two-sided Wald tests of the regression coefficient (β) and are uncorrected for multiple testing. #1328. Slow and dull Man Utd are just not good enough

Manchester United are like John Toshack’s duvet. You fix one problem – being far too vulnerable to conceding goals – only to create another – lacking the threat to score. It is all very Meh United not Man United. The indisputable fact is they are just not very entertaining to watch. They are slow and dull.

In the end it also points to another thing. The thing highlighted in midweek by Lisandro Martínez after the Champions League defeat at Atlético Madrid: they do not have the strength in depth to compete.

What they do have appears to not be fit for purpose. Certainly Michael Carrick, the under-pressure manager, is struggling to get the best out of the resources he has.

“It’s like a duvet,” Toshack, the former Real Madrid and Wales manager, famously said of football. “If you pull it up, your feet get cold. If you pull it down, your shoulders get cold.”

There will have been times in the last few days, with the intense criticism and scrutiny over his future, when Carrick will have simply felt like dragging that duvet up over his head and keeping it there.

Defeat by Leeds United would have been unthinkable. It would have put Carrick under potentially intolerable pressure in what appears to be a pivotal week, with Como away in the Champions League and a home Premier League fixture against Bournemouth in the coming days.

Was this a lifeline or the tightening of the noose for Carrick? Time will soon tell. The relief of avoiding defeat was tempered by the reality of it now being just one win in their opening seven league games – at home to newly promoted Ipswich Town – and they are down in 13th place. It is six games without a win in all competitions.

That is unacceptable and is their fewest number of league victories in a top-flight campaign since 1986-87. Back then they sacked their manager in November and brought in a certain Alex Ferguson.

The hard truth is Carrick needs to start collecting some “Ws” in those results columns. United are already 14 points behind leaders Manchester City and five outside the probable Champions League places. Qualifying again for that tournament must be the minimum expectation.

Ruben Amorim, Carrick’s predecessor, lost his job within 24 hours of the same 1-1 scoreline at Elland Road last season – dismissed after Martínez-like explosive comments again aimed at director of football Jason Wilcox. Carrick will not suffer the same fate after this, but the ice is becoming increasingly thin.

We have seen this movie before at United. A slow start to the season, a period of drift, falling out of contention, no reaction on the pitch, backing from the hierarchy that becomes increasingly unconvincing. And then a change.

Can Carrick, who genuinely does still retain support at the highest level, alter that pattern? Does he have it in him? Is he too passive like his team? Carrick said this draw felt like a “fresh start”, but on this evidence that comment can be classified as wildly optimistic.

Having directed his criticism at the United hierarchy, and specifically Wilcox, the former Leeds winger who was here, over a lack of summer signings, Martínez apologised and was named in the starting XI. But the Argentine only lasted to half-time, withdrawn injured with a tight thigh, and sat watching the second half with his hood up over his head.

What United did sign in the last window was three midfielders – at a cost of £155m – and all three started: Carlos Baleba alongside Andrey Santos with Youri Tielemans in the No 10 role, which meant Bruno Fernandes was pushed out to the left, from where he constantly wanted to come in-field, with Amad Diallo on the right.

Carrick talked of having a “fresh spine” as well as that fresh start. But it did not make for a potent combination even if, further forward, Bryan Mbeumo played through the middle and scored one. He should have scored another.

Bryan Mbeumo finds the net this time to put Manchester United 1-0 up at Leeds! 🔴 https://t.co/NKDIhlUND1

But beyond that United created little. “It was a dominant performance against Man United,” Daniel Farke, the Leeds manager, claimed. He was right. If one team deserved to win it was his. They had the chances but snatched at them with Anton Stach, in injury time, having a weak shot cleared off the line by Martínez’s replacement Noussair Mazraoui after a mistake by goalkeeper Senne Lammens. Stach had to score.

United were ahead at half-time. Mbeumo had headed wastefully wide when unmarked but did well to force his way past James Justin and meet a low cross from Tielemans to poke the ball home. The way the usually undemonstrative Carrick punched the air in his technical area showed the pressure he felt. It was something to build on. To gain control.

Leeds had started well but did not really pose much of a threat – beyond forcing Lammens to save well from Nico Elvedi’s downward header – and maybe the earlier kick-off subdued the crowd. This was far from a bear pit.

But after the break, Leeds were comfortably the better side. The nature of their equalising goal, with Dominic Calvert-Lewin too strong and alert for first Baleba and then Mbeumo to fire in from a corner, exposed the enduring softness at the heart of United.

Dominic Calvert-Lewin equalises for Leeds against Manchester United 👊 https://t.co/mnpyxZJKbm

And that must be addressed by Carrick, especially as he appeared to sacrifice attacking intent by shoring up defensively. But that duvet is looking far too inadequate right now. Or Carrick is making it appear so.

Michael Carrick says he has put on “the headphones” this week in an effort to drown out the noise, but admitted Manchester United have to stop their struggles from snowballing.

United sit just two points above the relegation zone after a 1-1 draw at Leeds left them with just one win from their opening seven Premier League matches.

Carrick claimed the result felt like a “fresh start” after a week in which Lisandro Martínez publicly apologised for criticising Jason Wilcox, the United director of football, and the Old Trafford board.

But the United manager acknowledged their position “doesn’t look too good” and that they must start winning soon to stop the club from entering another doom cycle.

“Listen, we’re not accepting it as everything’s great by any stretch, so I’m realistic with that,” said the United manager, who claimed “the headphones have been on this week”.

“But sometimes you do struggle, sometimes there’s a bit of it where you have to find a way through it. We haven’t really had to go through that yet [before now] and we have to find a way through it.

“There has been a cycle at times here over a period of time when it can go in different directions. We’ve got to be stable enough to keep doing the right things for the right reasons as a group, and we’re more than capable of winning football matches.

“I understand the situation doesn’t look too good if you look at it from a certain way, but I’ve no doubts we can go on a good run.”

United face Como in the Champions League in Italy on Wednesday before Bournemouth visit Old Trafford four days later.

Carrick said he remains convinced United can still have a strong campaign, despite their worst start to a season for 40 years. I know what we’ve got in the changing room, where we want to get to, how we want to get there,” he said. “We know we can do it.

“We’ve done it for some time, and we feel we’re a better group now, and I do feel that. Sometimes it doesn’t always show, but you get a feeling and I’m encouraged by a lot of things. And if we keep doing the right things, I think we can still have a really good season.”

Asked if he would be putting the headphones back on this week ahead of two more pivotal games, Carrick added: “Nah, it’s always quiet for me.”

Martínez was substituted at half-time at Elland Road with a tight thigh just days after his tirade at club executives and Marcus Rashford was left out for “purely tactical” reasons. “Nothing personal, the front players were doing a good job on and off the ball,” Carrick said. “Everyone is ready for Wednesday.”

The Leeds boss told Sky Sports: “We are slightly disappointed it is just a point. Overall, I felt it was not necessary to be losing at half time but it is still Manchester United. Second half, we got the equaliser, we should have kept up the dominance, too many strikes went over the crossbar but it was overall a solid performance. We should have won the game but we move on.

“We took it as a compliment that we have done many things right over the last month if we were seen as favourites against Manchester Untiedbut we have earned this. We wanted to prove the comments right.

“We were the dominant side but we couldn’t capitalise as we lacked quality in and around the box.

“It says a lot about how much respect we have earned. Overall, this is where we are at the moment and overall, it is a good place to be.

“It is still difficult in this league to win points. You have to be clinical and be very, very effective but we have to keep going.”

Speaking to Sky Sports, he said: “I think we could’ve played with a bit more quality in the final third, particularly in the first half. We were getting good quality in the box but just not enough numbers.

“We made sure in the second half we came out with more confidence going forward. I think we were unlucky not to win the game.

“They tried to [match us up formation-wise]. Not surprised given what happened last season. They were probably looking at our physical output and the way we liked to play and tried to go man-for-man.

“It took us a little bit to adjust to it, but I don’t think it was too difficult to adjust. It was more down to us and maybe a lack of quality in the final third.”

Brighton & Hove Albion 5 Crystal Palace 0

It’s all over at Elland Road, with Leeds and Man Utd playing out a competitive draw. Mbeumo’s opener was cancelled out by Calvert-Lewin’s equaliser in a game that was low on attacking quality and chances. Ultimately, a draw was a very fair reflection of the match. Man Utd are 14th and winless in six games across all competitions, while Leeds move into the top seven.

FULL-TIME: Dominic Calvert-Lewin earns a point for Leeds against Manchester United 💪 https://t.co/yDzLRE3Ir5

There are two yellow cards in quick succession as Ampadu is cautioned for a late tackle on Amad. Andrey Santos runs over and barges into the Leeds captain to earn himself a booking. The referee quickly calms then drama down.

Unconvincing goalkeeping from Lammens as he only punches Ampadu’s cross as far as Stach, whose tame shot squeezes through the Belgian’s legs. However, it’s blocked by the Man Utd defence and Lammens eventually gathers the ball.

There will be four minutes of added time. Can either side snatch a late victory?

Three times now United have looked like they’re about to get away down the flanks in the last few minutes and each time they’ve been flagged offside (Amad twice, Mbeumo once) and each occasion the player was able to look across the line. Carrick looked to the heavens. And he’s right to be frustrated. So avoidable.

Nmecha and Maguire challenge for the ball in the air, with the Man Utd defender bumping into the back of the Leeds substitute’s head. The crowd half-heartedly appeal for a penalty, but it’s quickly checked and cleared by VAR.

Carrick responds with a positive, attacking switch as Tielemans departs for Cunha.

Farke makes another change for Leeds as Longstaff replaces Tanaka in midfield.

Excellently goalkeeping from Trafford, who dashes out of his six-yard box to collect Andrey Santos’ pass and keep the ball in his grasp while staying in his box under the watchful eye of Mbeumo.

Dalot drives forward and leads a counter-attack. He passes to Amad, who forces a corner as Leeds get back well and recover. Man Utd take a clever short corner routine, but it ends with Mount scuffing an effort wide.

Both teams make changes. For Leeds, Nmecha replaces Okafor, while Mount enters the action for Man Utd as Baleba is withdrawn. The Englishman will sit alongside Andrey Santos in the away side’s midfield pivot.

From presentable range, Fernandes curls an effort straight into Trafford’s arms. Dalot then fails to adequately deal with a cross, heading the ball only as far as Stach. However, the Leeds midfielder wildly lashes his strike over the bar.

United were under that cosh in that period after Leeds equalised but they’ve gained a foothold back in the game now and a bit of frustration has crept in among the home fans. Stach the third player to fire high over the bar. Could go either way this.

How much longer will Carrick wait before making some changes in forward areas? His side need some renewed attacking impetus. The Man Utd head coach has Rashford, Cunha, Mount and Zirkzee all on the bench to choose from.

Okafor attempts to spearhead a Leeds break by playing in Calvert-Lewin. However, his pass is poor and it’s intercepted by Maguire. Amad is down after being caught by Tanaka earlier in that phase of play.

On the turn, Fernandes drags a low effort wide of the far post in a rare attacking flurry for Man Utd in this second half.

Ampadu feels Leeds should have a penalty as he collides with Maguire at a corner. The Man Utd defender hauls the Leeds captain to the floor. It’s been checked and cleared by VAR, but Maguire was taking a huge risk there.

Michael Carrick will surely be angry at the way Manchester United have started the second-half. One-nil up they have been far too slow and casual - highlighted by Dominic Calvert-Lewin’s goal which was embarrassingly easy to score from a corner. Leeds now on top and a huge few minutes ahead for Carrick.

Gudmundsson’s searching cross can’t quite find Calvert-Lewin as Man Utd scramble it clear. The away side’s backline has three defenders playing out of position, and they’ve been made to pay by Leeds’ leveller.

How will Man Utd cope with that setback? Leeds are putting them under serious pressure and have flown out of the blocks since the break as Tanaka volleys over from outside the penalty area.

The hosts finally have something to shout about at Elland Road! Leeds have a corner and Muharemovic beats Mazraoui to the delivery. The defender glances the ball to Calvert-Lewin, who holds off Mbeumo before smashing a close-range half-volley into the bottom corner. Elland Road goes wild and Leeds now have the momentum at the start of this second half.

Dominic Calvert-Lewin equalises for Leeds against Manchester United 👊 https://t.co/mnpyxZJKbm

It looks like a straight swap as Mazraoui slots in as a centre back, with Yoro continuing to deputise on the right.

We are back under way the second half. Martinez has been withdrawn at half-time, with Mazraoui on as his replacement, while Leeds are unchanged.

That is a really good half for Manchester United. More for the scoreline than the performance, although they have grown into the game after a sluggish start. Bryan Mbeumo’s goal will come as a huge relief to Michael Carrick. Leeds, in truth, have been a disappointment although they were denied the opening goal by Senne Lammens with a fine save. They needs to raise the tempo and the crowd. It is far too quiet. If Manchester United can hold on or build on this it will be a huge result for their under-pressure manager.

Carrick will be delighted with that first half. Man Utd have frustrated Leeds, defended valiantly and found the all-important breakthrough thanks to Mbeumo’s opener. Despite all the drama leading up to this game, Man Utd look really organised and unified, limiting Leeds to very little in forward areas.

Ahead at the break 👊🔴 https://t.co/rSSC8Pu4iG

There will be two minutes of added time. Can Man Utd protect their lead until the break?

Bogle drives into Man Utd’s box and squeezes a shot through a sea of bodies. However, it trickles into Lammens’ arms.

A big few minutes here for Manchester United. They need to see this half out. The goal has really steadied them but important they take that lead into the interval.

Calvert-Lewin attempts to latch onto Bogle’s clipped cross, but he directs it harmlessly wide.

Carrick’s game plan has worked perfectly so far. Man Utd soaked up the early pressure with their determined defending, before growing in confidence over the last 10 minutes. Mbeumo’s goal was much deserved.

You could see what that goal meant to Michael Carrick. He’s not one to show his emotions but he punches the air and wears the steely look of a man who knows how important it was to get the first goal here.

Mbeumo missed an earlier chance, but he makes no mistake with that one! Amad slips in Tielemans, who whips a magnificent cross into Mbeumo. The forward shows great composure and guides the delivery into the bottom corner.

Bryan Mbeumo finds the net this time to put Manchester United 1-0 up at Leeds! 🔴 https://t.co/NKDIhlUND1

The crowd loves that as Trafford sprints way out of his box almost to the halfway line to beat Amad to a ball over the top. Man Utd then make a promising break through Mbeumo, whose tame effort is easily gathered by Trafford.

Bogle attempts to take everyone on as he dribbles into Man Utd’s penalty area. He glides away from Dalot and Martinez, but overruns it, allowing Maguire to come across and shepherd the ball out of play.

Chants of “you soft southern b------” from the Leeds fans every time a Manchester United player goes down injured. Just a reminder that Leeds is actually only 22 miles further north than Manchester.

The away side are growing into this contest, with a slick move seeing Baleba find Dalot. The right back sprints into Leeds’ box, but he’s tackled well by Bogle.

Mbeumo misses a massive opportunity! Tielemans clips in a cross and an unmarked Mbeumo finds space between Elvedi and Muharemovic but heads wide. He has to get that on target.

Bryan Mbeumo comes close to giving Manchester United the lead 😬 https://t.co/j5PFXa2Uhe

Leeds test Lammens! Stach whips in a free kick, which is met by Elvedi, whose downward header is parried away by Lammens. That’s Leeds’ best chance so far, but the Man Utd goalkeeper did his job.

Leeds have enjoyed nearly 70% possession, but they’re yet to have a shot of any note. That’s testament to Man Utd’s competitiveness and organisation. Bogle then digs out a promising cross, but Yoro heads it away at the back post.

In fairness to Man Utd, they’re defending solidly and doing well to frustrate Leeds. Gudmundsson is then carded for catching Andrey Santos on his ankle with a very unpleasant challenge. It’s been such a physical and scruffy match so far.

Risky from Fernandes as he lunges in with a dangerous challenge on Muharemovic. Leeds then break as Martinez misses his tackle on Calvert-Lewin, but Stach’s cross is blocked. When the ball eventually goes out of play, Fernandes is booked for that earlier challenge. He can have no complaints.

United staff aggrieved that Fernandes should be booked but Ampadu escape a yellow card before then for arguably a worse challenge on Mbeumo, whom he caught thick on the ankle with his studs.

🫡 Ethan Ampadu starts as captain for the 100th time, becoming the youngest player to reach that milestone since Billy Bremner! https://t.co/80YrU08S3s

No early rhythm in this game so far. It’s still a little frantic at the moment, with Leeds having most of the ball and trying to force the issue.

Leeds crunch into a couple of heavy challenges on the Man Utd players in these early exchanges. Stach is eventually penalised for a strong tackle, but it’s a purposeful start from the hosts.

Interestingly, it looks like Fernandes is starting centrally in the ‘false nine’ position, with Mbeumo and Amad out on the wings. The Man Utd captain started out wide in Spain on Wednesday - an experiment that definitely did not work.

We are under way at Elland. Can Leeds pile more misery on Man Utd or will the visitors answer their critics with a much-needed win?

Leeds striker Dominic Calvert-Lewin was the only player not to take the knee prior to kick-off for the Premier League’s ‘No Room for Racism’ campaign. The gesture from the other players was roundly booed by a lot of the fans inside Elland Road.

Both teams are out on the pitch, with kick-off fast approaching.

With just 10 minutes until kick-off, here’s a recap of the two squads.

Leeds: Trafford, Justin, Elvedi, Muharemovic, Bogle, Ampadu, Tanaka, Gudmundsson, Stach, Okafor, Calvert-Lewin.

Subs: Zetterer, Longstaff, Wilson, Aaronson, Nmecha, Bijol, Bahoya, Bard, Gruev.

Man Utd: Lammens, Yoro, Maguire, Martinez, Dalot, Santos, Baleba, Fernandes, Tielemans, Diallo, Mbeumo.

Subs: Darlow, Mazraoui, de Ligt, Mount, Rashford, Cunha, Zirkzee, Lacey, Amass.

"I'm torn a little bit" Gary Neville says there should be some 'consequences' for Lisandro Martínez's comments after Man Utd's loss to Atlético Madrid ⤵️ https://t.co/oz8Mj24NuH

"We've moved on" Michael Carrick on Lisandro Martínez starting for Man Utd 🔴 https://t.co/mKVnI3gTrT

"We know what we need to do today" Ethan Ampadu speaks ahead of Leeds' clash with Man Utd ⚔️ https://t.co/wT5H5uzX7b

There have been wide open spaces in Manchester United’s side for opponents to exploit this season so it’s no surprise to see Michael Carrick keep faith with an extra body in midfield. It could make for a rather disjointed set up.

Lisandro Martinez keeps his place despite his rant at the Old Trafford board in midweek but the bigger concern has been his individual performances this season - they have been nowhere near good enough and he’s brought extra scrutiny on himself with the tirade. Bruno Fernandes is going to have to operate out wide you would think if Youri Tielemans plays centrally ahead of Carlos Baleba and Andrey Santos.

Leeds are the kind of compact, organised, aggressive in-your-face team United have tended to struggle against in recent years. They were good in defeat to Arsenal last weekend and showcased their considerable threat in the 4-1 win over Newcastle. Expect a white-hot atmosphere at Elland Road. They cannot stand Manchester United in these parts.

Lisandro Martínez delivered a strong and powerful message to his Manchester United team-mates: if you’re playing terribly, use the director of football as a punchbag and you might become a hero.

It is a popular play in a world in which certain players have become as adept at scapegoat-hunting as man-marking. Passionately speak about what someone else at your football club is doing wrong – particularly the unloved executives – and cast yourself as a whistleblower, selflessly exposing the truth that the long-suffering supporters deserve.

Such internal fights make for great drama, unless your own club is caught in the middle of it.

That’s why in the immediate aftermath of Martínez’s scathing comments about Jason Wilcox following the Champions League defeat by Atlético Madrid, there was a division between those who celebrated the Argentine speaking out and those who felt it was self-serving, a convenient deflection by an out-of-form player in the final year of his contract.

The narrative is completely dominated by the drama around Man Utd, which should suit Leeds perfectly. All eyes and pressure is on their opponents, and they have every reason to feel confident ahead of this huge clash at Elland Road.

Luke Shaw remains unavailable through injury, with Leny Yoro, who was sent off in midweek, deputising at full-back. Kobbie Mainoo is also sidelined, while Matheus Cunha and Marcus Rashford are benched. With Benjamin Sesko still out, Bryan Mbeumo starts up top and is likely to be supported out wide by Amad Diallo and Bruno Fernandes.

The big news is that Lisandro Martinez starts for the visitors, despite his scathing outburst earlier in the week. Michael Carrick also starts Carlos Baleba for the second match running, and he’s partnered in midfield by Andrey Santos and Youri Tielemans. Just 10 months on from Ruben Amorim’s final game in charge of Manchester United, the club return to Elland Road on Sunday afternoon with another manager under pressure and the director of football again in the spotlight.

The difference is Michael Carrick still has a chance to determine the course of his United future whereas Amorim had already sealed his fate after a furious bust-up with Jason Wilcox 48 hours before his last game ended in a 1-1 draw with Leeds and post-match fireworks.

But even for a club never far from a crisis, it seems remarkable to think they are back in a tailspin so soon after Amorim’s sacking in early January.

Good afternoon and welcome to our live coverage of this mouthwatering Premier League fixture between Manchester United and Leeds United at Elland Road.

Quiet week in the world of Man Utd? Don’t be silly. Following a 2-0 defeat in the Champions League against Atlético Madrid in Spain on Wednesday, defender Lisandro Martinez launched an extraordinary attack on Man Utd’s director of football Jason Wilcox and the club’s hierarchy because of a dreadful start to the campaign, which has yielded two victories in nine games across all competitions.

The Argentine criticised Man Utd’s recruitment and said he expected more, but didn’t suggest Carrick was to blame. Martinez has since apologised for his outburst and met with Wilcox, Man Utd chief executive Omar Berrada and Michael Carrick, with Telegraph Sport understanding that he’s free to play today, although his role remains unclear as we all eagerly await the team news.

Carrick is under immense pressure to get a result here in Yorkshire, with last weekend’s 1-1 draw with 10-man Tottenham at Old Trafford condemning Man Utd to their worst league start for 40 years.

With all eyes on the visitors, Leeds will be licking their lips at the prospect of piling further misery on their beleaguered opponents. Daniel Farke’s side suffered their first Premier League loss last weekend, falling 2-1 to Arsenal at the Emirates after going a goal up, but the mood remains positive after a solid start to the campaign.

Leeds are eighth and the club will be harbouring ambitions of a top-half finish in the Premier League for the first time since the 2019/20 season, with the prospect of qualifying for European football not out of the realm of possibility.

Unlike Man Utd, Leeds have a settled, reliable system that clearly suits their current squad. Elland Road will also be a cauldron of hostility and noise, given the fierce backdrop between these two bitter rivals.

This has all the ingredients to be a thrilling and fascinating watch as we bring you the latest updates, information and drama. Kick-off is at 14:00, with team news coming shortly.

#1327. 'It's certainly possible': Erik ten Hag sticks the knife in on Man United and warns his old club they could get relegated after poor start to the season

By LUKE AUGUSTUS, ASSISTANT SPORTS EDITOR

Published: 06:26 EDT, 2 November 2026 | Updated: 06:41 EDT, 2 November 2026

Erik ten Hag has warned his former club Manchester United that they could get relegated this season as their dismal season shows no sign of improving currently.

The Red Devils languish outside the Premier League relegation zone only on goal difference, as they sit 17th with seven points from nine matches - two more than bottom side Sunderland.

United have staggeringly only won one match in the top-flight, a 5-2 win over Premier League new boys Ipswich Town, a Premier League low that is equalled with Sunderland and 19th-placed Nottingham Forest.

Their plight worsened on Saturday afternoon after a 2-0 defeat at Chelsea - which saw them endure a second-half collapse and see Lisandro Martinez sent off.

As a result, pressure is mounting on under-fire head coach Michael Carrick and one of his predecessors Ten Hag – who won the Carabao Cup and the FA Cup during his two-and-a-bit seasons at United - believes the Old Trafford outfit could be mired in a relegation battle in the months to come.

'In the Premier League it's certainly possible, because all the teams are simply strong,' he said on ESPN NL, when asked about United's possibility of relegation.

Erik ten Hag has warned Manchester United that they could get relegated this season

Their 2-0 loss at Chelsea on Saturday means they're 17th - two points above 20th Sunderland

'They're all strong squads, all good managers. If you end up on the wrong side once and you really get into that vicious circle, then it can become very difficult.'

United have some tough fixtures coming up with a home encounter with Aston Villa on Sunday afternoon before a trip to bitter rivals Liverpool after the international break on November 22. After those two games, in-form Brentford travel to Old Trafford on November 28.

Ten Hag's comments come after his latest swipe at his former player Cristiano Ronaldo, claiming the Portugal icon's career was already over by the time he joined Juventus and eventually returned to Old Trafford.

'Every top team must embrace the top player, but the top player must also make way for the team. That was simply the problem with Ronaldo,' Ten Hag also told ESPN.

'Let there be no misunderstanding on my part, he is of course a great player. He belongs among the greats of the world.

'But the reality is also that he hasn't been able to deliver for the last seven or eight years. From Juventus onwards, it was simply over.'

#1325. Chivu: ‘Inter are still in the Champions League race, we’ll have a great game against Feyenoord’

Cristian Chivu insists Inter are “still in the race” in the Champions League, and has backed his players to respond to Saturday’s derby defeat in Rotterdam on Tuesday.

With quotes courtesy of the Corriere dello Sport, the Inter coach spoke at his pre-match press conference before the game against Feyenoord at De Kuip. It kicks off at 21:00 CET [20:00 GMT].

Inter are under pressure on two fronts. Saturday’s 3-1 loss to Milan was their first league defeat of the season. In Europe they have only three points from three games, after a late win over Shakhtar Donetsk and defeats to Real Madrid and Club Brugge.

“I believe in the work, in what this team is and what it has done so far. I’m confident. They’re champions, and they’ve shown it,” Chivu said. “There have been negative episodes and mistakes that we have to learn from, accept and move past, trying to fix them. But I’m confident.”

Chivu believes 16 points will be enough for a top-eight finish and a place in the round of 16.

“We’ve always said that the Champions League, like the league, has to be played game by game. To get into the top eight, it’s around 16 points,” he said. “For now we’ve won one game and lost two, but we’re still in it. We know what we are and what we want, and I’m convinced we’ll have a great game.”

He warned that Giovanni van Bronckhorst’s Feyenoord, who beat Como at home earlier in the competition, will be dangerous. “In this stadium they thrive. They have intensity, quality and a lot of players like Moussa and Zequiel. They’re quality players and inverted wingers. It won’t be easy, but at the same time we have to bring out all our qualities to put them in difficulty.”

“We’ve had to deal with some unpredictable situations and look for solutions with what we had available. We’ve got Provedel and Pavard back, and fortunately we haven’t had any problems in the last few days.”

#1324. Clostridium perfringens Delta toxin targets CD9 to drive NEC and brain injury

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC) is the most devastating gastrointestinal emergency in preterm infants, frequently causing mortality and long-term neurodevelopmental impairment1,2. Although the gut microbiota has been implicated in NEC pathogenesis3,4,5, the microbial factors driving NEC and the following brain pathology remain unclear. Here we identify Clostridium perfringens pathobionts containing Delta toxin in the gut microbiome of individuals with severe and fatal NEC. Clinically, infected infants show worse outcomes, including aberrant systemic inflammation, severe neurological damage and coagulopathy. We establish a mouse model in which Delta-toxin-positive C. perfringens infection, or Delta toxin exposure alone, recapitulates clinical features of NEC, including intestinal necrosis and acute cerebral injury. Mechanistically, Delta toxin preferentially targets macrophages, potently activating inflammasome signalling and pyroptosis, triggering a rapid inflammatory cascade that compromises blood–brain barrier integrity and drives neuroinflammation. Through a genome-wide CRISPR screen, we identify the tetraspanin CD9 as the host receptor for Delta toxin. Using systemic, myeloid-specific and intestinal-epithelial-specific Cd9-knockout mice, we show that systemic and myeloid Cd9 ablation protects mice against toxin-induced lethality, blood–brain barrier dysfunction and multiorgan injury, whereas epithelial Cd9 deletion shows partial protection, implicating macrophage targeting as a primary driver of C. perfringens CD9-dependent pathogenesis. Furthermore, a neutralizing anti-Delta toxin monoclonal antibody confers protection against disease progression. These findings suggest that a subset of NEC is a specific-toxin-mediated disorder and validate the Delta toxin–CD9 axis as a therapeutic target for this subset.

NEC remains a major cause of mortality and long-term morbidity in preterm infants1,2. NEC pathogenesis is multifactorial, involving the complex interplay of immature intestinal development, intestinal barrier dysfunction, gut dysbiosis and excessive inflammatory response3,4,5,6. The specific triggers of NEC and the mechanisms driving its rapid progression remain poorly understood.

The impact of NEC extends beyond the intestine. More than half of postoperative survivors develop brain injury and neurodevelopmental impairment7,8, with TLR4 inflammatory pathways implicated in this pathology9,10. Many insights are derived from experimental models that use hypoxia, cold stress and hyperosmolar formula feeding to increase intestinal vulnerability11,12. Although these models have been valuable for mapping inflammatory pathways, they may be less well suited to interrogating microbiome-driven early initiating events.

Gut microbiota are implicated in NEC susceptibility: NEC is associated with dysbiosis3,4,5, germ-free mice are resistant to NEC-like injury13 and microbiota-modifying interventions are protective14,15. Several studies identified enrichment of toxin-producing C. perfringens in NEC16,17,18, but causal virulence factors remain undefined.

C. perfringens is a ubiquitous, Gram-positive anaerobe producing diverse toxins19,20. Strains are classified into seven toxin types (A–G) based on toxin repertoire19. Type C strains produce Beta and Delta toxins, which are both pore-forming toxins (PFTs) that induce cell death by forming transmembrane pores21,22,23. While Beta toxin is well characterized, Delta toxin remains understudied. Here we identify C. perfringens Delta toxin as a virulence factor that drives intestinal necrosis and brain injury in a subset of NEC, providing an avenue for targeted therapeutic intervention.

To investigate the role of gut microbiota in NEC, we profiled faecal samples from 28 preterm infants without NEC and 16 preterm infants with NEC. 16S rRNA-sequencing analysis revealed an enrichment of C. perfringens in NEC samples (Fig. 1a), consistent with previous reports16,17. Two fatal cases of NEC showed high C. perfringens abundance (Extended Data Fig. 1a). To validate this finding, we performed anaerobic culture of faecal samples from 49 individuals without NEC and 17 patients with NEC (Supplementary Table 1). C. perfringens-positive cultures showed visible gas production and were confirmed by selective tryptose sulfite cycloserine (TSC) agar isolation and PCR targeting of C. perfringens-specific genes (Extended Data Fig. 1b–d). Overall, C. perfringens was more prevalent in patients with NEC compared with in infants without NEC (56% versus 18%), supporting its association with NEC (Fig. 1b,c).

a, 16S rRNA gene sequencing of faecal samples from infants with (n = 16) and without (n = 28) NEC. b,c, Summary (pie chart (b) and table (c)) of C. perfringens (Cp) and Delta toxin detection across the non-NEC (n = 49) and NEC (n = 27) cohorts as determined by anaerobic culture and serology. d, ELISA detection of anti-Delta toxin antibody in the serum (1:2,700 dilution) of infants without (n = 5) and with (n = 12) NEC. e, Clinical parameter fold changes between the Delta toxin+ (n = 2) and Delta toxin− (n = 5) NEC groups; the blue to magenta gradient indicates the change in magnitude. Mono%, monocyte percentage; T-CO2, total carbon dioxide; Neu%, neutrophil percentage; Lymph%, lymphocyte percentage. f,g, Representative T2W and T2 FLAIR brain MRI scans from the non-NEC (n = 3), Delta toxin− NEC (n = 4) and Delta toxin+ NEC (n = 2) groups (f), and quantification of the Evans index (>0.3 indicates ventricular enlargement) (g). h, Schematic of neonatal mouse NEC model induced by twice-daily intragastric gavage of formula containing C. perfringens. The representative image shows intestinal necrosis in a P11 mouse pup. i,j, Representative intestinal haematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining (i) and histopathology scores (j) of pups 4 days after infection with or without C. perfringens. n = 5 (NC), n = 6 (Delta toxin− C. perfringens) and n = 6 (Delta toxin+ C. perfringens). Scale bar, 100 μm. k, Survival curves of pups infected with Delta toxin− or Delta toxin+ C. perfringens. n = 8. l,m, Representative brain H&E staining (l) and quantification of lateral ventricular width (left; n = 4) and ependymal injury scores (right; n = 6) (m) of pups infected with Delta toxin− or Delta toxin+ C. perfringens. Scale bars, 100 μm (top) and 50 μm (bottom). Representative images from one of three independent experiments are shown. Data are mean ± s.d. P values were determined using one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA; j and m), two-tailed unpaired Student’s t-test (g) and the log-rank test (k). *P < 0.05, **P < 0.01, ***P < 0.001, ****P < 0.0001. The diagram in h was created using BioRender; Zhang, S. https://BioRender.com/o2lct20 (2026).

C. perfringens produces a repertoire of toxins, including Alpha, Beta, Epsilon, Iota toxin, enterotoxin (CPE), necrotic enteritis β-like toxin (NetB) and perfringolysin O (Pfo)19. We next examined whether specific toxin profiles correlated with severe outcomes. PCR-based toxin typing identified isolates from two deceased patients as type C C. perfringens strains containing the delta toxin gene (Delta toxin+ C. perfringens clinical-03 and clinical-15) (Extended Data Fig. 1e). Delta toxin production was further confirmed by western blot analysis of culture supernatants (Extended Data Fig. 1f,g). We further detected anti-Delta toxin antibodies in two patients with severe surgical NEC whose stool cultures were negative, probably due to antibiotic treatment, indicating previous infection with Delta toxin+ C. perfringens strains. Expanded serological analysis of ten additional patients with severe surgical NEC identified five anti-Delta toxin antibody-positive cases (Supplementary Table 2). Thus, 7 of 12 (58%) patients with severe NEC showed serological evidence of Delta toxin exposure, whereas Delta toxin was not detected in any infant without NEC by faecal isolate PCR or serology (Fig. 1b–d).

Clinically, Delta toxin+ infants showed more prominent systemic inflammation, coagulopathy and brain injury, compared with Delta toxin− cases characterized by elevated C-reactive protein and D-dimer, decreased monocytes, platelets and haemoglobin (Fig. 1e). Importantly, brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) in these patients indicated more severe injury, including lateral ventricular enlargement (Fig. 1f,g).

To assess Delta toxin pathogenicity, we selected representative clinical isolates, the Delta toxin+ strain C. perfringens clinical-03 and the Delta toxin− strain C. perfringens clinical-01 for genomic analysis and animal infection studies (Extended Data Fig. 1e,f). Phylogenetic analysis revealed that the clinical-03 strain clustered with NCTC3181 (a known Delta toxin+ type C strain24), whereas clinical-01 clustered with CVCC1160 (a Delta toxin− type C strain), with the two clinical isolates sharing around 96% DNA identity (Extended Data Fig. 1h). Neonatal mice orally gavaged with these strains and formula for 4 days developed severe NEC-like intestinal pathology only after Delta toxin+ infection, including disrupted intestinal architecture, villus and crypt damage, inflammatory infiltration and mucosal fibrin clots, accompanied by increased mortality (Fig. 1h–k). During infection with the clinical-03 strain, Delta toxin was detected predominantly in the intestine, with lower levels in the kidney and lung, but was undetectable in the brain based on western blotting and enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) (Extended Data Fig. 1i,j). Nevertheless, infected mice developed severe brain abnormalities, including lateral ventricular enlargement and ependymal cell damage (Fig. 1l,m). Reference strain comparison using NCTC3181 and CVCC1160 (around 99% identity) confirmed that Delta toxin+ infection caused more severe intestinal, brain and lung injury (Extended Data Fig. 1k–m). Finally, culture supernatants from Delta toxin+ strains induced cytotoxicity in HeLa cells, HT29 cells and intestinal organoids, which was neutralized by a Delta-toxin-specific polyclonal antibody (Extended Data Fig. 1n–p). These results support Delta toxin as a key secreted virulence factor responsible for cell damage.

Owing to technical challenges in performing some assays in postnatal day 7 (P7) neonatal mice, we included 4-week-old weanling mice for subsequent experiments. Intraperitoneal (i.p.) administration of purified Delta toxin caused dose-dependent lethality in both age groups, with neonates showing greater sensitivity (Fig. 2a,b and Extended Data Fig. 2a). We next quantified Delta toxin distribution in neonatal mice 4 h after i.p. injection of 10 μg toxin. Consistent with the infection model, toxin levels were highest in the intestine (around 61 μg per g), followed by kidney (approximately 15 μg per g) and lung (about 7 μg per g), with barely detectable toxin in the brain (Extended Data Fig. 2b). These levels were comparable to those in infected pups, supporting the physiological relevance of the toxin injection model.

a, Survival curves of P7 mice after Delta toxin challenge. n = 10. b, Representative images of neonatal mice after Delta toxin challenge (right), and the age-matched control mice (left). d, days. c,d, Intestine H&E staining (c) and histopathology scores (d) after low-dose (4 μg, analysed at day 5) or high-dose (20 μg, 4 h) Delta toxin challenge. n = 5. Scale bars, 200 μm (c). e–h, Brain (third ventricle and ependyma (e,f) and cerebral cortex and lateral ventricle (g,h)) histopathology scores (e,h) and H&E staining (f,g) from neonatal mice after Delta toxin challenge. n = 5. For f, scale bars, 100 μm (third ventricle) and 20 μm (ependyma). The black arrows show ependymal disruption; the blue arrows show periventricular vacuolation and oedema; and the red arrows indicate haemorrhage (f). For g, scale bars, 50 μm (cerebral cortex) and 100 μm (lateral ventricle). The black arrows indicate neuronal shrinkage with reduced volume, hyperchromatic cytoplasm and indistinct nuclear–cytoplasmic boundaries; the yellow arrows show neuronal degeneration; and the green arrows show inflammatory cell infiltration (g). i,j, Representative T2-weighted brain MRI images (i) and Evans index quantification (j) of 4-week-old mice after Delta toxin i.p. injection. n = 3 (control), n = 3 (20 μg) and n = 4 (100 μg). The yellow arrows indicate focal hyperintensity. k,l, In vivo photoacoustic imaging (PAI) of cerebral blood flow (k) and quantification of microvascular branching length (l) in the cortex of 4-week-old mice. n = 4. m, Schematic of the experimental design for the Evans blue assay to evaluate BBB disruption. D1, day 1. n,o, Representative whole-brain images after Evans blue perfusion (n) and quantification of Evans blue extravasation (o) in the brains of 4-week-old mice. n = 6. p,q, Immunofluorescence staining (p) and mean fluorescence intensity (MFI) quantification (q) of hippocampal ZO-1. The white arrows indicate a diminished ZO-1 signal. n = 4. For p, scale bars, 100 μm. Representative images are shown from one of three independent experiments. Data are mean ± s.d. P values were determined using one-way ANOVA (d, e, h, j, l and o) and a two-tailed unpaired Student’s t-test (q). The diagram in m was created using BioRender; Zhang, S. https://BioRender.com/o2lct20 (2026).

We next challenged P7 neonates and 4-week-old mice using either an acute high-dose model to mimic fulminant infection, analysed at 4 h, or a single low-dose challenge with prolonged follow-up to approximate residual toxin activity after antibiotic clearance, analysed at days 5–7. Across both age groups and dosing strategies, Delta toxin induced a severe NEC-like multiorgan pathology. Intestines showed mucosal disruption, villus destruction, epithelial detachment and oedema (Fig. 2c,d and Extended Data Fig. 2c,d). Concurrently, the brain exhibited haemorrhage, ependymal disorganization, periventricular oedema, ventricular dilation (Fig. 2e,f and Extended Data Fig. 2e,f), neuronal shrinkage and degeneration, and inflammatory cell infiltration (Fig. 2g,h and Extended Data Fig. 2g–i). We also observed intravascular coagulation within the cerebral microvasculature in the hippocampal region (Extended Data Fig. 2j,k). In 4-week-old mice, brain MRI further confirmed that Delta toxin caused brain injury and ventricle dilation (Fig. 2i,j), mirroring the neuropathology observed in patients with NEC. In vivo photoacoustic imaging of brains showed a significant reduction in cerebral blood flow, vascular density and branching index, indicating Delta-toxin-associated hypoxic–ischaemic injury and cognitive impairment (Fig. 2k,l).

Beyond the brain, Delta toxin induced widespread multiorgan pathology, with particularly severe injury observed in the kidney and lung. These tissues exhibited distinct signs of coagulopathy, haemorrhage and inflammatory cell infiltration, notably affecting the renal medulla, glomeruli and pulmonary parenchyma in both age groups (Extended Data Fig. 2l–o). Moreover, toxin-treated mice showed dilated ear vessels and increased Evans blue extravasation in the peritoneal lavage fluid, indicating vascular damage25 (Extended Data Fig. 3a,b). Delta toxin further induced systemic coagulation abnormalities, including elevated red blood cell counts, reduced platelets and altered coagulation parameters, including prolonged prothrombin time and activated partial thromboplastin time,  and reduced fibrinogen (Extended Data Fig. 3c–h). These findings recapitulate the severe disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) observed in Delta-toxin-positive patients with NEC (Fig. 1e). Inflammasome activation is known to drive coagulation through macrophage-mediated release of tissue factor26. Consistently, Delta toxin promoted tissue factor release from macrophages and Caco2 intestinal epithelial cells (Extended Data Fig. 3i), suggesting that both cell types contribute to toxin-induced coagulopathy.

To define the specific contribution of Delta toxin to neurological injury, we evaluated the effects of Beta toxin, which has been implicated in type C C. perfringens enteritis27. Beta toxin exhibited selective cytotoxicity for endothelial HUVECs but notably spared HT-29 intestinal epithelial cells and organoids (Extended Data Fig. 4a–c), aligning with a previous report that Beta toxin preferentially targets CD31+ vascular endothelial cells28. In vivo, it induced rapid, dose-dependent mortality (Extended Data Fig. 4d), but did not induce brain pathology at any dose tested (Extended Data Fig. 4e). These data demonstrate the specific pathogenic role of Delta toxin as a driver of NEC-like multiorgan pathology.

We next examined whether Delta-toxin-induced brain injury is associated with blood–brain barrier (BBB) dysfunction and neuroinflammation. In 4-week-old mice, Evans blue extravasation revealed dose-dependent BBB leakage after Delta toxin challenge, with lipopolysaccharide (LPS)29 as a positive control (Fig. 2m–o). Acute high-dose Delta toxin (100 μg, 8 h) caused more-severe BBB disruption than either prolonged low-dose Delta toxin (20 μg, analysed at day 7) or acute LPS (1 mg, 8 h), indicating that Delta toxin rapidly disrupts BBB integrity. ZO-1 immunofluorescence in the hippocampus confirmed structural damage with localized disorganization and reduced signal intensity (Fig. 2p,q).

BBB disruption is often accompanied by neuroinflammation30,31 and intestinal CD4+ T cells migrate across the BBB into the brain, where they accumulate with microglia to trigger neuroinflammation32,33. We next characterized brain immune cell populations after exposure to Delta toxin. In both age groups, acute high-dose Delta toxin triggered an increase in total CD45+ cells (Extended Data Fig. 5a). This increase was largely attributable to a marked expansion of the microglial population, predominantly reflecting microglial expansion (Extended Data Fig. 5b,c), confirmed by increased IBA1+ immunostaining (Extended Data Fig. 5d–g). Three-dimensional analysis revealed a shift of microglia from ramified to amoeboid morphology, characterized by shorter branch lengths and attenuated processes (Extended Data Fig. 5d–g). GFAP+ astrocytes also increased, with increased branching and cell volume (Extended Data Fig. 5h–k), indicating pro-inflammatory activation34. CD4+ and CD8+ T cells remained at similar levels at this timepoint (Extended Data Fig. 5l). In neonates after low-dose prolonged challenge, microglial expansion and activation (Extended Data Fig. 5m–r) were accompanied by increased CD4+ and CD8+ T cells (Extended Data Fig. 5s,t), consistent with T cell recruitment 4 days after NEC induction32.

As patients with NEC exhibit a pronounced systemic and central nervous system inflammatory response1, we analysed cytokine profiles in the serum and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) of patients with NEC positive for C. perfringens Delta toxin. The results revealed abnormally high cytokine levels, including IL-6, IL-10, TNF and IL-1β (Fig. 3a,b). To examine whether Delta toxin contributes to this inflammatory activation, we administered Delta toxin to 4-week-old mice through i.p. injection and observed a significant increase in IL-1β levels in both the serum and peritoneal fluid (Fig. 3c), along with a dose-dependent upregulation of Il1b, Il18, Tnf and Nlrp3 mRNA levels in peritoneal lavage cells (Fig. 3d). IL-1β and IL-18 are major effector cytokines released after NLRP3 inflammasome activation35, and activated macrophages represent the principal cellular source of mature IL-1β36. The specific NLRP3 inhibitor MCC950 suppressed Delta-toxin-induced Il1b and Il18 in peritoneal macrophages (Fig. 3e), improved survival rates (Fig. 3f and Extended Data Fig. 6a) and mitigated Delta-toxin-induced BBB disruption, as evidenced by reduced Evans blue extravasation (Fig. 3g,h). These findings suggest that Delta toxin activates the NLRP3 inflammasome to drive local and systemic inflammation as well as BBB damage.

a,b, Cytokine profiling of serum (a) and CSF (b) from Delta toxin+ patients with NEC. n = 2 (serum) and n = 1 (CSF). c, The IL-1β concentration in 4-week-old mice after Delta toxin challenge. n = 7 (control), n = 7 (20 μg) and n = 8 (100 μg) (left); n = 5 (right). d, Il1b, Il18, Tnf and Nlrp3 mRNA expression in peritoneal cells from Delta-toxin-challenged mice. n = 3. e, Il1b, Il18 and Nlrp3 mRNA expression in peritoneal macrophages treated with Delta toxin (0.005 μg ml−1), with or without MCC950. n = 3. f, Survival curve of 4-week-old mice challenged with Delta toxin treated with vehicle or MCC950. n = 12. g,h, Brain images (g) and quantification (h) of Evans blue extravasation in 4-week-old mice. n = 5 (no Delta toxin (−)), n = 7 (20 μg) and n = 6 (100 μg). i,j, Histograms (i) and quantification (j) of neonatal peritoneal macrophages (F4/80+Ly6G−) and neutrophils (F4/80−Ly6G+) after challenge with Delta toxin. n = 7 (control), n = 4 (20 μg) and n = 3 (4 μg). k,l, Histograms (k) and quantification (l) of neonatal intestinal macrophages and neutrophils after Delta toxin challenge. n = 5. m, Intestinal macrophage percentages (left) and numbers (right) in C. perfringens-colonized neonates at day 4. n = 4. n, MTT assay of primary peritoneal macrophages treated with distinct toxins. n = 3. o, Pro-inflammatory gene mRNA expression in peritoneal macrophages treated with distinct toxins for 24 h. n = 3. P values were determined using one-way ANOVA (c, j and m), two-tailed unpaired Student’s t-tests (h and l) and log-rank (Mantel–Cox) tests (f).

We next examined whether macrophages, well-established cells capable of NLRP3 inflammasome activation, are preferentially targeted by Delta toxin. In both neonates and 4-week-old mice, high-dose Delta toxin caused rapid, near-complete depletion of peritoneal macrophages within 1 h, and low-dose exposure resulted in reduced peritoneal macrophage numbers persisting for 5–7 days (Fig. 3i,j and Extended Data Fig. 6b–d). By contrast, neutrophils decreased at 1 h, accumulated by 4 h and persisted to days 5–7, suggesting a subsequent neutrophil-dominated inflammatory response (Fig. 3i,j and Extended Data Fig. 6b–d). In the neonatal intestine, Delta toxin selectively depleted macrophages, without significantly altering T cells, B cells, neutrophils or dendritic cells (Fig. 3k,l and Extended Data Fig. 6e,f). Consistently, neonatal mice infected with the NCTC3181 (Delta toxin+) strain showed both a reduced percentage and a reduced absolute number of intestinal macrophages at 4 days after infection, whereas infection with the CVCC1160 strain (Delta toxin−) resulted in no detectable change (Fig. 3m). To assess the inflammatory potency relative to other PFTs, we exposed primary peritoneal macrophages to Staphylococcus aureus α-haemolysin (α-Hla), C. perfringens Delta toxin, Beta toxin, Pfo or LPS. Macrophages were resistant to α-Hla, Beta toxin and Pfo, but exceptionally sensitive to Delta toxin (Fig. 3n). Delta toxin potently induced inflammatory cytokine mRNA at 1–5 ng ml−1, whereas Pfo and α-Hla required around 5,000 ng ml−1 and 50,000 ng ml−1, respectively; Beta toxin had a minimal effect even at high concentrations. Notably, Delta toxin was effective at approximately 100-fold lower concentrations than LPS (Fig. 3o). Consistently, IL-1β was detected in primary peritoneal macrophage culture supernatants after 10 ng ml−1 Delta toxin treatment (Fig. 3p).

To define the mechanism, we examined key inflammatory cell-death pathways in immortalized bone-marrow-derived macrophages (iBMDMs). Delta toxin induced a time-dependent increase in pyroptosis signatures, including accumulation of pro-caspase-1, cleaved caspase-1 and gasdermin D (Fig. 3q). By contrast, canonical apoptosis markers, BAX induction and caspase-3 cleavage37 were not detectably altered under the same conditions (Fig. 3r), supporting pyroptosis as the dominant cell-death program induced by Delta toxin in iBMDMs.

We next tested whether K+ efflux38, a conserved trigger for NLRP3 inflammasome activation after membrane permeabilization, mediates Delta-toxin-induced inflammation. Extracellular KCl, used to prevent intracellular K+ depletion, abrogated Delta-toxin-induced NLRP3 upregulation and caspase-1 cleavage (Extended Data Fig. 6g), identifying K+ efflux as a major upstream signal. Moreover, Delta toxin rapidly induced ERK phosphorylation (Fig. 3s), consistent with pore-forming toxin-induced calcium influx, which subsequently activates MAPK–ERK signalling39. In vivo, bone marrow cells from Delta-toxin-treated mice showed increased GSDMD cleavage (Fig. 3t), confirming pyroptotic signalling. Collectively, these findings reveal that Delta toxin drives potent inflammation through the NLRP3–Caspase-1–GSDMD pathway and activates MAPK–ERK signalling.

We next examined whether Delta toxin engages a specific host receptor to mediate cell binding and cytotoxicity. We first evaluated the sensitivity of various cell lines. HeLa and HT29 cells were found to be highly susceptible, indicating that they abundantly express receptor (Extended Data Fig. 7a). We therefore performed a genome-wide CRISPR–Cas9 screen in HeLa cells using the GeCKO v2 library40 against Delta toxin (0.01 μg ml−1) (Fig. 4a). Next-generation sequencing of surviving cells revealed Cd9 as the top hit (Fig. 4b). CD9 expression was confirmed across relevant cell lines, and higher CD9 expression was associated with increased sensitivity to Delta toxin (Fig. 4c and Extended Data Fig. 7a). Although Delta toxin has been reported to bind to GM221, genetic disruption (UGCG knockout (KO)) or pharmacological inhibition (EtDO-P4 treatment) of GlcCer-derived glycosphingolipids (including most gangliosides such as GM2) did not change cellular sensitivity (Extended Data Fig. 7b,c). By contrast, CD9-KO rendered HeLa cells resistant to Delta toxin with toxicity reduced by around 40,000-fold (Fig. 4d). Moreover, CD9-overexpressing (CD9-GFP-oe) A549 cells showed markedly increased sensitivity (Fig. 4e). KO of other candidate genes (LRP6 and CLEC12B) did not alter toxin sensitivity (Fig. 4b and Extended Data Fig. 7d). GST-tagged Delta toxin can bind to wild-type (WT) HeLa cells and CD9-GFP-oe A549 cells, but not to CD9-KO cells and A549 cells (Fig. 4f–h). Biolayer interferometry (BLI) assays confirmed specific binding between GST–CD9 and Delta toxin, but not Beta toxin (Fig. 4i). The measured interaction (KD) fell in the micromolar-range binding affinity, indicative of specific, low-affinity binding (Extended Data Fig. 7e,f). It is possible that a proper membrane environment is required for the high-affinity binding of Delta toxin on cell surfaces. Together, these data identify CD9 as a receptor for Delta toxin.
