Published: 12:23 EDT, 2 November 2026 | Updated: 12:48 EDT, 2 November 2026

Five framed photographs hang on the walls of the clubhouse lounge at Holm Park: the Titan crane, the Singer sewing factory and Kilbowie Park, as well as the rubble-strewn streets of the Blitz and the long-lost Seven Seas pub. Together, they tell the story of a town, its triumphs and its traumas.

‘There’s an old Bankies song,’ says Clydebank FC chair Grace McGibbon, who had the pictures installed at the start of this season. ‘It goes, “We make ships, sewing machines, we build famous football teams, we’re the Bankies from Kilbowie Park”. It’s kind of a homage to that.’

To McGibbon, the pictures are a reminder of what Clydebank is and has always been.

‘Clydebank is not just a football team, or a shopping centre, or whatever else you might think,’ she tells Daily Mail Sport. ‘It’s so much more than any of that. This is a community that never gives up. There’s almost a defiance about the place. That’s what these photos represent.

‘Other people might look at it and go, “It’s just pictures on a wall, I don’t get it”. But we get it. It reminds us why we’re here and why we’re doing this.’

Without question, ‘this’ is one of the Scottish football stories of the season so far. As well as being in contention for the Lowland League West title – and with it, the chance of a Lazarus-like return to the Scottish football league – Clydebank have reached the third round of the Scottish Cup for the third successive season where Championship side Livingston await.

Clydebank finished top of a KDM Evolution Trophy league phase containing mainly senior sides

More immediately, they host League One strugglers Alloa Athletic in the last 32 of the KDM Evolution Trophy on Tuesday, the Bankies having qualified for the knockout stages of the Challenge Cup by finishing top of the league phase, unbeaten, and ahead of the likes of Ross County, Airdrieonians and Cove Rangers.

Be under no illusions: something special is happening in West Dunbartonshire just now. To fully understand how special requires a short history lesson. Between 1888 and 1931, three clubs bearing the Clydebank name came and went. It was in the 1960s that things changed materially.

Frustrated by poor attendances, and inspired by Major League Baseball franchise relocations, Jack and Charlie Steedman – the majority owners of East Stirlingshire FC – merged their club with Clydebank Juniors. ES Clydebank, as they were called, relocated to New Kilbowie Park in Clydebank, enraging supporters of the hitherto Falkirk-based East Stirlingshire.

A legal challenge brought by local shareholders saw the merger invalidated and the brothers being deposed. Undeterred, they formed a brand-new club, Clydebank FC, which successfully applied for entry into the Scottish football league in time for the 1966/67 season. A decade later, inspired by a 20-year-old Davie Cooper, the club was promoted to the Premier Division for the first time, narrowly missing out on the First Division title to Alex Ferguson’s St Mirren.

For a while, everything was gravy. The Bankies established themselves as a solid if unspectacular outfit, represented at various times by the likes of Owen Coyle, Tommy Coyne and Bobby Williamson. The ‘two Jims’, Fallon and Gallacher, became club icons alongside record-goalscorer Ken Eadie. Gary Teale rose through the club’s youth academy. They even lured Cooper home to see out his career.

Kilbowie Park was one of the iconic stops for away fans before it was razed to the ground

In 1996, the rug was pulled. The Steedmans sold New Kilbowie Park to developers who demolished the ground and built a retail park on top of it. That sparked a chain of events that included ground-sharing with Dumbarton and Greenock Morton, ownership changes, and ill-conceived plans to relocate to Dublin, then Carlisle, the Scottish Borders and more.

After the inevitable tumble into administration, the club was acquired by the newly formed Airdrie United, itself a product of the liquidated Airdrieonians. To all intents and purposes, Clydebank FC was renamed and relocated, leaving devastated Bankies without a club.

McGibbon remembers it well. ‘I’m Clydebank born and bred,’ she beams. ‘My husband had been a Clydebank fan all his days and, when we first met, he took me along to a couple of games. I immediately got the bug.

‘So, when the demise happened, you felt it. This thing that was so important to you was suddenly gone. It was heartbreaking. The season after it happened, you’d bump into people wandering around the shopping centre because that was the only place left to go.’

As Scottish football carried on without them, a group of fans formed a collective called the United Clydebank Supporters and recovered the club name and crest from Airdrie United. ‘At that point,’ recalls McGibbon, ‘we basically had to take a crash course in how to run a football club. People talk about starting again from scratch. That’s what this was. Absolute scratch.’

Scottish football icon Davie Cooper started and finished his playing career with the Bankies

Item one on the agenda was an application to join the Scottish Junior Football League. After that was accepted, and after a year out of the game, Clydebank returned in time for the start of the 2003-04 campaign. Club legend Billy ‘Budgie’ McGhee was named manager, a new home at Glenhead Park in Duntocher was secured, and an improbable new chapter began.

Fast-forward roughly a quarter of a century, and the progress made is quite remarkable. Via various rungs of the former Scottish Junior Football Association and ground-hopping arrangements, Clydebank joined the West of Scotland League – the sixth tier of the Scottish football pyramid – in 2020. In 2024-25, they won promotion to the Lowland League West to move to within a step of a sensational return to the Scottish football league.

Win the league and they will go into a three-way, end-of-season play-off with the champions of Lowland League East and the Highland League. The winner of that round-robin will advance to a two-legged, home-and-away play-off against the team finishing bottom of SPFL League Two, sometimes referred to as ‘Club 42’. Win that tie and you’re playing League Two football next season.

‘We have a three-year plan to be in League Two,’ says McGibbon. ‘Within five years, League One. And after that, who knows? The most important thing is that we remain sustainable and fan-owned.

‘We can’t sell out to a big money man. Do that and you sell the soul of the club. I know because we’ve been there before. We can never again be in a position where one person has sole ownership of this club. It just can’t happen.’

Which raises the question of governance. The ten-person board, chaired by McGibbon, is entirely voluntary. ‘We don’t take a penny out of the club,’ she insists. ‘No expenses, nothing.’

Pop group Wet Wet Wet sponsored their hometown club Clydebank between 1993 and 1997

Another 30 or so volunteers manage various other parts of club business, from running the social media accounts to curating the matchday programme to operating the club shop. If it feels as though the community is showing up for its team, that’s because it is.

‘I think it harks back to the town’s working-class roots,’ says McGibbon. ‘And we try to embrace it in kind. We understand that it’s difficult for people to buy season tickets and such like with the cost of everything these days. That’s why we’ve put things in place to help, like payment plans. If we know someone genuinely can’t afford a ticket, we try to make it happen. Sometimes, it’s more important to have that person there than bringing in an extra few quid on the day.’

Crucially, the club has also invested in the Bronze Licence required for promotion into the upper tiers of the pyramid, a significant outlay that has the full backing of manager Gordon Moffat.

‘The whole trajectory of the club is so positive,’ he says. ‘For me, my coaches and the players, it’s really reassuring to see the way the club is run. Grace and the board are basically lifelong fans and it’s obvious to anyone they’ve got the club’s long-term future at heart.

‘When I came in seven years ago, I said to Grace that we’d need to increase the playing budget if we wanted to be competitive and, to her credit, she’s managed to do that whilst keeping us on a sure footing. She’s not scared to say no but, at the same time, she’s a fan and she wants to watch a good team.’

Clydebank chair Grace McGibbon is proud of the way the club has battled through adversity

Currently, that team includes an eclectic mix of joiners, electricians, engineers, firefighters, a barber and more. There’s a potent mix of youth and experience, with leaders in every position. Nicky Low, for example. The former Aberdeen and Dundee midfielder joined the Bankies in February 2023, back when they were still in the West of Scotland Football League.

‘I knew a few boys who were there at the time,’ says the 34-year-old. ‘I said to them, “Listen, is it professional the way it’s run, because I’m not coming if it’s a bag of washing”. Honestly, they couldn’t have spoken more highly of the place, and they were right to.

‘It’s the volunteer aspect that really gets me. Clydebank’s lucky that a lot of people give up their free time to help out, and you see what it means to them when you win and they’re all high-fiving you. Just seeing people smiling at football is what makes it all worthwhile.’

For Low, playing for Clydebank also represents something of a ‘full circle’ moment. ‘I was brought up in Greenock,’ he says, ‘so when Clydebank were ground-sharing with Morton back in the day, I was their ball boy. I’ve had a soft spot for them since I was a kid.’

All of which is lovely but football – as we are constantly reminded – is a results business, and Low is determined to continue Clydebank’s momentum with a win over Alloa in the Challenge Cup.

‘We’re under no illusions about how difficult a game it’s going to be,’ he says. ‘Alloa are a strong team. They play good football and Andy Graham will have them well organised. They’ll be favourites but we’ll go in believing that if we can bring the best version of ourselves, we’ll have a chance of progressing.

Holm Park will play host to a cup clash against Alloa that could provide a real fairytale

‘As a team and as individuals, we’re playing well and we always believe we can score, so if we can keep it tight at the back, I believe we’re capable of giving anybody a game.’

Manager Moffat agrees. ‘We’ve shown against League One and League Two teams over the last few seasons that we can compete. People will say, “It’s a one-off game, anything can happen.” But we’ve got a decent sample size in our favour now. Sure, we’ll lose some games to SPFL opposition, but I think we’ve proven we’re more than capable of winning plenty, too.’

As for McGibbon, she’s mostly just happy to have her team back. ‘I work in retail,’ she says. ‘Monday to Thursday. Nothing exciting. My passion comes from this football club, from the people, the fans, the coaches, the players. Every single person at the club, I absolutely love them for what they’ve given. That’s what makes it all worthwhile. I mean, you wouldn’t do this if it didn’t mean something to you. But it does. It’s very special.’

And who knows? Maybe one day there will be space on the wall for a photo of the team that restores Clydebank to the Scottish football league. They, too, will have earned their place.

■ Clydebank FC face Alloa Athletic in the last 32 of the KDM Evolution Trophy at Holm Park on Tuesday, November 3. Kick-off 7.45pm.

#1296. F1 champion Antonelli’s love for Bologna FC: from wannabe striker to Coppa Italia celebrations

Bologna have invited Kimi Antonelli to celebrate his Formula 1 world title with them, and the Mercedes driver’s love for the Rossoblù goes back to his childhood.

The 20-year-old from Bologna became the youngest world champion in F1 history in Mexico on Sunday, and the first Italian to win the title since Alberto Ascari in 1953. His hometown club sent their congratulations and asked him to join them for the celebrations.

According to TuttoMercatoWeb, Antonelli once dreamed of a career in football. He played as a striker as a boy, but told Corriere della Sera it was less about technique than stamina. “I ran a lot on the pitch too. Let’s say I just ran,” he joked.

His father Marco took him to watch Bologna as a child, and he is still a regular at the Dall’Ara. He was in the stands for a 2-0 win over Como in February 2025. His first footballing idol, though, was Lionel Messi, which made him a Barcelona fan during the Argentine’s peak years.

When Bologna beat Milan to win the Coppa Italia in May 2025, ending a 51-year wait for the trophy, Antonelli was preparing for the Imola Grand Prix and couldn’t get to Rome. He joined the celebrations in the streets of Bologna instead.

That same weekend, a delegation led by then-coach Vincenzo Italiano and captain Lorenzo De Silvestri visited him in the Imola paddock. They gave him a signed Bologna shirt, and he returned the favour with a Mercedes one.

#1295. Ballon d'Or Power Rankings: Why Harry Kane should win over Lamine Yamal, Kylian Mbappe, and Lionel Messi

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The deadlines have passed, the votes have been tallied and verified, all that is left is to crown the outstanding male footballer of the 2025-26 season. That might be easier said than done.

Twelve months ago it was quite obvious that Ousmane Dembele would be taking home this prize. He had the narrative, he had the performances and he had the silverware. In years without major international tournaments it is often the case that being the best team on the Champions League winner is enough and so it proved for Dembele, who only really fulfilled the promise of a career in the back half of Paris Saint-Germain's breakout season. Mohamed Salah and Raphinha had cases based on individual performance but when it came down to medals, it really was hard to see past Dembele. He fulfilled all the criteria.

This time the very best performers of the club season did not take home that one extra trophy to buttress their campaign. Bayern Munich and Barcelona won their domestic leagues. Big whoop. The English champions almost exist as a counter to the individual qualities the Ballon d'Or glorifies. Arsenal won the league in spite of the absence of their star forwards, a triumph of depth and resilience that is unlikely to earn them many podium spots. Paris Saint-Germain repeated the league and Champions League double but half their strongest XI barely showed up in Ligue 1. Dembele can hardly repeat off around 2500 minutes for club and country last season.

As is always the case, the World Cup promises to warp voting. It clarifies little among the front runners. Harry Kane and Kylian Mbappe had great individual tournaments but one of the Ballon d'Or's three criteria is "team performances and achievements". England and France fell short there. Lamine Yamal fulfills that, but Spain's triumph was one of the collective, the greatest prize in the sport won despite their forward struggling with injury.

Meanwhile, the best at the tournament do not sit easily in this ranking. Rodri might have held Spain together, but his domestic season was hampered by injury. Lionel Messi's historic standing was only buttressed by what he did as a 39-year-old, but your mileage may vary as to the significance of an MLS Cup-winning run beforehand.

This year more than most, then, there is no right answer. This, at least, is the least wrong I can offer. And we'll end this preamble with a customary reminder: this is not a prediction for who will win the Ballon d'Or. If you want that, consult your preferred sportsbook, I guess, or our own Golazo rankings. This is who ought to win it. You will probably disagree.

Perhaps it was the endings to his tilts at the Champions League and World Cup that make it so hard to lock in on Kane as the best player in the world last season. If the 33-year-old really were that good, would he not have found a way to bend the biggest games in his direction? That semifinal against Argentina in particular was one of those late-summer Kane games where he looks too leggy to impact the game either in the penalty area or the midfield roles he drops into, usually with such success.

That's one game though. There are another 64 where he was frequently spectacular. A remarkable 73 goals for club and country is the sort of output that belonged back in Messi's prime years. The absolute biggest game may not have gone his way but Kane was unforgettable against the Ivory Coast, thrilling in both legs against PSG and incisive in putting Real Madrid to the sword.

Then there are the Bundesliga numbers. Gaudy output is the baseline for a Bayern striker against domestic opposition but still the only players to have bettered Kane's 36 goals in 31 league games are Gerd Muller and Robert Lewandowski. The former won the Ballon d'Or, the latter probably would have if it had been awarded in 2020. There is no reason why Kane should not get it this time.

PSG were ultimately the best side in Europe last season and yet judging which of their players deserves the Ballon d'Or is a challenge. Ligue 1 might not demand much of them but it does feel unreasonable to reward a player who spent half his weekends watching on from the sidelines because his head coach can afford to save him for the trickier tests that come with retaining the Champions League. At some point there has to be a minutes restriction. If you're not seeing the pitch for half of your team's league minutes, then it is really hard to make a case for you to be one of the 10 best performers in the world last season. Either you were injured, unfortunate but still a disqualifying factor, or your team are not frequently playing opponents of a sufficient standard.

All of which is to say that Dembele, Joao Neves, Nuno Mendes and even you Khvicha Kvaratskhelia, you've got to go. Yes, you looked like some of the best players in the world in the spring. It's just that you had most of the autumn off.

As for Vitinha, there's a reason why he played nearly 4000 club minutes and only one other starter in the Champions League final cleared 3000. The Portuguese midfielder was the engine without which his side could not motor forward. Across Europe's top five leagues, he ranked third for progressive carries per 90 minutes and second for progressive passes. Unlike most tempo setters in midfield, he also weighed in with crucial goals and assists, firmly establishing himself as the best midfielder on the planet.

The sport's assist king last season. If we consider domestic cups and leagues, European matches and the World Cup, then Michael Olise ended the year with 10 more goals laid on for his teammates than anyone else. The summer definitively proved that he could be the lead attacker in a frontline made up of some of the best forwards in the world, but then again, his form with Bayern Munich had shown as much.

In general, when we're reflecting back on the season, we shouldn't lean too heavily on expected goals and assists. What we're really looking at is actual returns and if that meant a player was out over the skis, well, more power to them. Having said that, I mean, talk about separating yourself from the field.

In pure output terms, Yamal, still just 19 years of age, was perhaps a little off the peak of Europe's attackers, 37 goals and assists when Kane, Olise and Mbappe were all in the 40s or higher. Still, it was enough that a starring role in the World Cup might just have swung Yamal into top spot. Unfortunately, a biceps femoris injury put paid to the prospect of him showing more than flashes of his best self in the summer.

Unfortunately for Yamal, that was the story of his 25-26, where 96 days were lost to injuries that included a nagging groin issue in the autumn. That is among the most common problems faced by young footballers who are still growing into the bodies of seasoned athletes. On the evidence of when he was on the pitch, Yamal will be a Ballon d'Or winner when he has reached full physical maturity.

Here's maybe the trickiest candidacy to get a read on. In terms of goal contributions, only Kane beats him, and when the lights shone brightest at the World Cup, Mbappe was phenomenal. By the time he retires, likely with at least two more tournaments under his belt, his high watermark for World Cup scoring might look a bit like Michael Phelps' Olympic gold record or Wilt Chamberlain's scoring titles.

For an individual award, individual output really matters. If the Ballon d'Or were about team performance, then you would have the ludicrous scenario where Real Madrid campaigned for Dani Carvajal to win the prize in 2024 if Rodri was going to get it anyway. After all, he was there for the Euro 2024 win and the Champions League too. That'd be mad. Aaah.

However, team success is one of the criteria and it's one that needs to be at least partially weighed when you play for Real Madrid and France. You can't make the Russell Westbrook 2017 case for Mbappe. His goals and assists need to lead to something. In the summer they very nearly did.

A reminder once again that this is not a prediction. Gabriel Magalhaes probably is not going to make the top 10. The best odds you can find of him winning the Ballon d'Or are +6600, an implied probability of 1.5%. That's defenders and this prize, folks. Only three of them have won it in history. Franz Beckenbauer is the only one to have managed it without winning the major international tournament of that year.

There is a reason for that. The most valuable and difficult skill in this sport is scoring goals. In the era of three points for a win, attack tends to deliver the biggest prizes. That's what made Arsenal's Premier League win so remarkable. It and the near miss in the Champions League final were built on one of the most exceptional defenses in the history of this sport, anchored by the brilliant Gabriel, whose blend of skill and tenacity made him the best Arsenal player last season.

With shot-disrupting qualities that are Victor Wembanyama-esque -- 13.2% of shots Arsenal faced when Gabriel was on the field were blocked by their No. 6 -- the man the Emirates Stadium calls the king of Brazil made it far harder for the other team to do that most valuable and difficult thing on the pitch. It takes something special for a defense to carry an injury-riddled team to a league title. That Gabriel anchored that something special merits a very high place in the final voting.

Now, here's a weird one. As what might broadly be viewed as the third attacker on Bayern Munich, it's really hard to make a case for Luis Diaz winning the Ballon d'Or. Even he has been arguing that his teammate Kane should get it. "For me, he's number one to win it," Diaz said earlier this month. "Hopefully he gets it. We're trying to make his case to win it."

What we are really arguing here is that Diaz was so excellent in his particular role that it makes him one of the 10 best footballers in the world last season. With 39 goals and assists combined, it is not that hard a case to make. Diaz was also an exceptional passer, an outstanding creator for others and vital at moving Bayern into dangerous areas. There are players below him in this list who have more of a case to have been the best player in the world but really no one ranked sixth, seventh or eighth is actually going to win the Ballon d'Or. Consider this a reflection on how impactful Diaz was.

The inverse of a player such as Diaz might be Bruno Fernandes, who took a far inferior team on his back and propelled them to levels that they would not have gotten close to otherwise. When Fernandes started moving through the gears in the back half of the season, Manchester United flew from midtable to the Champions League.

Along with Gabriel, Fernandes is the player who tells the story of the great tactical trend of 2025-26 as well as anyone. Nine of his record-breaking 21 Premier League assists came from set pieces and for a time there might have been no attacking scenario more difficult to defend than Fernandes standing over a corner, lobbing it into a mass of bodies from which Casemiro would often rise the highest.

It wasn't just set pieces for Fernandes, whose 99 open-play chances created were 22 more than any other player in Europe's top five leagues last season. For a sense of just how impactful he was, one need only observe how United are struggling now that he has come back down to earth.

For these last two, the question really is how much importance you place on the World Cup. Obviously, it is the peak of the sport but what happens when you've spent the rest of your time playing at a level that ClubELO and Opta would consider to be a fair way below England's second tier, at or around the level of the Norwegian, Ecuadorian and Swiss domestic leagues? If you're as historically excellent as Messi, you're probably going to look sprightlier and more incisive than those who have spent the preceding nine months slogging their way through the Champions League and European domestic seasons.

If that sounds like a means of diminishing Messi's brilliance at the World Cup, it shouldn't be. Being the best player on the runners-up at 39 is an exceptional achievement, one that only serves to reinforce his status as the greatest of all time. It also should have resulted in him being named player of the tournament. The Ballon d'Or, however, is awarded for the period from Aug. 3, 2025 to July 19, 2026. For too much of that, Messi was playing at a level that was simply beneath his talents.

Somewhat as above, really. At the World Cup, Rodri was Rodri, the player who was so eminently worthy of winning the 2024 Ballon d'Or. When Spain had the ball, Rodri, now at Barcelona, was the man who moved them through the lines, who carried the ball almost as effectively as he passed it. When Spain didn't have the ball, Rodri got it back for them.

Flashes of that Rodri had emerged as he stepped up his recovery from an ACL injury in his final months as a Manchester City player. He was brilliant for a half against Chelsea in January, the best player on the pitch when City beat Arsenal in the EFL Cup final. Even Pep Guardiola, however, knew that the "real Rodri" would not emerge until later on in the season. That puts a hard cap on where he can rank.

#1294. Where have all the saucers flown?

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Jeff Hecht is based in the Boston area where he writes factual articles about science and technology to make a living and science-fiction stories to stimulate the imagination, many of them for Nature Futures.

Holding her lunch box, Lili scanned the noon break area at the Exotic Destinations travel show. The middle-aged travel agents chattering among themselves ignored her, but a tall Black woman with snow-white hair waved.

Recognizing her from the session on tourism on the Extraterrestrial Highway, Lili walked over to ask, “May I join you?”

“Certainly,” the woman said. “My name’s Bettye, with an e at the end. I noticed you at the Extraterrestrial Highway session.”

“I’m Lili, with two l’s, two i’s and no y at all, and I saw you there. What did you think of their space alien experience?” She sat down to unpack her lunch.

“It’s changed tremendously since I was young,” Bettye said. “My parents just hoped to see a flying saucer on a long trip across the southwestern desert. Now they have cheesy roadside attractions with animated space aliens waving outside the door.”

Intrigued, Lili asked “What was it like back then?”

Read more science fiction from Nature Futures

Read more science fiction from Nature Futures

“Flying saucers were a mystery in the sixties; everybody wanted to see one. Papa was an Air Force mechanic, and pilots told him they had seen saucers. The Byrds sung about hitching a ride on a saucer. Papa always looked for saucers.”

“Do your stories help sell tours?” Lili asked.

“I wish I had travel stories, but my parents were too poor to take vacations after they immigrated from Hong Kong.”

Bettye grinned. “Oh, we loved telling those stories about looking for flying saucers, but we had to be careful we didn’t scare anyone.”

Bettye sipped her iced tea and sat back. “I saw my first saucer when we were driving through the desert. Papa drove at night because our old station wagon didn’t have air conditioning. The Moon was bright so we could see the foothills and the cacti. I fell asleep, but woke when Papa stopped. He and Mama whispered and pointed at a moonlit saucer parked a little ways away. A hatch opened and two aliens got out and walked towards us. Mama said we better go, but the car wouldn’t start. The aliens wore pale green suits and carried metal boxes that looked like old telephones. I waved, and they waved back.”

“A little,” Bettye said. “Then the boxes started talking English voices like we heard on the radio. Mama hushed me when I giggled.”

“They asked us to fly them over the mountains and tell them about the scenery. Papa laughed and said our car couldn’t fly. They said theirs could, and Mama got them to pay us to guide them. Mama was scared because she had never flown, but Papa and I had a great flight. After we landed, the aliens asked if we would guide other aliens on trips.”

“Oh yes. Papa took me along and we had a great time guiding the alien tours. They were very friendly and what they paid let me go to college.”

“That was a very successful business,” Lili said. “How long did it last?”

Bettye nodded. “Several years, until a saucer flew too close to an Air Force base. A pilot at the base jumped into a fighter and flew towards us. Papa told the aliens to fly away because the fighter might shoot us down, but their speaking boxes said ‘no civilized beings would do that’.”

“The fighter shot a missile at us. Then one alien pointed something at the missile and it vanished. The other alien pointed a box at the plane and made it move with what he called a force field. He made it land on the road. The pilot opened the door and ran away while we watched the alien melt the plane.”

#1293. Aston Villa 2.0 are making mockery of the early-season doom merchants

Two months ago there were many doom merchants insisting that Aston Villa were heading for a season of struggle, but they are looking foolish now.

After a summer of uncertainty and much change, Villa are stepping into a brave new era and find themselves joint-top of the Champions League table after three matches.

With co-owner Nassef Sawiris in attendance, Villa fans are dreaming of another magical season almost four years after Emery walked through the doors at this historic club.

Sawiris was the key figure driving Emery’s appointment in October 2022 and few could have predicted the success that has followed with the Basque manager at the helm.

Villa 2.0 have made a flawless start to their European campaign and are running into form in the Premier League after a sticky start.

In this comfortable victory over Viking, Villa became the second fastest team to win 20 matches at this level from 30 matches, only behind Real Madrid (who won 20 of their first 29). They have also won 12 home games in Europe in a row.

Much tougher assignments are to come, with powerhouses Barcelona, Paris St-Germain and Borussia Dortmund still to come in the league phase.

Yet Villa are currently level on points with Paris St-Germain, Liverpool and Real Madrid, and Emery remains determined to make an impact in this competition.

He said: “We are delighted with how we are responding and improving things. The Champions League is very difficult, but we have nine points and you can feel confidence. We are comfortable for the next challenge.”

What a difference a few months make. Over the course of the summer, many observers wondered if the Emery fairy tale was in danger of ending.

With six of the starting XI from last season’s Europa League final victory moving on, it could have been a difficult period of transition. We have all learnt, however, that Emery can never be written off or doubted.

Just a week after their biggest European win, the 6-0 destruction of Fenerbahce, expectations were understandably high. Before kick-off a huge tifo was unfurled in the Holte End with the words: “We’ve conquered before. We’re prepared for more.”

#1292. Footy Fix: Who will win Ballon d'Or as Harry Kane, Kylian Mbappe, Lamine Yamal, Lionel Messi vie for prize

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The attention of the soccer world will be fixed on London to start the week, where a months-old question will finally be answered: Who's going to win the Ballon d'Or? I'm Pardeep Cattry with a lookahead to Monday's ceremony, plus a preview of what's to come as action resumes in the EFL Cup.

Monday, Oct. 26🇫🇷 Ligue 1: Paris Saint-Germain vs. Lyon, 3:30 p.m. ➡️ beIN Sports🏆 Ballon d'Or ceremony, 4 p.m. ➡️ DAZN

Tuesday, Oct. 27🇮🇹 Serie A: Roma vs. Cagliari, 3:45 p.m. ➡️ Paramount+🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿 EFL Cup: Fleetwood Town vs. Arsenal, 4 p.m. ➡️ Paramount+

Lionel Messi and Cristiano Ronaldo may no longer be the frontrunners for the Ballon d'Or, but their decades-long command over soccer's most prestigious individual accolade still colors the way we all look at the award. The air of mystery that should be a fixture in the run-up to an awards show still feels foreign, the ability to gauge the eventual winner a fresh challenge for many. That's especially true this year, particularly on the men's side, where none of the usual indicators apply.

A handful of deserving players make up the list of nominees once again, but none fit the prototype of an eventual Ballon d'Or winner, rightly or wrongly. The award often goes to the best player on a team that won the biggest prize on offer in the last year, a path that would lead you straight to Spain's golden ball winner, Rodri. The midfielder hardly feels like a slam-dunk pick after spending much of last season building his form following an ACL injury, which might lead you to a member of Paris Saint-Germain's UEFA Champions League-winning team. Vitinha, the Portuguese midfielder, might actually have a shot but there are buzzier names in the mix that are equally worthy. The favorite might actually be someone else entirely – Harry Kane, the England captain and Bayern Munich talisman who has steadily established himself as his generation's greatest goalscorer over the years. Here's James Benge on Kane's case in the final batch of Ballon d'Or power rankings.

There is no obvious candidate on the women's side, either, though Alexia Putellas might just be the favorite if the usual patterns apply. The voting body will be inclined to select someone from Barcelona's UEFA Women's Champions League-winning side and with three-time Ballon d'Or winner Aitana Bonmati out of the running after dealing with a broken leg last season, Putellas playing a central role with eight goals and six assists in Europe before leaving for London City Lionesses in the summer. She is one of eight members of that squad among the list of nominees, the list of 30 an eclectic selection of some of the world's best players. The NWSL's nominees include Temwa Chawinga, the league's back-to-back MVP with the Kansas City Current and the headliner for a Malawi side that made a run to the Women's Africa Cup of Nations, and U.S. women's national team standout Rose Lavelle, who scored the game-winner for Gotham FC in last year's NWSL Championship.

#1291. Oliver Glasner's great Nottingham Forest gamble: Squad running through fields as punishment, why he thinks players are not serious enough and how alienating stars could see him pay ultimate price

Published: 12:00 EDT, 2 November 2026 | Updated: 12:55 EDT, 2 November 2026

If football management were gambling, Oliver Glasner has just done the equivalent of walking into one of Nottingham’s top casinos and chucking everything on red.

Not satisfied with hammering his Forest players publicly after Saturday’s 2-0 defeat at Brentford, Glasner then had the squad running on the banks of the River Trent for their customary Sunday recovery session. The social media footage has to be seen to be believed – Premier League footballers jogging through an overgrown field, filmed by a baffled dog-walker.

Even if Forest were doing well and their players were easy to manage, these would still be risky moves. Instead, Glasner's side are 19th in the table and he is trying to handle a notoriously restless dressing room.

Forest are believed to pay Glasner more than £10million a year and until now owner Evangelos Marinakis has been patient. But in the Premier League most fans are sceptical when club officials talk about long-term projects and three-year plans. Only three of the current 20 managers have lasted three years in their current job.

Any manager who loses regularly is under pressure, particularly at a club who sacked three managers last season and another in the summer. Glasner has lost six of 10 as Forest boss and won only once. Forget the spin: results alone mean Glasner is under the pump.

If there are no signs of a reaction against Manchester City on Saturday, it promises to be an uncomfortable November international break.

If there are no signs of a Nottingham Forest reaction against Man City on Saturday, it promises to be an uncomfortable November international break for Oliver Glasner

There was not one single moment that broke Glasner’s patience but the 30th minute at Brentford on Saturday probably contributed heavily.

Forest centre back Murillo, who has regressed alarmingly this season, watched idly as Bees goalkeeper Caoimhin Kelleher launched the ball way over his head and into the path of Dango Ouattara. Ouattara then breezed past Murillo before Nikola Milenkovic turned the cross into his own net. Glasner was unhappy with the shape Murillo was in when he returned for pre-season training and was furious at such slack work.

It was not the first time Forest had been exposed like this, either. Jay Dasilva’s winner for Coventry at the City Ground in September came from a similar diagonal pass from keeper Carl Rushworth, though that time Daniel Munoz – one of Glasner’s pupils – was at fault. Again, slack. Again, sloppy.

Daily Mail Sport understands Glasner does not see enough seriousness in his squad. This group of players get on well but nonetheless, there is a view that poor results do not hurt them enough. Is it really time for laughing and joking around the training ground when you have taken one point from a possible 15?

Most of this squad have never won a European trophy, or one in Europe’s top five leagues. Glasner has three. Some around him believe there are Forest players who carry themselves like superstars when they do not deserve to.

It is thought Glasner is also frustrated with himself. Looking back, perhaps he wishes he had started with a bang, because the 52-year-old was alarmed at the physical data from previous seasons.

In 2024-25, Forest covered fewer kilometres than any other team, and last season only Liverpool and Chelsea covered fewer. In 2024-25, only Arsenal made fewer sprints; last season, only Everton were below Forest. Glasner’s Palace sides were never lower than 12th in those four categories.

When Glasner has been outspoken in the past, it has usually worked. At Wolfsburg and Frankfurt, performances improved. At Crystal Palace last season, Glasner let rip at his bosses after a game at Sunderland last January and most expected him to be sacked. Instead, he left in the summer after delivering the Conference League. The dynamic at Forest is very different though – and Glasner may soon understand why.

Glasner was unhappy with the shape Murillo (left) was in when he returned for pre-season training and was furious at the Brazilian's slack work at Brentford

Player power was a major factor in Ange Postecoglou and Sean Dyche's sackings last season. When players believe they can go above the manager’s head and vent to those in charge, they will. This is the danger for Glasner.

Daily Mail Sport understands there are players who love neither the new style – Glasner is a committed three-at-the-back man and many of the squad feel more comfortable in a back-four – nor the Austrian’s strict approach. He is very different from the avuncular Vitor Pereira, whose easy charm and light-touch approach united the squad post-Dyche and kept Forest in the top flight.

Others are surprised Glasner has not made it a priority to bring the dressing room’s strongest characters onside. Along with Morgan Gibbs-White, both Ola Aina and Callum Hudson-Odoi are powerful voices in the squad and alienating any of them is dangerous. Equally, Ibrahim Sangare and Nico Dominguez are well-respected, and both have been left on the fringes like Aina and Hudson-Odoi.

While Gibbs-White is clearly Forest’s best player, he can be a complex character. If the skipper is not 'having’ a Forest manager, his position becomes vulnerable.

It was a turbulent summer for Gibbs-White, who was frustrated no Champions League club came in for him and ultimately changed agents. He was also left out of England’s World Cup squad. Some believe that Glasner’s rigid tactical framework does not bring the best from Gibbs-White, who likes to roam across the front line and drop deep when he wishes. While Pereira understood this, Glasner does not operate like that.

At times this season, Gibbs-White’s body language has been striking. Team-mates who make mistakes feel his anger but the 26-year-old has only one goal (a penalty) and two assists this term.

Gibbs-White watched team-mate Elliot Anderson leave Forest for City last summer and perhaps questioned why he was not on the same path to the Champions League.

It is tempting to wonder about some of the advice Gibbs-White has received from those around him, though. Because if Gibbs-White is wondering why he is still playing for a bottom-half Premier League club, it is never a bad idea to look in the mirror.

Callum Hudson-Odoi is a powerful voice in the dressing room and Glasner would do well not to isolate him

If  Morgan Gibbs-White is wondering why he is still playing for a bottom-half Premier League club, it is never a bad idea to look in the mirror

Marinakis did not make Glasner the highest-paid manager in Forest’s history just to show him the door at the first sign of trouble. When the pair held talks, Glasner is thought to have stressed the need for time to make his vision work.

Neither man suffers fools and it is easy to imagine that Marinakis would have approved of parts of Glasner’s outburst. That does not give Glasner a free pass, because Marinakis factored in player feeling when dismissing Postecoglou and Dyche.

If the Glasner experiment fails, George Syrianos will come under scrutiny. Forest’s chief football officer has more power at the club than at any other time and he pushed hard for Glasner, whom he has known for some time through links to German football.

It is believed the pair had some contact over possible transfer business during Glasner’s time at Palace, and Glasner would likely have welcomed the chance to work with Syrianos at Selhurst Park.

In December 2023, Syrianos wanted Glasner to replace Steve Cooper but Marinakis chose Nuno Espirito Santo instead. Marinakis’ son, Miltiadis, is at the training ground regularly and will report back to his father. These are testing times for Glasner and his champion.

Dyche has had his say, too. During a poor run of results last season, he gathered the Forest players and staff for their views on what needed to change.

Anticipating their opinions on formations and tactics, Dyche was bewildered when one player queried the decision to move the weekly barber visit from Friday to Thursday. Nevertheless, that player is still at Forest and Dyche lasted less than four months.

Dyche  made many mistakes at Forest but his latest posts on Threads felt relevant.

If the Glasner experiment fails, George Syrianos will come under scrutiny. Forest’s chief football officer has more power at the club than ever before and he pushed hard for Glasner

The problem at Forest is that even if the players fail to stand up and be counted, they are rarely the ones to pay the ultimate price

They read: ‘The badge is bigger than all… and yet it seems not nowadays! I can only hope it turns and the culture we were insisting upon is now being assessed and realised as what was and is needed. Oliver is out there saying what I was saying… in his own style.

‘Nottingham Forest are still finding the goals hard to come by – and I had it along with my staff – we scored but nowhere near what the metrics were telling us, so not enough to stay in our job?

'We had 35 efforts at goal v Wolves and yet a 0-0 result and it culminated in myself and staff being sacked. I hope Oliver is given more time, the fans stay with him and the players stand up and be counted.'

The problem at Forest is that even if the players fail to do so, they are rarely the ones to pay the ultimate price.

#1290. Serie A | Atalanta 0-3 Parma: Gilardino gets first win as Daffara frustrates Sarri’s side

Giovanni Fabbian, a Davide Zappacosta own goal and Simone Lontani’s long-range strike gave Parma a shock 3-0 win at Atalanta, Alberto Gilardino’s first since taking charge.

Atalanta went into the game 11th in Serie A on 11 points. They hadn’t won at home since beating Venezia on 12 October, and had drawn 2-2 at Fiorentina on Thursday. Maurizio Sarri’s side are in the middle of an injury crisis, with only 19 players called up. Gianluca Gaetano and Thomas Kristensen joined Raoul Bellanova, Gianluca Scamacca, Giacomo Raspadori, Sead Kolašinac, Franck Kessié, Isak Hien, Odilon Kossounou and Pompei on the sidelines, while Giorgio Scalvini returned in defence.

Parma were in the bottom three on five points after a 0-0 draw with Udinese, still waiting for Gilardino’s first win. They were without Adrián Bernabé, who picked up a muscle problem in training on Sunday, so Fabbian started in midfield and Lontani up front alongside El Bilal Touré.

Atalanta dominated the opening half hour, with 73% possession. Charles De Ketelaere was the main threat: he dragged an early effort wide, forced Giovanni Daffara into a save at his near post, then fired just past the far post after weaving through the defence. Ederson whistled a long-range drive inches wide, and Nikola Krstović scuffed a shot past the post.

Parma’s first real chance came from a set piece, when Enrico Delprato headed wide from Vincent Sierro’s corner. They didn’t waste the next one. Sierro swung in another corner on 41 minutes, and Fabbian headed home from close range.

Daffara made a sharp save to deny Nicola Zalewski just before half-time.

Things got worse for Atalanta two minutes after the restart. Zappacosta stretched to cut out a cross and diverted it inside his own left post.

Jonathan Rowe wasted two good chances to pull one back. On 58 minutes, Fabbian teed up Lontani, who curled a superb shot from outside the area into the bottom-right corner.

Sarri brought on Eljif Elmas, Kamaldeen Sulemana, Lazar Samardžić and Javison Idele, but Daffara was in inspired form. He produced a fine save to keep out Krstović’s low drive, and Mario Pašalić headed against the crossbar from close range.

Krstović had a header saved by Daffara and then drilled another chance wide as Parma held on for a clean sheet.

Fabbian 41, Zappacosta og 47, Lontani 58 (P)

Sarri doesn’t know how to defend. No idea why Atalanta hired him. They are totally incompatible. Wolf pack to Tiki Taka?

#1289. Premier League Power Rankings: Manchester United falling fast; Tottenham Hotspur, Bournemouth rise

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Eight games into a campaign, patterns are supposed to emerge as teams begin to lock into midseason form. This season of the Premier League is no exception, except the pattern is a new one – expect chaos until further notice.

Several teams are experiencing a regression to the mean after rocky starts to the season, evidenced by the weekend's most notable games. Aston Villa are surging up the table after a 2-1 win over Manchester City, Bournemouth defeated Manchester United in style with a 3-0 triumph at Old Trafford and Tottenham Hotspur have gone from zero wins to two in a week, a 2-0 win at Chelsea their most impressive performance in months. Others are also putting their early season results behind them, but it feels like they are crashing back down to earth – Brentford were held to a 1-1 draw at Hull City, while Ipswich Town were unimpressive in a 1-1 draw against Nottingham Forest.

A fascinating theme is beginning to emerge along the way. It feels like there are more midtable teams than usual, even if some sit as high as seventh (someone has to, after all). Then there are those that seem like relegation contenders but are several spots above the drop zone because, somehow, there are that many teams worse than them. There's a frenetic feeling to the Premier League table and, by extension, the latest edition of power rankings but the show must go on.

Here's how each Premier League team is looking after the latest round of games.

Arsenal's 2-0 win over Everton was not glamorous but the Gunners won't care. They're level on points with Manchester City and well-positioned to compete for the title, much as they have been all season.

Manchester City's short-lived grip on first place is gone after their defeat to Aston Villa, one that raises questions about their ability to go the distance in Enzo Maresca's first season in charge.

Liverpool are slowly but steadily figuring things out with Andoni Iraola at the helm, a 2-0 win over Brighton and Hove Albion their most impressive result yet. A top-four spot feels like a realistic aim for this season, even if they are not the finished product just yet.

Fabian Hurzeler's side played a fairly even game with Liverpool, so their stock should not drop too much but the Reds did map out a plan to neutralize their attack-minded tendencies, which might be something opponents borrow from in the coming weeks and months.

This is where the extreme midtable energy of the Premier League comes in – Chelsea were deeply unimpressive against Spurs, unconvincing at almost every turn. Most teams in England's top flight, though, are worse off so the Blues hang onto fifth for now but they will be worth keeping an eye on.

Between a 3-0 win over AC Milan in the UEFA Europa League and their triumph at Old Trafford, it has been a fun week to be a Bournemouth fan. Those wins are a sign that things are finally clicking – they might be 13th in the league but they rank third on expected goal differential, a signal that things were always trending in the right direction.

Aston Villa's slow start is officially a thing of the past, Unai Emery's side smartly outmaneuvering City to prove just that. They are officially a team on the rise.

Leeds United's unstylish but effective consistency means they continue to hang out in the top half of the table but playing even against an unimpressive Sunderland side is not the kind of thing a team earns plaudits for.

There's no reason Brentford should not target a top-half finish but much like Leeds above them, an even game against relegation contenders Hull City is not indicative of the team's overall qualities.

Manchester United really have their hearts set on scaling down the table as fast as they can, don't they? The Red Devils should be better than this but their mistake-prone nature continues to be costly.

A win over Coventry City is one thing but a victory at Chelsea is another. More specifically, it's the kind of thing that ensured Spurs would dig themselves out of their early season hole and perhaps sets them up for some more normal results in the short-term.

There is no shame in losing to the reigning champions but Everton did not make much of a dent in the match, the Toffees seemingly resigned to being permanent residents of the middle of the Premier League's table for the foreseeable future.

For all their faults, Fulham have done well enough to pick up the points expected of them, the latest coming in a win over Coventry City. Barely cracking 0.5 expected goals along the way, though, is not something to write home about.

Conventional wisdom suggests that the other shoe will drop for Hull City but it hasn't yet, especially after picking up a well-earned point against Brentford.

Add Nottingham Forest to the list of anomalies this season, sitting firmly in the relegation zone despite ranking fifth in the league on expected goal differential. Case in point – they tallied 2.29 expected goals to Ipswich's 0.46 but tied 1-1 anyway. Until they solve that problem, they are doomed to less-than-ideal spots on the table.

Ipswich were lucky to pick up a point against Forest but the early season success is a thing of the past for them, too.

Eighth-place Newcastle United seem to be riding their luck – they rank 19th in the league on expected goal differential – but creating a five-point cushion above the drop zone by way of a win over Crystal Palace counts for something.

Sunderland will value the point they picked up against Leeds but they are in the midst of an unexciting season, which is hardly a position of strength for a team in desperate need of points.

Palace will take some solace from the fact that they outplayed Newcastle but in their case, the results actually reflect their form.

Coventry were neck-and-neck with Fulham on expected goals in defeat but considering the Cottagers put up a paltry number, there's not much the newly promoted side can brag about.

#1288. Who's to blame for Manchester United's decline? Ranking the biggest culprits

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

It's happened again. Another season, another Manchester United crisis. No longer does the end of daylight savings time herald the harsh winter ahead. Instead, it is the boos that ring around Old Trafford as the United faithful turn their ire on the same owners, the same executives and the same players, well aware it will be a different coach that pays the price.

Sunday's 3-0 defeat to AFC Bournemouth was remarkable only for the sheer unremarkability of it. In the 74 years after their first meeting in the 1949 FA Cup third round, Bournemouth won three games against Manchester United. In the last two years they have won three games: all at Old Trafford, all 3-0. Freddie Kruger is treading the boards at the Theatre of Dreams.

Although maybe that analogy is not quite apt. After all, the one positive that you could say about a Krugerian nightmare is that it tends to be a one-and-done situation. No such luck if you happen to be a Manchester United supporter. Could any of them now believe that sacking Michael Carrick would fix anything about this club? They've tried the Eddie Howe-esque Premier League mainstay, the relentless winner a la Antonio Conte, the graduate of the Ralf Rangnick pressing academy in the mold of Julian Nagelsmann. Their shortlist only needs an ex-Ajax coach to sweep the quadrants of post-Sir Alex Ferguson ineptitude. Fred Grim to Manchester United? Well, doesn't that sound about right?

This is a club suffering under profound mismanagement, the sort that no one individual can marshal on their own. So there's plenty of blame to spread around. Let's start doing so, in reverse order of course. Gotta keep you on the page as long as we can. Build some suspense. Who might be top, you wonder? Well you probably know. But you know most every AAA movie is going to end with the hero triumphant. The joy is in the journey to the inevitable end point.

Now look, the soon to be former Manchester United manager is not without his faults, as Bruno Fernandes so robustly articulated after the 4-1 defeat in Como. There have been some very weird technical decisions here this season and a head coach with a scintilla of authority probably could have got this team to stop taking so many shots from outside the box. And yet did anyone at Manchester United genuinely think they'd unearthed the next great coach when they threw him the salvage our season post-Ruben Amorim job?

That Carrick did so much more than that, guiding United to Champions League qualification through a third-placed finish, spoke to his ability to keep things simple. He retained what had worked from his predecessor, tidied up some of the complexities of the formation and rode Bruno Fernandes' player of the season form as far as he could go. It is not his fault that United have not kicked on since. What had the 45 year old achieved in three seasons at Middlesbrough that suggested a coach who would do much more than what most coaches do, get a team to perform at or around its talent level?

Maybe when the stars align, when his team has a game a week and a fully fit squad he could achieve something better than the field but it is no more sensible to project out Carrick's future off the spring hot streak than it is to discount his coaching ability because he has struggled to cope with the first confluence of injuries, unfortunate results and player ill-discipline of his tenure.

Old Trafford seemed to have the right sense of it on Sunday. "It's Carrick you know," reverberated around the ground until the minute he was down the tunnel. Then it was both barrels for everyone else.

No one associated with Manchester United should apologize for having exacting standards. A well-run version of this club would make every decision based on improving their title-winning prospects either in the short or medium term. There should be no need to take the long way to the Premier League summit.

Having said all that, goodness it does not take much to send this club into a doom spiral of nostalgia and despair. When Lisandro Martinez served notice on Jason Wilcox and the hierarchy United had performed pretty well in defeat away to Atletico Madrid, a result that few in the Champions League field could credibly bemoan. Their form had wobbled but only a dodgy Erling Haaland goal had taken Manchester City past them and the last two Premier League results had been disappointing but not disastrous draws.

In short things were not going well but the difficulties were explicable. Up to the loss at the Metropolitano at least one of United's major problems was they had scored fewer goals than their expected goals (xG) for and conceded more than the xG value of their opponents shots. Their actual goal difference was minus-one, their expected goal difference was a shade under plus four. There's some heavy lifting being done in there by thrashing Ipswich Town and Sabah but the aggregate of a good team probably does contain a couple of thrashings as well as games where you play even against seemingly inferior teams like Fulham.

In short, just as United weren't as good as last season's rise to third place -- the defense started wobbling quite dramatically into the spring -- they aren't really as bad as 16th in the table, a point clear of the relegation zone might have you believe. A clear-eyed assessment both of the relative talent of United and the rest of the league would say that this is a good team vulnerable to a wobble. Just stay the course, keep calm in the dressing room and block out the noise.

But, of course... this is Manchester United we're talking about.

Sir Jim Ratcliffe certainly talked a good game when he finally got his hands on the sporting infrastructure at Old Trafford in February 2024, his $1.6 billion investment for around a quarter of the club affording him INEOS Group control of football operations at United. No longer would this be a club in hock to the first team head coach, the Ferguson way of thinking to be replaced by a brain trust that included the sporting director, "probably the recruitment guys" and, for reasons, the chief executive and Ratcliffe himself. "In modern football, you need to decide what's your path and stick to your path," the new minority owner insisted.

In the two and a half years since Manchester United's path has led them to: openly canvass the market for a replacement for manager Erik ten Hag, trigger an extension clause in his contract when they couldn't find anyone better, spend over $400 million outfitting the Dutchman with new players, sack him within four months, hire a coach in Ruben Amorim who had talked himself out of better jobs thanks to his insistence on playing a 3-4-3, finish 15th, sack Amorim just as their analytical profile was on an upswing because he had fallen out with his employers, bring in Carrick temporarily and then permanently, spend almost all their budget on midfielders, get dragged in public by Martinez.

That's just the condensed lowlights. It's fair to say that you don't hear much any more about Project 150, the ambitious vision to mark a century and a half of the club with a 21st top flight title. Perhaps by 2028 sporting director Wilcox will have got round to fixing the defense having blown so much of the 2025 summer budget on attack before then spending nearly $200 million on a midfield that needed upgrades but got Youri Tielemans, Andrey Santos and Carlos Baleba while the left back spot was left untouched.

It would say everything about the cataclysmic mismanagement at a senior level if Wilcox -- like so many at the club a man with little top level experience of the role he has been thrust into -- gets the man said to be his preferred choice to succeed Carrick, Eddie Howe.

The same Eddie Howe who spent a hugely successful two years with Dan Ashworth at Newcastle United. The same Dan Ashworth who Manchester United spent £4.1 million on the poaching of and, five months later, firing of. The same Manchester United who in INEOS' period running the show rank ninth in the Premier League for points, 10th for expected goal difference. Still, at least they sacked staff and cut costs. Who ever could have imagined that as a fix for a business' problems?

Speaking after Sunday's 3-0 loss to Bournemouth, Harry Maguire pulled no punches. "At the moment it's nowhere near good enough and something needs to change," he said. He's not wrong. And yet the only constants at this club sit second and first in our rankings. Cast your mind back to the 4-0 thrashing at the hands of Brentford in August 2022, Erik ten Hag's second game in charge and oh, what, half a dozen crises ago. The starting back four for Manchester United on that Saturday evening in west London? Diego Dalot, Harry Maguire, Lisandro Martinez, Luke Shaw. The starting back four in draws against Fulham and Everton more than four years later? Dalot, Maguire, Martinez, Shaw.

There are players at this club who have seen off half a dozen permanent managers. Some might not have lasted that long but in their time they have been frozen out or put up for sale. Few have paid the price for inconsistency. Why would you respect the authority of the head coach if you have spent three or four years in the Old Trafford dressing room and seen so many cycle through without any apparent accountability for the playing staff. It seems notable that Cristiano Ronaldo's bombing out by Ten Hag was followed by one of the most impressive runs of results in the last half decade. Players discovered their actions had consequences and started playing like that.

Now, they talk like they are bulletproof. Imagine Martin Odegaard used a post-match interview to mouth off about Mikel Arteta's tactics. Would he ever play for Arsenal again? That's a question Mesut Ozil and Pierre-Emerick Aubameyang can answer. When a player did not perform for Pep Guardiola's Manchester City, he was swiftly sold. Meanwhile United's squad is preserved in aspic. Their defense moves like it is.

These are not players who lack for talent. United's first choice attack rivals any bar Manchester City and Liverpool. Their midfield needs careful construction to mitigate for its lack of pace but it has quality. When the mood takes them Maguire, Martinez and Shaw are perfectly solid defenders. As the graphic above suggests, this is a team that can have moments of extreme competence. That is how United got to third a few months ago. Were they helped by the coach's tactics or the hierarchy's recruitment? Not really but that does not make these expensive, well-remunerated players innocent bystanders, unable to arrest the decline.

More than two decades after Malcolm Glazer loaded debt onto Manchester United to fund his purchase of the club, what has been accomplished beyond a steady degradation of this behemoth of English culture. Being owned by the Glazers, who have not put any money into the club since the takeover, is estimated to have cost the club at least $1.5 billion, much of it spent on servicing debt from the initial takeover. It should be noted that 15 major trophies have been won in the time the Glazers have owned the club but 10 of them came in the period where Ferguson's sheer magnetism held the club together.

There is an argument to be made that United's commercial income skyrocketed under current ownership and certainly this was a club that was among the first to realize that every region could have its own bespoke set of sponsors, that there was always another billboard or patch on the jersey to splash with a logo. Those brands were not, however, flocking to United because of anything the Glazers had done. United were the dominant force in English football at just the right moment to benefit from the Premier League moving from national to global obsession.

Far from custodians, the Glazers are the most deleterious of landlords. An extractive force, they provide minimal service and value while taking their management fees, dividends, repayments and then the riches Ratcliffe paid for a slice of the pie. All of their money could have gone into retaining United's preeminence in the English game or at least staving off the impact of their indifference. As if to make the metaphor particularly on the nose, on their watch Old Trafford has decayed such that the cost of renovation, an estimated $1.6 billion, might just make a case for the planned new stadium that no supporter seems to want.

A club that even in fallow years ranks among the top 10 revenue generators in football has found itself on a cost-cutting drive for which Ratcliffe is the face both because the Glazers' debt acts as a competitive drag and because ownership showed no interest nor aptitude in improving the on-field product. If the players represent a culture that is accountability-lite then it is ownership that enables it. When we start this piece by warning that nothing will change post-Carrick it is because we have seen enough to know that nothing changes until those who tolerate this degradation of Manchester United are no longer in a position of power.

#1287. Cristiano Ronaldo is left out of Al-Nassr match due to 'security concerns' as countryman Joao Felix stars in his absence

By PRESS ASSOCIATION and HARRY BAMFORTH, LIVE SPORTS COVERAGE REPORTER

Published: 11:37 EDT, 2 November 2026 | Updated: 14:01 EDT, 2 November 2026

Cristiano Ronaldo did not travel for Al-Nassr's AFC Champions League fixture against Pakhtakor on Monday amid ongoing security concerns.

The 41-year-old Portugal star was among a number of players left out by coach Ange Postecoglou for the trip to Tashkent, Uzbekistan.

In Ronaldo's absence, fellow Portugal international Joao Felix netted a brace in a momentous 6-2 win for Postecoglou's side.

The Australian coach also rested Kingsley Coman and Mohamed Simakan, telling a news conference he had made the decision 'given the pressure of matches and the amount of travel involved'.

It came a week after Al Nassr's match at home to Al Wasl was postponed, with the UAE club refusing to travel due to the situation in Saudi Arabia.

Airports in the country have come under a series of attacks undertaken by Houthi rebels.

Cristiano Ronaldo was rested from Al-Nassr's clash with Pakhtakor due to security concerns

Operating with backing from Tehran, the Houthis are seeking to disrupt Saudi Arabia's oil exports. One recent attack from the militants killed 13 people.

Last week Ronaldo scored a hat-trick against Al Kholood in the Saudi Pro League on Thursday, taking him to nine goals in 12 appearances this season.

Ronaldo's treble has taken him to 985 career goals as he edges nail-bitingly close to the ultimate milestone that he has been chasing for many years, since breaking the record for top goalscorer in football history in 2021.

Addressing the target with his former team-mate Rio Ferdinand in 2024, Ronaldo said: 'I want to reach 1,000 goals. If I don't have any injuries, this for me is the most important (thing), I want that.

'For me, the best mark that I can have in football is to reach, first, 900 goals. After, my challenge is to be at 1,000 goals.'

Despite surpassing Josef Bican five years ago as the all-time top goalscorer for club and country, that number is contested due to a lack of data from some historical records.

Last month, Ronaldo became football's first multi-billionaire after the veteran forward raked in £225million this year, according to Forbes.

Ronaldo reportedly passed the $2billion mark in career earnings earlier this year, just six years after he was the first footballer to surpass $1billion.

Ronaldo's status comes as he again topped Forbes' football rich list, aided by a lucrative salary at Saudi Arabian side Al-Nassr which is estimated at £488,000-per-day.

Forbes has determined that Ronaldo has also earned £42million off the pitch over the course of the year, which has come via endorsements and his business ventures.

#1285. Harry Kane proves there is only one Ballon d’Or winner

Let’s cut to the chase. If there is any justice, sanity or logic in football then Harry Kane will win the Ballon d’Or when the ceremony takes place in London on Monday.

Arsenal would have deservedly won this Champions League match away to Bayern Munich if Kane was not on the pitch. Instead, they almost lost it but for another bit of brilliance from Declan Rice, Kane’s vice-captain for England, and probably his successor to wear the armband.

A brilliantly worked team-goal finished off by Declan Rice, and Arsenal are level 💥 📺 Stream on TNT Sports & HBO Max: https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/Y25zI80A0z

“I’m lucky I can play with him and not so lucky I have to play against him,” Rice said, and that summed it up succinctly.

And that Ballon d’Or? There is bias, but Rice – who is also on the 30-strong list of nominees – added of Kane: “He is the clear winner. His numbers speak for themselves, the year he has had has been remarkable. When you play with him you realise how good he is and when you play against him you see how much of a pain it is.”

Arsenal stood toe-to-toe with Bayern in an open match. Both sides went for it, partly because they knew under the Champions League format, that defeat was not a disaster. There has been some chat about whether Arsenal can be, well, a bit dull. Not here. It would be no surprise to see these two face off again deep into this competition.

The only setback for Arsenal was a worrying injury to Bukayo Saka early on, limping off and tapping his thigh, indicating an issue with his muscle. Mikel Arteta’s reaction betrayed his understandable concern.

Kane won a penalty and then expertly took it to give Bayern the lead. Other strikers could have scored the penalty but few would have created the wonderful assist that drew Bayern level.

It has been a fact for quite some years that Kane is not only the best goalscorer for England but the best passer. Indeed, if Kane could provide for Kane he would have scored even more goals.

“Unsere nummer neun,” shouted the stadium announcer after Kane’s goal and that needed no translation. Kane is a god in Bavaria, where they know a few things about having great centre-forwards. But the 33-year-old is surpassing them all.

Kane’s goal meant he had scored in 10 straight Champions League games, one short of the record held by Cristiano Ronaldo. It was also the former Tottenham Hotspur forward’s 16th goal in 23 games against Arsenal. No one has ever scored more against them.

Kane is the complete player, carrying out his defensive duties – winning headers to clear Bayern’s lines from Arsenal free-kicks – to linking the play to being the focus of his team’s attacks. He is a centre-half, central midfielder and centre-forward. Who pops up on the wing to deliver pinpoint crosses.

Maybe Kane will be pipped at the Palladium – the theatre where the ceremony takes place – by Barcelona’s Lamine Yamal or Real Madrid’s Kylian Mbappé, or even an absurd sympathy vote for Lionel Messi. But Kane deserves it. His time is now.

Some passages of play in the first half deserve analysis. Just to highlight how good Kane was. After an Arsenal corner, wastefully volleyed over by Riccardo Calafiori, Bayern countered and suddenly it was three on two. Serge Gnabry, the former Arsenal winger, had to do better than shoot weakly when picked out on the overlap. David Raya saved. That was a let-off.

But who sprung that counter? It was not Manuel Neuer, the Bayern goalkeeper, taking the goal-kick, but Kane, with his sharp thinking. And then Kane launched a superb pass from deep which Ismael Saibari should have dealt with better. It should have been another opportunity. Potentially a goal.

Is there anything Harry Kane can't do? 🧐 His goal kick very nearly led to a Bayern Munich goal 😲 https://t.co/fqbsN7KOjw

And then Bayern did score. The ball was played inside to Kane, in centre field and afforded too much space. He delivered a perfectly weighted through ball for Alphonse Davies to run on to. The pace was perfect, allowing the Canadian not to break stride and stroke it past Raya. Kane did not fire the ball in, he did not make Davies work to reach it and he did not give Jurrien Timber any chance of cutting it out. It was perfect. Few players could do that. “Harry Kane puts the ball in a space from 30 metres that doesn’t exist,” Arteta said. True.

Initially it was ruled out for offside, but that was overturned after a VAR check to provide Eze with a bit of redemption after being hooked against Nottingham Forest at the weekend.

When Timber was punished for handball, as he blocked Kane’s shot, the penalty was given. Up stepped Kane and we knew the rest. At that point it felt like Bayern would win, but Arsenal continued to play courageously and pushed on, as they had done throughout, risking conceding further goals.

It was a game in chunks. They had moments, we had moments. In our moments, I think we exploited the spaces in behind a little bit better maybe but we played against a top team and the result is a result between two big teams.

Last year they reaped the benefits of a top-two finish: home ties all the way to the final and a guarantee of avoiding the other club in the top two.

They have a chance to pick off Real Madrid at the Emirates, and will anticipate Aston Villa (who still have to play Barcelona and PSG) and Real Betis dropping points.

Given PSG have already dispatched Manchester City and Barcelona, it is hard to envisage them dropping a point, though they do have the odd off night.

Arsenal’s chances of grabbing second could come down to winning their remaining games and Liverpool slipping up. But with five games to go, these permutations are probably premature.

Wow, what a game. That is one of the highest levels that we have played. The level of opposition, what the game required, and our level as well. Two teams who wanted to press each other and wanted to attack and wanted to play. It was a fascinating game.

I think we started the game incredibly well, we were so dominant, we did everything to deserve the first goal. We didn’t score the goal and lost Bukayo and had to adapt to it.

We gave a terrible chance away after our corner which could have cost us, then we scored the goal. In the second half, the game was even,  they started probably a little bit better before they scored and they you have to react and we certainly did.

The spirit of the team, the quality we have showed on the second goal as well.

They are a bit concerned. A player having to come off with a sharp pain is never good news but we have to wait and see.

I thought it was a good performance. Probably the draw was a fair result overall. We probably just didn’t get quite enough right tonight to get the win.

When you play against teams like Bayern who are man to man all over the pitch you have to apply certain principles, and I just kept running and managed to get away from my man. When they are following you all over, I just kept running and I was in on the goal.
